title: Constitutive active variants of TpoR
shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for its constitutive activation. This dataset contains scores for protein variants.

experiment.title: Constitutively active variants of TpoR
experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for its constitutive activation.
experiment.abstractText: The human thrombopoietin receptor (hTpoR/MPL) plays a crucial role in platelet production and is the target of several biologic and small-molecule agonists used to treat thrombocytopenia. Mutations that cause constitutive hTpoR signalling through JAK2 can drive myeloproliferative diseases such as essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Several of the above drugs, and most disease-associated hTpoR mutations, act at or near the transmembrane (TM) domain, and specific TM and/or juxtamembrane (JM) structural transitions have been implicated in their mechanisms of action. Whether these non-native stimuli have shared or distinct structural mechanisms, and how these relate to activation by Tpo, remain unclear, and there is no high-resolution structure of the intact receptor that visualizes this crucial region. We employed deep mutational scanning to interrogate sequence-function relationships in the hTpoR TM-JM regions in response to four classes of stimuli: the native ligand Tpo, three small-molecule agonists eltrombopag, avatrombopag and lusutrombopag, a peptide mimic of the biologic agonist romiplostim and two disease-associated mutations S505N and W515K.
experiment.methodText:
The variant libraries were constructed using overlap extension PCR with degenerate oligos targeting the transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions of TpoR. We selected the libraries on cytokine dependent cell lines, where cell growth depended on TpoR activation to measure function in the context of different stimuli.

Cells were harvested after selection and RNA extracted to generate cDNA, which was indexed and prepared for direct Illumina sequencing. Raw sequenced data were trimmed and deduplicated before being analyzed with the DiMSum pipeline. We ensured at least two biological replicates were performed per datasets.

Functional scores were derived by comparing non-treated cells against plasmids library.

experiment.title: copP combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for COP-associated protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of COP-associated protein protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1YG0.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: copP trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of COP-associated protein.

experiment.title: copP trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of COP-associated protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of COP-associated protein protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1YG0.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: CPEB2 Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein, ZZ domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the CPEB2 Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein, ZZ domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: CPEB2 Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein, ZZ domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the CPEB2 Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein, ZZ domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein, ZZ domain in CPEB2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q7Z5Q1_PF16366_513.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: cspA combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Cold shock protein CspA.

experiment.title: cspA combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Cold shock protein CspA.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Cold shock protein CspA protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1MJC.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: cspA (G17A) chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of Cold shock protein CspA (G17A).

experiment.title: cspA (G17A) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Cold shock protein CspA (G17A).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Cold shock protein CspA (G17A) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1MJC.pdb_G17A.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the cspB Cold-shock protein, DNA-binding domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Cold-shock protein, DNA-binding domain in cspB using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P41016_PF00313_1.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

title: C-terminal of L-Selectin
shortDescription: A deep mutational scanning experiment targeting the CLS helix region on the bacterial inner membrane.

experiment.title: C-terminal of L-Selectin (CLS)
experiment.shortDescription: A deep mutational scanning experiment targeting the CLS helix region on the bacterial inner membrane.
experiment.abstractText: This study mutated the residues on CLS helix region of the bacterial inner membrane. The experiment links the insertion and self-association property of the tested region to the survive of bacteria and studied the membrane-protein energetics landscape of missense mutations of the target.
experiment.methodText: The C-terminal of L-Selectin is used as the membrane-spanning segment for dsT$\beta$L in this experiment. The authors created forward and reverse primers of lengths 40-85 base pairs with the central codon replaced by NNS which encodes all possible amino acid substitutions on the target sequence. They leveraged a traditional assay, the TOXCAT-$\beta$-lactamase (T$\beta$L) screen, and adapted it to deep mutational scanning studies (dsT$\beta$L). The tested sequence is expressed in between a chimera of ToxR dimerization-dependent transcriptional activator of a chloramphenicol-resistance gene and $\beta$-lactamase. In this construct, the membrane integration of target sequence determines the bacterial resistance to ampicillin and the self-association correlates with the chloramphenicol resistance. Besides, the orientation to the membrane of this chimera is also crucial for survival. The selection result was determined by deep-sequencing using Illumina.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Mutational scanning reveals the determinants of protein insertion and association energetics in the plasma membrane.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Insertion of helix-forming segments into the membrane and their association determines the structure, function, and expression levels of all plasma membrane proteins. However, systematic and reliable quantification of membrane-protein energetics has been challenging. We developed a deep mutational scanning method to monitor the effects of hundreds of point mutations on helix insertion and self-association within the bacterial inner membrane. The assay quantifies insertion energetics for all natural amino acids at 27 positions across the membrane, revealing that the hydrophobicity of biological membranes is significantly higher than appreciated. We further quantitate the contributions to membrane-protein insertion from positively charged residues at the cytoplasm-membrane interface and reveal large and unanticipated differences among these residues. Finally, we derive comprehensive mutational landscapes in the membrane domains of Glycophorin A and the ErbB2 oncogene, and find that insertion and self-association are strongly coupled in receptor homodimers.

title: C. thermocellum cohesin binding affinity
shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of C. thermocellum cohesin binding affinity for dockerin.

experiment.title: C. thermocellum cohesin binding affinity
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of C. thermocellum cohesin binding affinity for dockerin.
experiment.abstractText: This study determined the effect of amino acid substitutions on cohesin-dockerin binding using deep mutational scanning. Cohesins from *Clostridium thermocellum* and *Clostridium cellulolyticum* were analyzed using yeast display.
experiment.methodText:
Single site mutagenesis was performed using NNN PCR (Pfunkel) to create a site saturation mutagenesis library. *C. thermocellum* cohesin was segmented into four tiles and sequenced using 150-bp paired-end reads.

Cohesin mutants were displayed on the surface of yeast and incubated with biotinylated dockerin. A C-terminal c-myc tag on the cohesin domain was used to measure protein expression and streptavidin-conjugated fluorophores were used to measure binding. Cells in the top 5% by fluorescence were used as the “selected” population for score calculation.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Determination of binding affinity upon mutation for type I dockerin-cohesin complexes from Clostridium thermocellum and Clostridium cellulolyticum using deep sequencing.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The comprehensive sequence determinants of binding affinity for type I cohesin toward dockerin from Clostridium thermocellum and Clostridium cellulolyticum was evaluated using deep mutational scanning coupled to yeast surface display. We measured the relative binding affinity to dockerin for 2970 and 2778 single point mutants of C. thermocellum and C. cellulolyticum, respectively, representing over 96% of all possible single point mutants. The interface ΔΔG for each variant was reconstructed from sequencing counts and compared with the three independent experimental methods. This reconstruction results in a narrow dynamic range of -0.8-0.5 kcal/mol. The computational software packages FoldX and Rosetta were used to predict mutations that disrupt binding by more than 0.4 kcal/mol. The area under the curve of receiver operator curves was 0.82 for FoldX and 0.77 for Rosetta, showing reasonable agreements between predictions and experimental results. Destabilizing mutations to core and rim positions were predicted with higher accuracy than support positions. This benchmark dataset may be useful for developing new computational prediction tools for the prediction of the mutational effect on binding affinities for protein-protein interactions. Experimental considerations to improve precision and range of the reconstruction method are discussed. Proteins 2016; 84:1914-1928. © 2016 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: High-resolution sequence-function mapping of full-length proteins.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Comprehensive sequence-function mapping involves detailing the fitness contribution of every possible single mutation to a gene by comparing the abundance of each library variant before and after selection for the phenotype of interest. Deep sequencing of library DNA allows frequency reconstruction for tens of thousands of variants in a single experiment, yet short read lengths of current sequencers makes it challenging to probe genes encoding full-length proteins. Here we extend the scope of sequence-function maps to entire protein sequences with a modular, universal sequence tiling method. We demonstrate the approach with both growth-based selections and FACS screening, offer parameters and best practices that simplify design of experiments, and present analytical solutions to normalize data across independent selections. Using this protocol, sequence-function maps covering full sequences can be obtained in four to six weeks. Best practices introduced in this manuscript are fully compatible with, and complementary to, other recently published sequence-function mapping protocols.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Determination of binding affinity upon mutation for type I dockerin-cohesin complexes from Clostridium thermocellum and Clostridium cellulolyticum using deep sequencing.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The comprehensive sequence determinants of binding affinity for type I cohesin toward dockerin from Clostridium thermocellum and Clostridium cellulolyticum was evaluated using deep mutational scanning coupled to yeast surface display. We measured the relative binding affinity to dockerin for 2970 and 2778 single point mutants of C. thermocellum and C. cellulolyticum, respectively, representing over 96% of all possible single point mutants. The interface ΔΔG for each variant was reconstructed from sequencing counts and compared with the three independent experimental methods. This reconstruction results in a narrow dynamic range of -0.8-0.5 kcal/mol. The computational software packages FoldX and Rosetta were used to predict mutations that disrupt binding by more than 0.4 kcal/mol. The area under the curve of receiver operator curves was 0.82 for FoldX and 0.77 for Rosetta, showing reasonable agreements between predictions and experimental results. Destabilizing mutations to core and rim positions were predicted with higher accuracy than support positions. This benchmark dataset may be useful for developing new computational prediction tools for the prediction of the mutational effect on binding affinities for protein-protein interactions. Experimental considerations to improve precision and range of the reconstruction method are discussed. Proteins 2016; 84:1914-1928. © 2016 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: High-resolution sequence-function mapping of full-length proteins.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Comprehensive sequence-function mapping involves detailing the fitness contribution of every possible single mutation to a gene by comparing the abundance of each library variant before and after selection for the phenotype of interest. Deep sequencing of library DNA allows frequency reconstruction for tens of thousands of variants in a single experiment, yet short read lengths of current sequencers makes it challenging to probe genes encoding full-length proteins. Here we extend the scope of sequence-function maps to entire protein sequences with a modular, universal sequence tiling method. We demonstrate the approach with both growth-based selections and FACS screening, offer parameters and best practices that simplify design of experiments, and present analytical solutions to normalize data across independent selections. Using this protocol, sequence-function maps covering full sequences can be obtained in four to six weeks. Best practices introduced in this manuscript are fully compatible with, and complementary to, other recently published sequence-function mapping protocols.

experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. experiment.title: CUE2 Ubiquitin system component CUE domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the CUE2 Ubiquitin system component CUE domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Ubiquitin system component CUE domain in CUE2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P36075_PF02845_9.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: CXCR4 Ab 12G5 binding
shortDescription: Deep mutational scan selecting for CXCR4 binding to Ab 12G5 in Expi293F cells.

experiment.title: CXCR4 Ab 12G5 binding
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan selecting for CXCR4 binding to Ab 12G5 in Expi293F cells.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment utilised site-saturation mutagenesis (SSM) to measure the functional consequences of mutations in the human chemokine receptor, CXCR4 and to map ligand interaction sites. Cells were selected for binding to Ab 12G5.
experiment.methodText:
The human CXCR4 sequence was generated by oligo assembly and fused to a c-myc tag. SSM libraries were generated by overlapping PCR using primers with an NNK codon, as described by Procko et al, 2013.
The SSM library was transfected into CXCR4-knockout human Expi293F cells using pCEP4. 
Surface receptor expression was measured by anti-myc-FITC staining and cells were sorted on a BD FACSAria II.
To test the validity of deep mutational scanning for mapping GPCR interactions sites, cells were selected for binding to fluorescent Ab 12G5, a previously mapped (by small-scale alanine mutagenesis) interacting ligand. 
Total RNA was extracted and PCR-amplified before sequencing by Illumina MiSeq v 3 or HiSeq 2500. 

Raw data available from GEO under accession [GSE100368](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE100368).

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Mapping Interaction Sites on Human Chemokine Receptors by Deep Mutational Scanning.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Chemokine receptors CXCR4 and CCR5 regulate WBC trafficking and are engaged by the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp120 during infection. We combine a selection of human CXCR4 and CCR5 libraries comprising nearly all of ∼7000 single amino acid substitutions with deep sequencing to define sequence-activity landscapes for surface expression and ligand interactions. After consideration of sequence constraints for surface expression, known interaction sites with HIV-1-blocking Abs were appropriately identified as conserved residues following library sorting for Ab binding, validating the use of deep mutational scanning to map functional interaction sites in G protein-coupled receptors. Chemokine CXCL12 was found to interact with residues extending asymmetrically into the CXCR4 ligand-binding cavity, similar to the binding surface of CXCR4 recognized by an antagonistic viral chemokine previously observed crystallographically. CXCR4 mutations distal from the chemokine binding site were identified that enhance chemokine recognition. This included disruptive mutations in the G protein-coupling site that diminished calcium mobilization, as well as conservative mutations to a membrane-exposed site (CXCR4 residues H79

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Computational design of a protein-based enzyme inhibitor.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: While there has been considerable progress in designing protein-protein interactions, the design of proteins that bind polar surfaces is an unmet challenge. We describe the computational design of a protein that binds the acidic active site of hen egg lysozyme and inhibits the enzyme. The design process starts with two polar amino acids that fit deep into the enzyme active site, identifies a protein scaffold that supports these residues and is complementary in shape to the lysozyme active-site region, and finally optimizes the surrounding contact surface for high-affinity binding. Following affinity maturation, a protein designed using this method bound lysozyme with low nanomolar affinity, and a combination of NMR studies, crystallography, and knockout mutagenesis confirmed the designed binding surface and orientation. Saturation mutagenesis with selection and deep sequencing demonstrated that specific designed interactions extending well beyond the centrally grafted polar residues are critical for high-affinity binding.

experiment.title: cylR2 (P41A) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of CylR2 (P41A).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of CylR2 (P41A) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2LYP.pdb_P41A.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep mutational scanning of CYP2C19 reveals a substrate specificity-abundance tradeoff
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Cytochrome P450s (CYPs) are a family of enzymes responsible for metabolizing nearly 80% of small molecule drugs. Variants in CYPs can substantially alter drug metabolism, which may result in improper dosing and severe adverse drug reactions. CYPs have low sequence conservation, making it difficult to anticipate whether variant effects measured in one CYP may extend to others based on sequence alone. Even closely related CYPs, like CYP2C9 and its closest homolog CYP2C19, have distinct phenotypic properties despite sharing 92% amino acid sequence identity. Thus, we used Variant Abundance by Massively Parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) to measure the steady-state protein abundance, a proxy for protein stability, of 7,660 missense variants in CYP2C19 expressed in cultured human cells. Our results confirmed positions and structural features critical for CYP function and revealed how variants at positions conserved across all eukaryotic CYPs influence abundance. We jointly analyzed 4,670 variants whose abundance was measured in both CYP2C19 and CYP2C9, finding that the homologs have different variant abundances in substrate recognition sites within the hydrophobic core, and that substitutions in some regions reduced abundance in CYP2C19 but not CYP2C9. We also measured the abundance of all single and some multiple WT amino acid exchanges between CYP2C19 and CYP2C9. While most exchanges had no effect, substitutions in substrate recognition site 4 (SRS4) reduced abundance in CYP2C19. When nearby amino acids were exchanged in double and triple mutants, we found distinct interactions between the sites in CYP2C19 and CYP2C9, revealing a region that is partially responsible for the difference in thermodynamic stability between the two homologs. Since these positions are also important for determining substrate specificity, there may be an evolutionary tradeoff between stability and altered enzymatic function. Finally, we used our data to analyze 368 previously unannotated human variants, finding that 43% had decreased abundance. Thus, by comparing variant effects between two closely related and important human genes, we have uncovered regions underlying their functional differences and paved the way for a more complete understanding of one of the most versatile families of enzymes.

title: CYP2C9 abundance scores as measured by VAMP-seq
shortDescription: This study measured the functional consequences of mutations in CYP2C9, as measured by two different assays, one using Variant Abundance by Massively Parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) in HEK293T cells, and one using a yeast activity-based protein profiling assay (Click-seq). This entry contains amino acid scores from the abundance assay using VAMP-seq in HEK293T cells.

experiment.title: CYP2C9 abundance scores
experiment.shortDescription: CYP2C9 protein abundance measured by Variant Abundance by Massively Parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq).
experiment.abstractText:
This study measured the functional consequences of mutations in CYP2C9, as measured by two different assays, one using Variant Abundance by Massively Parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) in HEK293T cells, and one using a yeast activity-based protein profiling assay (Click-seq).

This entry contains amino acid scores from the abundance assay using VAMP-seq in HEK293T cells.
experiment.methodText:
CYP2C9 variant libraries were generated using inverse PCR with NNK primers. Variants were tagged with 18bp random sequence barcodes and the association between barcodes and variants was determined using PacBio sequencing. The barcoded abundance library was introduced into a HEK293T landing pad cell line.

Cells expressing CYP2C9 variants fused to EGFP were sorted into 4 bins by FACS. Genomic DNA was extracted and barcodes from each bin were sequenced. Three replicate sorts were performed. Barcodes from each bin were counted and associated with variant sequences using Enrich2. Variant abundance scores were calculated from the weighed average of variant frequencies in each bin, such that high abundance variants have a higher score and low abundance variants have a lower score. Abundance scores were normalized to the median synonymous variant score (set to 1) and the median nonsense variant score (set to 0). Confidence intervals and variance estimates are based on replicate scores.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Massively parallel characterization of CYP2C9 variant enzyme activity and abundance.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: CYP2C9 encodes a cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for metabolizing up to 15% of small molecule drugs, and CYP2C9 variants can alter the safety and efficacy of these therapeutics. In particular, the anti-coagulant warfarin is prescribed to over 15 million people annually and polymorphisms in CYP2C9 can affect individual drug response and lead to an increased risk of hemorrhage. We developed click-seq, a pooled yeast-based activity assay, to test thousands of variants. Using click-seq, we measured the activity of 6,142 missense variants in yeast. We also measured the steady-state cellular abundance of 6,370 missense variants in a human cell line by using variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq). These data revealed that almost two-thirds of CYP2C9 variants showed decreased activity and that protein abundance accounted for half of the variation in CYP2C9 function. We also measured activity scores for 319 previously unannotated human variants, many of which may have clinical relevance.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Multiplex assessment of protein variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Determining the pathogenicity of genetic variants is a critical challenge, and functional assessment is often the only option. Experimentally characterizing millions of possible missense variants in thousands of clinically important genes requires generalizable, scalable assays. We describe variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq), which measures the effects of thousands of missense variants of a protein on intracellular abundance simultaneously. We apply VAMP-seq to quantify the abundance of 7,801 single-amino-acid variants of PTEN and TPMT, proteins in which functional variants are clinically actionable. We identify 1,138 PTEN and 777 TPMT variants that result in low protein abundance, and may be pathogenic or alter drug metabolism, respectively. We observe selection for low-abundance PTEN variants in cancer, and show that p.Pro38Ser, which accounts for ~10% of PTEN missense variants in melanoma, functions via a dominant-negative mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate that VAMP-seq is applicable to other genes, highlighting its generalizability.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Matreyek KA, et al. Multiplex assessment of protein variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing. Nat. Genet. 2018; 50:874-882.

title: DBT Peripheral subunit-binding domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DBT Peripheral subunit-binding domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: DBT Peripheral subunit-binding domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DBT Peripheral subunit-binding domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Peripheral subunit-binding domain in DBT using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P11182_PF02817_171.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: DDHD2 Sterile alpha motif domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DDHD2 Sterile alpha motif domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Sterile alpha motif domain in DDHD2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O94830_PF00536_389.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

title: DDX3X SGE Exon 1
shortDescription: DDX3X SGE Exon 1

experiment.title: DDX3X SGE Exon 1
experiment.shortDescription: DDX3X SGE Exon 1
experiment.abstractText: This dataset contains the cLFC and cLFC-trend for DDX3X saturation genome editing (SGE) data from Exon 1. Variants were assayed based on viability in LIG4-KO HAP1 cells after direct editing of the endogenous DDX3X locus using CRISPR-based editing.
experiment.methodText: Oligo pools containing the designed variants (eg. exonic and intronic SNV, inframe codon deletion) were synthesized and cloned into the HDR plasmids with ~800bp of each targeted exon homology arm. The designed oligos contain the variants being assayed and 1-3 fixed synonymous substitutions at the PAM and protospacer to prevent re-editing by Cas9 after a successful repair. LIG4-KO HAP1 cells with Cas9 overexpression were co-transfected with a plasmid expressing sgRNA and the puromycin-resistant gene together with the HDR plasmid library. The transfected cells were selected with puromycin for 48 hours and sampled on Day4, Day 7, Day11, Day15 and Day21. cLFC was calculated for Day 7, Day 11, Day15 and Day21 with Day4 as a baseline. cLFC-trend was calculated for Day15 with Day4 as a baseline. Samples were sequenced with 300 bases single-end read using Illumina Hiseq 2500 Rapid.

title: DDX3X SGE scores for clinical use
shortDescription: DDX3X SGE scores for clinical use

experiment.title: DDX3X SGE scores for clinical use
experiment.shortDescription: DDX3X SGE scores for clinical use
experiment.abstractText: This dataset contains a score intended for clinical use in the context of a patient being assessed for DDX3X-related neurodevelopmental disorder. This is a score of nucleotide-variant functional effect derived from saturation genome editing performed in LIG4-KO HAP1 cells for the gene DDX3X. Saturation genome editing identifies variants that result in loss of DDX3X function. Variants are created by directly editing the endogenous DNA locus. Therefore, this technique will identify variants that alter splicing.
experiment.methodText:
We performed Saturation genome editing on DDX3X and quantified variant abundance at 5 time points. A Random Forest supervised classifier was constructed, using combined log fold-change of variant abundance (cLFC, a combined measure of variant abundance from two independent sgRNA experiments) at day 7, 11 and 15 compared to day 4, post-transfection. For raw cLFC values, see exon-specific MAVEdb entries listed above.
Variant training dataset: Variants observed in the GnomAD and UKBB population databases and benign/likely benign variants deposited in ClinVar and DECIPHER were used as ‘negative truth set’ variants (n=540). ‘Positive truth set’ variants (n=168) were de novo likely pathogenic and pathogenic variants curated from ClinVar; DECIPHER; Genomics England 100,000 genomes study; Kaplanis and Samocha et al. 2020 and Lennox et al., 2020. Please see Radford and Tan et al. 2023 for more details. Stratified sampling was used to select 80% of these truth set variants to train the model. 
Model performance: Random Forest model performance estimated from ‘test truth variants’ not used to train the model, using a posterior probability threshold of 50%, was 97.1% sensitivity and 100% specificity. However, we accept that in some clinical decision-making contexts a posterior-probability of variant function higher than 50% may be desirable. Therefore, we propose that for clinical use a posterior probability of > 90% be considered high confidence, and posterior probability 50-90% be considered intermediate confidence.

The score given in the table below is the posterior-probability from this Random Forest model that a variant is non-functional in the context of DDX3X-related neurodevelopmental disorder. In the column “SGE_prediction_of_variant_function_in_NDD_context” variants are classed as ‘abnormal’ if their Random Forest posterior probability is > 0.5. primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Saturation genome editing of DDX3X clarifies pathogenicity of germline and somatic variation.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Loss-of-function of DDX3X is a leading cause of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) in females. DDX3X is also a somatically mutated cancer driver gene proposed to have tumour promoting and suppressing effects. We perform saturation genome editing of DDX3X, testing in vitro the functional impact of 12,776 nucleotide variants. We identify 3432 functionally abnormal variants, in three distinct classes. We train a machine learning classifier to identify functionally abnormal variants of NDD-relevance. This classifier has at least 97% sensitivity and 99% specificity to detect variants pathogenic for NDD, substantially out-performing in silico predictors, and resolving up to 93% of variants of uncertain significance. Moreover, functionally-abnormal variants can account for almost all of the excess nonsynonymous DDX3X somatic mutations seen in DDX3X-driven cancers. Systematic maps of variant effects generated in experimentally tractable cell types have the potential to transform clinical interpretation of both germline and somatic disease-associated variation.

shortDescription: First generation of selection on codon-optimized AID variants

experiment.title: Deaminase activity of AID in generation 1
experiment.shortDescription: First generation of selection on codon-optimized AID variants
experiment.abstractText: The author developed Sat-Sel-Seq method to iteratively select the deaminase activity of AID. A saturated AID library is incoporated to _E. coli_ and selected for rifampin resistance. Functioning AID, together with uracil DNA glycosylase inhibitor (UGI), can cause mutations in RNA polymerase B (_rpoB_) which will become resistant to rifampin and make the host survive. Growth rate of the bacteria can reflect the deaminase activity of AID.
experiment.methodText:
The variant library is built by a cassette mutagenesis approach with NNS degenerate codons at the target codon and a silent mutation on subsequent codon as barcode. The library is then expressed in _E coli._ and selected for rifampin resistance. The initial and selected count of each variant are determined by 454 pyrosequencing and used to quantify the deaminase activity for each variant.
In this experiment, the colonies are selected for 1 generation (cycle).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: High-throughput mutagenesis reveals functional determinants for DNA targeting by activation-induced deaminase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Antibody maturation is a critical immune process governed by the enzyme activation-induced deaminase (AID), a member of the AID/APOBEC DNA deaminase family. AID/APOBEC deaminases preferentially target cytosine within distinct preferred sequence motifs in DNA, with specificity largely conferred by a small 9-11 residue protein loop that differs among family members. Here, we aimed to determine the key functional characteristics of this protein loop in AID and to thereby inform our understanding of the mode of DNA engagement. To this end, we developed a methodology (Sat-Sel-Seq) that couples saturation mutagenesis at each position across the targeting loop, with iterative functional selection and next-generation sequencing. This high-throughput mutational analysis revealed dominant characteristics for residues within the loop and additionally yielded enzymatic variants that enhance deaminase activity. To rationalize these functional requirements, we performed molecular dynamics simulations that suggest that AID and its hyperactive variants can engage DNA in multiple specific modes. These findings align with AID's competing requirements for specificity and flexibility to efficiently drive antibody maturation. Beyond insights into the AID-DNA interface, our Sat-Sel-Seq approach also serves to further expand the repertoire of techniques for deep positional scanning and may find general utility for high-throughput analysis of protein function.

title: Scores from deep mutational scanning CRX transcription factor in HEK 293-derived cells
shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of CRX variants in HEK 293-derived cells expressing a synthetic fluorescent reporter

experiment.title: Deep mutational scanning CRX transcription factor in HEK 293-derived cells
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of CRX variants in HEK 293-derived cells expressing a synthetic fluorescent reporter
experiment.abstractText: The transcription factor (TF) cone-rod homeobox (_CRX_) is essential for the differentiation and maintenance of photoreceptor cell identity. Several human _CRX_ variants cause degenerative retinopathies, but most are variants of uncertain significance. We performed a deep mutational scan (DMS) of nearly all possible single amino acid substitutions in _CRX_ using a cell-based transcriptional reporter assay, curating a high-confidence list of nearly 2000 variants with altered transcriptional activity. In the structured homeodomain, activity scores closely aligned to a predicted structure and demonstrated position-specific constraints on amino acid substitution. In contrast, the intrinsically disordered transcriptional effector domain displayed a qualitatively different pattern of substitution effects, following compositional constraints without specific residue position requirements in the peptide chain. These compositional constraints were consistent with the acidic exposure model of transcriptional activation. We evaluated the performance of the DMS assay as a clinical variant classification tool using gold-standard classified human variants from ClinVar, identifying pathogenic variants with high specificity and moderate sensitivity. That this performance could be achieved using a synthetic reporter assay in a foreign cell type, even for a highly cell type-specific TF like _CRX_, suggests that this approach shows promise for DMS of other TFs that function in cell types that are not easily accessible. Together, the results of the _CRX_ DMS identify molecular features of the _CRX_ effector domain and demonstrate utility for integration into the clinical variant classification pipeline.
experiment.methodText: The deep mutational scanning (DMS) method used a HEK293-derived cell line containing both a synthetic _CRX_ transcriptional reporter and a genomic landing pad system. A library of _CRX_ single amino acid substitution variants was integrated into the landing pad so each cell expressed exactly one variant. Cells were then sorted into four bins based on reporter fluorescence, followed by extraction of genomic DNA and sequencing of variant barcodes from each bin. The relative abundance of each variant across the bins was used to calculate a quantitative activity score, allowing measurement of how each substitution affected _CRX_ transcriptional activity.

experiment.title: Deep Mutational Scanning in FKRP and LARGE1 with Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF)
experiment.shortDescription: Our inability to interpret the consequences of rare variants is an unappreciated challenge in the diagnosis of rare diseases. We developed a democratized workflow called Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional assays (SMuRF) to inspect the direct impact variants have on enzymatic activity. We employed SMuRF to score all possible coding single nucleotide variants (SNVs) of Dystroglycanopathies-related enzyme-coding genes, FKRP and LARGE1. The utility of SMuRF scores was enhanced through the assignment of confidence scores and orthogonal assays for validation. SMuRF recapitulated and significantly expanded the knowledge gained from clinical reports and population databases, aiding in alleviating ethnic disparity in biomedical databases and improving variant classification. SMuRF expanded the training datasets of the computational predictors with the potential to improve their variant classification capability. SMuRF highlighted the critical regions in the enzyme structure which shed light on different disease mechanisms. SMuRF is the first high-throughput functional workflow to study dystroglycanopathy variants and opens the door for better variant interpretation underlying other rare diseases.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep Mutational Scanning in Disease-related Genes with Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF)
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Interpretation of disease-causing genetic variants remains a challenge in human genetics. Current costs and complexity of deep mutational scanning methods hamper crowd-sourcing approaches toward genome-wide resolution of variants in disease-related genes. Our framework, Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional assays (SMuRF), addresses these issues by offering simple and cost-effective saturation mutagenesis, as well as streamlining functional assays to enhance the interpretation of unresolved variants. Applying SMuRF to neuromuscular disease genes FKRP and LARGE1, we generated functional scores for all possible coding single nucleotide variants, which aid in resolving clinically reported variants of uncertain significance. SMuRF also demonstrates utility in predicting disease severity, resolving critical structural regions, and providing training datasets for the development of computational predictors. Our approach opens new directions for enabling variant-to-function insights for disease genes in a manner that is broadly useful for crowd-sourcing implementation across standard research laboratories.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep Mutational Scanning in Disease-related Genes with Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF)
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Interpretation of disease-causing genetic variants remains a challenge in human genetics. Current costs and complexity of deep mutational scanning methods hamper crowd-sourcing approaches toward genome-wide resolution of variants in disease-related genes. Our framework, Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional assays (SMuRF), addresses these issues by offering simple and cost-effective saturation mutagenesis, as well as streamlining functional assays to enhance the interpretation of unresolved variants. Applying SMuRF to neuromuscular disease genes FKRP and LARGE1, we generated functional scores for all possible coding single nucleotide variants, which aid in resolving clinically reported variants of uncertain significance. SMuRF also demonstrates utility in predicting disease severity, resolving critical structural regions, and providing training datasets for the development of computational predictors. Our approach opens new directions for enabling variant-to-function insights for disease genes in a manner that is broadly useful for crowd-sourcing implementation across standard research laboratories.

title: SGCA variants effects on α-sarcoglycan surface expression
shortDescription: SGCA variants effects on α-sarcoglycan surface expression

experiment.title: Deep Mutational Scanning in SGCA with Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF)
experiment.shortDescription: Comprehensive functional assessment of all possible coding single-nucleotide variants in SGCA using saturation mutagenesis and a cell-surface localization assay.
experiment.abstractText: Pathogenic variants in SGCA, encoding α-sarcoglycan, cause an autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, LGMDR3/2D, yet clinical interpretation of SGCA variants remains challenging due to the high prevalence of rare missense variants. α-sarcoglycan is an essential component of the sarcoglycan complex at the muscle cell membrane, and pathogenic variants frequently impair its membrane localization. Here, we systematically assess the effects of all possible single-nucleotide variants across the SGCA coding sequence using a saturation mutagenesis-based experimental assay that quantifies α-sarcoglycan surface expression. We generate a comprehensive functional atlas that distinguishes tolerated and damaging variants, aligning with independent genetic and clinical evidence, and reveals domain-specific properties of the cytoplasmic region, in which C-terminal truncating variants retain membrane localization, suggesting possible pathogenic mechanisms beyond impaired trafficking. This work provides a scalable functional framework to support genetic diagnosis and variant interpretation in sarcoglycanopathies.
experiment.methodText:
Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF) is an accessible workflow for deep mutational scanning (DMS) studies. The manuscript is currently in preparation. This workflow involves a 2-way extension PCR-based saturation mutagenesis and high-throughput functional assays that can be evaluated with short-read Next-generation sequencing.  

For SGCA, all possible coding single-nucleotide variants were generated across five non-overlapping mutagenesis blocks. Variant effects were evaluated using a FACS-based assay measuring α-sarcoglycan cell-surface expression in HEK-BDG cells stably expressing β-, δ-, and γ-sarcoglycan. Surface α-sarcoglycan was detected by live-cell staining of an extracellular FLAG epitope, and cells were separated into high- and low-surface-expression populations. Variant enrichment was quantified by NGS, and membrane localization scores (MLSs) were generated from three biological replicates.  

 

We have organized scripts used for SMuRF across three repositories:  

Balthazar repository is used to create the oligo library needed for the saturation mutagenesis as well as perform QC for the resulting construct.  

Gargamel repository is used to process the raw data from NGS to quantify the enrichment of the variants.  

DeniSa repository is used to generate and analyze the membrane localization scores (MLSs), SMuRF scores, process the nonsense variant library, analyze clinical data, and plot the results.

experiment.title: Deep mutational scanning of >23,000 single amino acid substitutions across TYK2, measuring variant effects on IFN-α signaling and protein abundance in engineered HEK293T cells with and without pharmacological inhibition.
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scanning of >23,000 single amino acid substitutions across TYK2, measuring variant effects on IFN-α signaling and protein abundance in engineered HEK293T cells with and without pharmacological inhibition.
experiment.abstractText: Tyrosine Kinase 2 (TYK2) is a genetically defined target for autoimmune disease, with first-generation inhibitors showing clinical success in some but not all associated indications. To build a deeper understanding of TYK2 structure-function, protein-ligand interactions, and the impact of human variants, Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) was applied to assess >23,000 amino acid substitutions across two TYK2 functions: IFN-α signaling and protein abundance. This enabled high-resolution structure-function mapping and the identification of novel allosteric sites. By coupling DMS with inhibitor treatment, variants that modulate compound potency were uncovered. Human variants, both common and rare, that are protective against autoimmune phenotypes were shown to reduce TYK2 protein abundance. Together, these findings demonstrate that DMS can prospectively reveal novel druggable sites, clarify structure-activity relationships (SAR), and highlight TYK2 degradation as a potential therapeutic strategy in autoimmunity.
experiment.methodText:
Variant library construction: The TYK2 coding sequence (UniProt: P29597) was divided into 17 sub-libraries of ~210 bp each. Pools of ~270 bp DNA oligos (Twist Bioscience) encoding every possible single amino acid substitution were synthesized. DNA barcodes were appended to variant alleles during initial amplification, and variant-barcode linked amplicons were cloned into sub-library-specific destination plasmids. A second cloning step integrated the full reporter cassette between the variant allele and barcode. Libraries were co-transfected with Bxb1 recombinase into engineered HEK293T cells and selected with 10 µg/mL Blasticidin for ~14 days, yielding a library of HEK293T cells each containing a single TYK2 allele-barcode combination integrated in single copy at the H11 safe harbor locus.

Model system and functional assays: The base cell line was HEK293T with all endogenous TYK2 alleles knocked out via CRISPR/Cas9. IFN-α signaling competence was reconstituted by stable piggyBac integration of STAT2 and IRF9 transgenes. For the IFN-α signaling assay, a barcoded luciferase reporter under the control of an eight-copy Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) was used with doxycycline-inducible TYK2 expression. Cells were stimulated with human IFN-α 2a at 1, 10, or 100 U/mL, and reporter RNA was harvested 6 hours post-stimulation. Inhibitor conditions used BMS-986202 (20 nM, 1 µM, 10 µM) and NDI-034858 (7 nM, 1 µM) at 100 U/mL IFN-α. For the protein abundance assay, a VAMP-seq-adapted reporter with N-terminal GFP-tagged TYK2 and co-transcriptionally linked BFP normalization control was used. Cells were sorted into four equal quartile bins by GFP:BFP fluorescence ratio via FACS on a Sony MA900.

Sequencing: Variant-barcode associations were mapped with 2×150 paired-end reads on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 (300-cycle P3 kit). Final DMS assay libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 with a 50-cycle P3 kit and 30% PhiX spike-in using custom read and index primers.

Replicates: Both IFN-α and abundance DMS libraries were assayed in biological triplicate. IFN-α sequencing libraries were amplified in duplicate per biological replicate to account for PCR/sequencing errors.

Statistical analysis: Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. Using these models, we computed per-condition variant effect estimates as well as contrasts of estimates between conditions. Variant effects were modeled using a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model, fitting one model per position and incorporating all variant and wild-type counts from the corresponding segment. For TYK2-VampDMS data, we obtained four activity bins per replicate, each producing one sample. Consequently, we computed normalized log abundance estimates for each variant within each bin. Then, we applied a weighted Bayesian model to identify an abundance midpoint (on the 0-1 scale) per variant, and contrasted the computed midpoint with the WT sequence midpoint.

Coverage: The IFN-α library included 23,737 of 23,740 possible variants (>99.9%); the abundance library included 23,716 (>99.9%).

title: Deep Mutational Scanning of alpha-Synuclein Aggregation in Yeast
shortDescription: The aggregation of alpha-synuclein single missense variants in yeast

experiment.title: Deep Mutational Scanning of alpha-Synuclein Aggregation in Yeast
experiment.shortDescription: The aggregation of alpha-synuclein single missense variants in yeast
experiment.abstractText: The cellular environment plays a critical role in shaping protein conformations, including aggregated states implicated in disease. One challenge to studying this relationship is that most techniques offering high-resolution insight into the nature of these aggregates cannot be deployed in living cells. Systematic mutagenesis presents an opportunity to bridge this gap but requires general and robust methods to detect protein aggregation across large numbers of variants. Here, we use clickable protein tags to generate FRET pairs in situ that can report protein aggregation in high throughput in living cells. We applied this strategy to probe the nature of cellular inclusions of alpha-synuclein in a popular yeast model. Our results demonstrate that cellular aggregates of alpha-synuclein in yeast are likely dominated by protein–membrane interactions, making the aggregation pathway in this cellular model very different than in many in vitro experiments.
experiment.methodText:
A DNA library encoding all possible single-amino acid variants of alpha-synuclein was obtained from a previously reported plasmid library generated by commercial oligonucleotide synthesis and assembly. This DNA library was cloned into the pYes2- alpha-synuclein WT-HaloTag construct using the EZClone method. To reduce sequencing costs, the plasmid library was bottlenecked to 80,000 members in E. coli. The resulting plasmid library was then transformed into Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain W303 using the LiAc/PEG/ssDNA method, generating approximately 0.9 million yeast transformants. 
For library selection experiments, protein expression was induced with 1% [w/v] galactose. After 12h of induction, cells were harvested and labeled with green and red HaloTag ligands and incubated for 1h at 30C in the dark. Cells were washed three times with PBS and resuspended for flow-cytometric sorting. Cell sorting was performed based on FRET signals, and FRET-positive and FRET-negative populations were collected for plasmid DNA isolation.
The alpha-synuclein coding region was amplified by PCR from plasmid DNA obtained from library samples collected during the sorting experiments. A sequential PCR approach was used to append the Illumina adapters and primer binding sites for sequencing. Amplicons were gel-purified, quantified by Qubit fluorometry, pooled, and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform in PE 300 mode.

experiment.title: Deep Mutational Scanning of alpha-Synuclein based on Expression Level in Yeast
experiment.shortDescription: The expression level of alpha-synuclein missense variants was determined by cell sorting of yeast expressing each variant fused to GFP.
experiment.abstractText: alpha-Synuclein is a conformationally dynamic protein linked to a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson’s. Conformational transitions of this protein are believed to contribute to disease etiology, but the conformations that drive pathology remain unclear. To address this question, we screened an exhaustive library of alpha-synuclein missense variants for their toxicity in yeast, a well-validated cellular model for alpha-synuclein pathobiology. By examining the pattern of mutations that disrupts cellular toxicity, we were able to build a model for the structure of the toxic species.
experiment.methodText:
A double-stranded DNA library based on human alpha-synuclein cDNA was produced by commercial oligonucleotide synthesis and assembly. The designed library encodes all single missense variants of alpha-synuclein, each encoded by a single codon. This library was cloned in frame with a C-terminal GFP fusion, and 26bp random barcodes were appended 3’ to the stop codon to facilitate repeated selection. This construct was cloned under control of an inducible promoter and transformed into E. coli. Following restrictive transformation, the final library diversity was ~60,000 unique clones, corresponding to ~20 barcodes per missense variant. The barcoded coding region was amplified and analyzed by long-read MiSeq in order to associate barcodes with coding sequences. The resulting lookup table expedites subsequent quantification of variant frequencies.

This plasmid library was then transformed into yeast. Selection was performed by inducing expression and collecting aliquots over time. Additional experiments were performed in yeast treated with small molecules. Finally, the expression level of each variant was estimated by cell sorting yeast cells based on the fluorescence of the GFP fusion.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep mutational scanning reveals the structural basis for α-synuclein activity.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Defining the biologically active structures of proteins in their cellular environments remains challenging for proteins with multiple conformations and functions, where only a minor conformer might be associated with a given function. Here, we use deep mutational scanning to probe the structure and dynamics of α-synuclein, a protein known to adopt disordered, helical and amyloid conformations. We examined the effects of 2,600 single-residue substitutions on the ability of intracellularly expressed α-synuclein to slow the growth of yeast. Computational analysis of the data showed that the conformation responsible for this phenotype is a long, uninterrupted, amphiphilic helix with increasing dynamics toward the C terminus. Deep mutational scanning can therefore determine biologically active conformations in cellular environments, even for a highly dynamic multi-conformational protein.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Newberry RW, et al. Deep mutational scanning reveals the structural basis for α-synuclein activity. Nat. Chem. Biol. 2020; 16:653-659.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep mutational scanning reveals the structural basis for α-synuclein activity.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Defining the biologically active structures of proteins in their cellular environments remains challenging for proteins with multiple conformations and functions, where only a minor conformer might be associated with a given function. Here, we use deep mutational scanning to probe the structure and dynamics of α-synuclein, a protein known to adopt disordered, helical and amyloid conformations. We examined the effects of 2,600 single-residue substitutions on the ability of intracellularly expressed α-synuclein to slow the growth of yeast. Computational analysis of the data showed that the conformation responsible for this phenotype is a long, uninterrupted, amphiphilic helix with increasing dynamics toward the C terminus. Deep mutational scanning can therefore determine biologically active conformations in cellular environments, even for a highly dynamic multi-conformational protein.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Newberry RW, et al. Deep mutational scanning reveals the structural basis for α-synuclein activity. Nat. Chem. Biol. 2020; 16:653-659.

shortDescription: Single-site saturation mutagenesis of EnvZ at 37C using activation of gfp expression downstream of cognate regulator OmpR as a readout.

experiment.title: Deep mutational scanning of EnvZ
experiment.shortDescription: Single-site saturation mutagenesis of the DHp domain of the bacterial histidine kinase EnvZ
experiment.abstractText: We carried out deep mutational scanning of EnvZ at multiple temperatures to investigate the temperature-sensitivity of its mutational landscape. We used a fluorescent reporter downstream of EnvZ's cognate regulator OmpR as a readout of activity. Expression of this reporter is activated by phosphorylated OmpR upon EnvZ activation.
experiment.methodText:
A comprehensive single mutant library was constructed using oligonucleotide-directed mutagenesis of the EnvZ DHp domain. To mutate each position in the EnvZ DHp (positions 230–289), two complementary 30-nucleotide primers (one sense, one antisense) were synthesized that introduce an NNS codon at the targeted position. One round of PCR was carried out with one reaction containing the antisense NNS primer and a primer located 105 bp upstream of the 5' end of the DHp domain, containing a SacI restriction site, and a second reaction containing the sense NNS primer and a primer flanking the 3' end of the gene, containing a SalI restriction site. A second PCR round using both first round products and both flanking primers produced the full-length double stranded product. All reactions yielded a band of the correct size on an agarose gel, which was extracted and purified (Zymo). PCR product concentrations were quantified (NanoDrop), pooled in equimolar ratios, digested with SacI and SalI, and ligated into the pSC101/specR expression vector. Each ligation was dialyzed on Millipore VSWP 0.025-μm membrane filters for 60 min and the entire volume was electroporated into 20 μL Invitrogen One Shot TOP10 Electrocomp E. coli to yield ~10e6 total transformants. Plasmids from these transformants were then purified by miniprep (Zymo), dialyzed, and electroporated into the experimental strain, containing a p15a/CmR plasmid with gfp downstream of the PompC promoter, which is regulated by OmpR, yielding ~10e9 transformants for each strain.

For three biological replicates, overnight cultures of the library were back diluted 1:100 and grown to OD600 = 0.2 at the relevant temperature. Cultures were then split into two, with one culture induced by addition of 5 mM aspartate to activate EnvZ. After 3 h of further growth at the tested temperature, cells were diluted into PBS and GFP expression was used to sort cells into bins on a BD FACS Aria machine. For each replicate, both on and off cultures were sorted into 8 bins. Up to ~3 million cells were sorted into bins per sample. Sorted cells were grown in 2× YT medium containing chloramphenicol and spectinomycin overnight.

After FACS, plasmids were purified (Zymo) from overnight cultures of each sorted bin. To add Element/Illumina sequencing adaptors and barcodes, two PCR reactions were performed using KAPA HiFi. First, EnvZ DHp domain sequences were amplified for 12 cycles (95 °C for 30 s, 68 °C for 15 s and 72 °C for 30 s) with inner amplification primers. Second, a PCR to add barcoding primers was carried out on product from the first PCR for 9 cycles (95 °C for 30 s, 68 °C for 15 s and 72 °C for 30 s). Final purified PCR products were quantified (NanoDrop), normalized, pooled. 37C samples (collected in 2022) were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq and 30C and 42C samples (collected in 2023) on an Element AVITI, with up to ~3 million reads collected per bin.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Marginal specificity in protein interactions constrains evolution of a paralogous family
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The evolution of novel functions in biology relies heavily on gene duplication and divergence, creating large paralogous protein families. Selective pressure to avoid detrimental cross-talk often results in paralogs that exhibit exquisite specificity for their interaction partners. But how robust or sensitive is this specificity to mutation? Here, using deep mutational scanning, we demonstrate that a paralogous family of bacterial signaling proteins exhibits marginal specificity, such that many individual substitutions give rise to substantial cross-talk between normally insulated pathways. Our results indicate that sequence space is locally crowded despite overall sparseness, and we provide evidence that this crowding has constrained the evolution of bacterial signaling proteins. These findings underscore how evolution selects for “good enough” rather than optimized phenotypes, leading to restrictions on the subsequent evolution of paralogs.

title: Deep mutational scanning of the hormone receptor PYL1 stability at 250 µM (+)-ABA
shortDescription: This experiment set quantifies the effects of single amino acid substitutions in the Arabidopsis thaliana abscisic acid hormone receptor PYL1 using a pooled growth-based assay in yeast. The resulting data capture mutation-dependent changes in homodimer abundance of PYL1.

experiment.title: Deep mutational scanning of the hormone receptor PYL1 stability at 250 µM (+)-ABA
experiment.shortDescription: This experiment set quantifies the effects of single amino acid substitutions in the Arabidopsis thaliana abscisic acid hormone receptor PYL1 using a pooled growth-based assay in yeast. The resulting data capture mutation-dependent changes in homodimer abundance of PYL1.
experiment.abstractText:
Many receptor proteins act as allosteric switches, but the genetic basis by which mutations in these can alter signal processing remains poorly understood. To systematically map how mutations modulate a receptor protein’s response during small molecule ligand binding, we performed a series of deep mutational scanning experiments on the Arabidopsis thaliana (+)-ABA hormone receptor PYL1.

Using a Glueable Protein-fragment Complementation Assay (GluePCA), PYL1 variants were assayed in a pooled format for their ability to undergo allosteric, (+)-ABA-dependent interaction with ABI1. This approach links protein-protein dimerization strength to yeast cellular growth via reconstitution of MTX-resistant dihydrofolate reductase (see DOI: 10.1126/science.1153878). It enables a direct, quantitative measurement of receptor activity across many genotypes simultaneously.

We quantify variant effects of ligand-independent (apo) and saturating-ligand conditions for PYL1 homodimer abundance. Additional experiments measure PYL1-ABI1 dimerization across twelve (+)-ABA concentrations, spanning several orders of magnitude, allowing us to capture full mutant dose-response characteristics. Together, our experiments provide a comprehensive view of how mutations reshape hormone receptor sensitivity, efficacy, and basal activity, revealing the modular nature of PYL1 switch function.
experiment.methodText:
Mutant libraries covering all single amino acid substitutions of PYL1 [residues 33-209] were generated using site-saturation mutagenesis in four separate tiles [residues 33-78, 79-124, 125-170, 171-209], and assayed in the GluePCA system in S. cerevisiae. Following transformation, pooled cultures were grown under selective conditions at defined (+)-ABA concentrations, such that growth rate reflects the strength of PYL1-PYl1 homodimer abundance (or PYL1-ABI1 binding in dedicated experiments).

For each condition, plasmid DNA was extracted before and after selection, and variant frequencies were quantified by Illumina sequencing. Variant-level enrichment scores were computed from relative changes in read counts between input and output populations. To account for sequencing depth and global fitness effects, these scores were then normalized to (i) overall culture OD of each library vs. (+)-ABA concentration, and (ii) synonymous wild-type and stop variant controls between all four library tiles. Triplicate measurements were combined to improve uncertainty estimates.
