title: Cellular abundance of MLH1
shortDescription: Cellular abundance of MLH1 variants using DHFR-PCA in yeast.

experiment.title: Disentangling the mutational effects on protein stability and interaction of human MLH1
experiment.shortDescription: Cellular abundance and PMS2 interaction of MLH1 variants using DHFR-PCA and Y2H, respectively, in yeast.
experiment.abstractText: This study assessed the cellular abundance and PMS2 interaction of nearly all possible missense variants and 40 nonsense variants in the C-terminal domain of MLH1. The cellular abundance of MLH1 variants was measured using the DHFR-PCA in a wild-type yeast strain. The PMS2 interaction of MLH1 variants was measured using the Y2H assay in the MaV203 yeast strain.
experiment.methodText: The C-terminal domain of MLH1 was divided into 7 tiles, and site saturated mutagenesis libraries was synthetised in each tile and cloned into pDONR221 by Twist Bioscience. The libraries were cloned into tailored destination vectors and transformed into appropriate yeast strains. The DHFR-PCA was performed on solid SC+histidine+leucine+methionine medium (control) and SC+histidine+leucine+methionine medium with 200 μM MTX and 1 mM sulfanilamide (selection). The Y2H assay was performed on solid SC-leucine-tryptophan medium (control) and SC-leucine-tryptophan-histidine medium with 20 mM 3-AT (selection). Plasmids were isolated to prepare amplicons that were subjected to pair-end next-generation sequencing using the Illumina NextSeq 550 System. The resulting sequencing data was used to calculate a single abundance score and interaction score for each MLH1 variant. The scores were calculated using Enrich2 based on three replicates.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Disentangling the mutational effects on protein stability and interaction of human MLH1
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense mutations can have diverse effects on proteins, depending on their location within the protein and the specific amino acid substitution. Mutations in the DNA mismatch repair geneMLH1are associated with Lynch syndrome, yet the underlying mechanism of most disease-causing mutations remains elusive. To address this gap, we aim to disentangle the mutational effects on two essential properties for MLH1 function: protein stability and protein-protein interaction. We systematically examine the cellular abundance and interaction with PMS2 of 4839 (94%) MLH1 variants in the C-terminal domain. Our combined data shows that most MLH1 variants lose interaction with PMS2 due to reduced cellular abundance. However, substitutions to charged residues in the canonical interface lead to reduced interaction with PMS2. Unexpectedly, we also identify a distal region in the C-terminal domain of MLH1 where substitutions cause both decreased and increased binding with PMS2, and propose a region in PMS2 as the binding site. Our data successfully distinguish benign from pathogenic MLH1 variants and correlate with thermodynamic stability predictions and evolutionary conservation. This work provides mechanistic insights into variant consequences and may help interpret MLH1 variants.Author SummaryMutations in proteins, including single amino acid substitutions, can disrupt normal cellular function and lead to diseases. Hence, there is great interest in understanding their consequences from both basic science and clinical genetics perspectives. Loss-of-function variants in the human mismatch repair protein MLH1 are associated with Lynch syndrome, a hereditary condition that significantly increases the risk of certain cancers. Detailed insights into the molecular consequences of MLH1 variants are essential for understanding the mechanisms underlying Lynch syndrome. In this study, we use high-throughput experimental approaches to test how missense mutations affect the cellular abundance of MLH1 and the interaction with its partner, PMS2. We find that many variants disrupting the interaction with PMS2 also lead to reduced cellular abundance levels, suggesting a strong relationship between protein stability and interaction in MLH1. Additionally, we identify a potential novel interaction site between MLH1 and PMS2, where mutations in MLH1 either increase or decrease interaction without affecting abundance. Our datasets are in line with the classification of clinically annotated MLH1 variants and may aid in interpreting variants of uncertain significance, while also providing new insights into the molecular details of the interaction with PMS2.

title: DLG3 PDZ domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DLG3 PDZ domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: DLG3 PDZ domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DLG3 PDZ domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the PDZ domain in DLG3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q92796_PF00595_383.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. experiment.title: DMS of SARS-CoV-2 PLpro to discover escape variants of Jun12682
experiment.shortDescription: A deep mutational scanning study to identify drug escape variants of SARS-CoV-2 Papain-Like protease (PLpro) against potent inhibitors Jun12682.
experiment.abstractText: Papain-Like protease (PLpro) is one of the most critical drug targets for SARS-CoV-2 therapeutic development. Recently, several compounds have demonstrated promise in treating infected murine models, including Pfizer's PF-079757472, Jun12682 and WEHI-P8–exhibiting distinct chemical scaffolds. We applied our DMS pipeline to investigate potential escape variants against these potent compounds.
experiment.methodText:
We employed a cellular FRET assay to differentiate between active and inactive PLpro variants using cell sorting techniques. Subsequently, RNA was extracted from the sorted cells, reverse-transcribed, and indexed for Illumina sequencing. Enrichment scores and error estimates were calculated with DiMSum.

Note that while the initial methionine was originally labeled as residue 0, in this uploaded data it is designated as residue 1–with subsequent residues following accordingly–because MAVEDB automatically translates the sequence starting from residue 1.

experiment.title: DMS of SARS-CoV-2 PLpro to discover escape variants of PF-07957472
experiment.shortDescription: A deep mutational scanning study to identify drug escape variants of SARS-CoV-2 Papain-Like protease (PLpro) against potent inhibitors PF-07957472, from Pfizer.
experiment.abstractText: Papain-Like protease (PLpro) is one of the most critical drug targets for SARS-CoV-2 therapeutic development. Recently, several compounds have demonstrated promise in treating infected murine models, including Pfizer's PF-079757472, Jun12682 and WEHI-P8–exhibiting distinct chemical scaffolds. We applied our DMS pipeline to investigate potential escape variants against these potent compounds.
experiment.methodText:
We employed a cellular FRET assay to differentiate between active and inactive PLpro variants using cell sorting techniques. Subsequently, RNA was extracted from the sorted cells, reverse-transcribed, and indexed for Illumina sequencing. Enrichment scores and error estimates were calculated with DiMSum.

Note that while the initial methionine was originally labeled as residue 0, in this uploaded data it is designated as residue 1–with subsequent residues following accordingly–because MAVEDB automatically translates the sequence starting from residue 1.

title: DMTF1 SANT/Myb domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DMTF1 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: DMTF1 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DMTF1 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SANT/Myb domain in DMTF1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9Y222_PF00249_226.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: DNAJA1 combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for DnaJ homolog subfamily A member 1.

experiment.title: DNAJA1 combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for DnaJ homolog subfamily A member 1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily A member 1 protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2LO1.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 117 variants that failed validation.

title: DNAJA1 trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily A member 1.

experiment.title: DNAJA1 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily A member 1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily A member 1 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2LO1.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: DNAJB2 combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 2.

experiment.title: DNAJB2 combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 2.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 2 protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2LGW.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 345 variants that failed validation.

title: DNAJB2 trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 2.

experiment.title: DNAJB2 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 2.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of DnaJ homolog subfamily B member 2 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2LGW.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: DNAJB5 DnaJ domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DNAJB5 DnaJ domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: DNAJB5 DnaJ domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DNAJB5 DnaJ domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the DnaJ domain in DNAJB5 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O75953_PF00226_4.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

title: DVL1 DIX domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DVL1 DIX domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: DVL1 DIX domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the DVL1 DIX domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the DIX domain in DVL1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O14640_PF00778_4.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: E. coli LetA defines a structurally distinct transporter family involved in lipid trafficking
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of intermembrane transport protein LetA from Escherichia coli
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the function of LetA variants exposed to outer membrane stress (LSB or cholate). The results here, combined with our cryo-EM structure and molecular dynamic simulations, are used to propose a model for how LetA transport lipids.
experiment.methodText: LetA variants were tested in pooled formant in a ∆pqiAB ∆letAB knock out strain. Variants were constructed using PCR mediated site-directed mutagenesis of all possible amino acid substitutions. LetA variants were sequenced using paired-end Illumina reads in a manner to ensure that pairs overlapped the region of interest.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: LetA defines a structurally distinct transporter family
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Cristina C. Santarossa, et al. LetA defines a structurally distinct transporter family. Nature. 2026; (Unknown volume):(Unknown pages). 10.1038/s41586-025-09990-0

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: LetA defines a structurally distinct transporter family involved in lipid trafficking
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Membrane transport proteins translocate diverse cargos, ranging from small sugars to entire proteins, across cellular membranes. A few structurally distinct protein families have been described that account for most of the known membrane transport processes. However, many membrane proteins with predicted transporter functions remain uncharacterized. We determined the structure ofE. coliLetAB, a phospholipid transporter involved in outer membrane integrity, and found that LetA adopts a distinct architecture that is structurally and evolutionarily unrelated to known transporter families. LetA functions as a pump at one end of a ~225 Å long tunnel formed by its binding partner, MCE protein LetB, creating a pathway for lipid transport between the inner and outer membranes. Unexpectedly, the LetA transmembrane domains adopt a fold that is evolutionarily related to the eukaryotic tetraspanin family of membrane proteins, including TARPs and claudins. LetA has no detectable homology to known transport proteins, and defines a new class of membrane transporters. Through a combination of deep mutational scanning, molecular dynamics simulations, AlphaFold-predicted alternative states, and functional studies, we present a model for how the LetA-like family of membrane transporters may use energy from the proton-motive force to drive the transport of lipids across the bacterial cell envelope.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Cristina C. Santarossa, et al. LetA defines a structurally distinct transporter family involved in lipid trafficking. (None). 2025; (Unknown volume):(Unknown pages). 10.1101/2025.03.21.644421

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of EEHEE_rd3_1627 protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is EEHEE_rd3_1627.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of EEHEE_rd3_1627.

experiment.title: EEHEE_rd3_1627 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of EEHEE_rd3_1627.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of EEHEE_rd3_1627 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is EEHEE_rd3_1627.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.title: Effects on ACE2-binding affinity of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1
experiment.shortDescription: This experiment measures the effects on ACE2-binding affinity of variants in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1
experiment.abstractText: The experiment aimed to determine the impact of mutations in the Omicron BA.1 RBD of the SARS-CoV-2 virus on their binding affinity to the human ACE2 receptor. Deep mutational scanning was used to analyze every possible single amino acid substitution in the Omicron BA.1 RBD, and their subsequent binding affinity with human ACE2 receptor was identified. Several mutations reduced the binding affinity of the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1 for its receptor, as expected. However, several new mutations were found which increased binding affinity, indicating the potential evolution of the virus. These mutations were clustered at several sites and caused subtle shifts to regions critical for receptor-ACE2 interactions. The experiment is described in more detail in the paper.
experiment.methodText: The experiment involved the generation of a yeast display library with every possible single amino acid mutation in the Omicron BA.1 RBD. The library was incubated with human monomeric ACE2 receptor, and binding strength was quantified using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) followed by deep sequencing. The effects of mutations on ACE2-binding affinity were analyzed and reported using heatmaps.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep mutational scans for ACE2 binding, RBD expression, and antibody escape in the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 receptor-binding domains.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 continues to acquire mutations in the spike receptor-binding domain (RBD) that impact ACE2 receptor binding, folding stability, and antibody recognition. Deep mutational scanning prospectively characterizes the impacts of mutations on these biochemical properties, enabling rapid assessment of new mutations seen during viral surveillance. However, the effects of mutations can change as the virus evolves, requiring updated deep mutational scans. We determined the impacts of all single amino acid mutations in the Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 RBDs on ACE2-binding affinity, RBD folding, and escape from binding by the LY-CoV1404 (bebtelovimab) monoclonal antibody. The effects of some mutations in Omicron RBDs differ from those measured in the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 background. These epistatic shifts largely resemble those previously seen in the Alpha variant due to the convergent epistatically modifying N501Y substitution. However, Omicron variants show additional lineage-specific shifts, including examples of the epistatic phenomenon of entrenchment that causes the Q498R and N501Y substitutions present in Omicron to be more favorable in that background than in earlier viral strains. In contrast, the Omicron substitution Q493R exhibits no sign of entrenchment, with the derived state, R493, being as unfavorable for ACE2 binding in Omicron RBDs as in Wuhan-Hu-1. Likely for this reason, the R493Q reversion has occurred in Omicron sub-variants including BA.4/BA.5 and BA.2.75, where the affinity buffer from R493Q reversion may potentiate concurrent antigenic change. Consistent with prior studies, we find that Omicron RBDs have reduced expression, and identify candidate stabilizing mutations that ameliorate this deficit. Last, our maps highlight a broadening of the sites of escape from LY-CoV1404 antibody binding in BA.1 and BA.2 compared to the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 background. These BA.1 and BA.2 deep mutational scanning datasets identify shifts in the RBD mutational landscape and inform ongoing efforts in viral surveillance.

experiment.title: Effects on antibody escape of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1
experiment.shortDescription: This experiment measures the effects on antibody escape of variants in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1
experiment.abstractText: We present a deep mutational scanning (DMS) assay to measure the effect of single amino acid mutations across the entire Receptor Binding Domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein on antibody escape for Omicron BA.1. The generated escape map revealed that Omicron BA.1 has a higher number of escape mutations compared to its predecessor Delta, suggesting that it may be less susceptible to neutralization by currently available antibody therapies. The data also demonstrated that a large proportion of Omicron BA.1 escape mutations make the RBD more similar to the bat-CoV RBD, which may suggest an increased adaptation to transmission dynamics or host cells and which creates a novel evolutionary trajectory. Furthermore, several Omicron BA.1 mutations lie in close proximity to RBD-ACE2 interaction residues and may directly block antibody binding while maintaining ACE2 binding. See the paper for more information.
experiment.methodText: We synthesized a pooled library of DNA sequences encoding all single amino acid mutations in the Omicron BA.1 RBD and expressed them on the surface of yeast cells. We then incubated the library with a monoclonal antibody known as LY-CoV1404, which targets the RBD of SARS-CoV-2. Next, we used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to select and sequence the variant yeast cells that survived LY-CoV1404 treatment. By comparing the frequency of each mutation in the surviving population versus the starting diversity, we were able to quantify the neutralization effect of each mutation. Importantly, we performed experiments in triplicate and reported robust statistical analysis to validate our results.

experiment.title: Effects on antibody escape of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.2
experiment.shortDescription: This experiment measures the effects on antibody escape of variants in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.2
experiment.abstractText: We present a deep mutational scanning (DMS) assay to measure the effect of single amino acid mutations across the entire Receptor Binding Domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein on antibody escape for Omicron BA.2. The generated escape map revealed that Omicron BA.2 has a higher number of escape mutations compared to its predecessor Delta, suggesting that it may be less susceptible to neutralization by currently available antibody therapies. The data also demonstrated that a large proportion of Omicron BA.2 escape mutations make the RBD more similar to the bat-CoV RBD, which may suggest an increased adaptation to transmission dynamics or host cells and which creates a novel evolutionary trajectory. Furthermore, several Omicron BA.2 mutations lie in close proximity to RBD-ACE2 interaction residues and may directly block antibody binding while maintaining ACE2 binding. See the paper for more information.
experiment.methodText: We synthesized a pooled library of DNA sequences encoding all single amino acid mutations in the Omicron BA.2 RBD and expressed them on the surface of yeast cells. We then incubated the library with a monoclonal antibody known as LY-CoV1404, which targets the RBD of SARS-CoV-2. Next, we used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to select and sequence the variant yeast cells that survived LY-CoV1404 treatment. By comparing the frequency of each mutation in the surviving population versus the starting diversity, we were able to quantify the neutralization effect of each mutation. Importantly, we performed experiments in triplicate and reported robust statistical analysis to validate our results.

experiment.title: Effects on binding of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD
experiment.shortDescription: This experiment measures the effects on binding of variants and individual mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD
experiment.abstractText: The receptor binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein mediates viral attachment to ACE2 receptor, and is a major determinant of host range and a dominant target of neutralizing antibodies. Here we experimentally measure how all amino-acid mutations to the RBD affect expression of folded protein and its affinity for ACE2. Most mutations are deleterious for RBD expression and ACE2 binding, and we identify constrained regions on the RBD's surface that may be desirable targets for vaccines and antibody-based therapeutics. But a substantial number of mutations are well tolerated or even enhance ACE2 binding, including at ACE2 interface residues that vary across SARS-related coronaviruses. However, we find no evidence that these ACE2-affinity enhancing mutations have been selected in current SARS-CoV-2 pandemic isolates. We present an interactive visualization and open analysis pipeline to facilitate use of our dataset for vaccine design and functional annotation of mutations observed during viral surveillance. See the [preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.17.157982v1) for more information.
experiment.methodText:
We constructed duplicate libraries of mutant variants of the SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding domain (RBD), and cloned the library into a yeast surface-display platform. We used FACS-seq assays to determine variant expression and binding scores: 1) We labeled RBD variants for cell surface expression levels (a correlate of folding stability), and/or binding of soluble ACE2 ligand across a range of ACE2 concentrations. 2) We used FACS to partition our library into bins of expression or binding. 3) We sequenced the variants from within each bin. 4) From the distribution of sequence reads across FACS bins, we can reconstruct each variant's mean expression. 5) For binding values, by comparing binding as a function of ACE2 concentration, we calculate binding constants from per-variant titration curves.

We provide our duplicate library measurements at the level of individual variants within our library, which are described by unique molecular identifier barcodes downstream from the variant RBD coding sequence. We also provide decomposed single-mutant scores, which are the primary mutation scores we use in our analysis of the data. In each of these datasets, the binding score is a delta-log<sub>10</sub>(_K_<sub>D,app</sub>) metric from the variant titration curves, and the expression score is a delta-log(mean fluorescence intensity) measurement of cell surface expression. Both metrics are relative to the unmutated SARS-CoV-2 reference sequence phenotype, polarized such that a positive value indicates higher affinity or expression compared to unmutated SARS-CoV-2, and a negative value indicates decreased affinity or expression compared to unmutated SARS-CoV-2.

See the [preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.17.157982v1) or [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jbloomlab/SARS-CoV-2-RBD_DMS) for additional information.

experiment.title: Effects on RBD expression of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1
experiment.shortDescription: This experiment measures the effects on RBD expression of variants in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD Omicron BA.1
experiment.abstractText: The experiment aimed to determine the impact of mutations in the Omicron BA.1 RBD of the SARS-CoV-2 virus on the expression of the RBD on the surface of yeast cells. Deep mutational scanning was used to analyze every possible single amino acid substitution in the Omicron BA.1 RBD, and their subsequent expression was identified. Results showed that the Omicron BA.1 RBD mutants have lower surface expression levels relative to Wuhan-Hu-1, indicating a potential reduction in viral infectivity. The experiment is described in more detail in the paper.
experiment.methodText: The assay method used for this experiment involved the generation of a yeast display library with every possible single amino acid mutation in the Omicron BA.1 RBD. The library was incubated with a C-terminal epitope tag on the surface of the yeast cells, and the RBD mutant library's surface expression level was determined using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) followed by deep sequencing. The effects of mutations on RBD surface expression were analyzed and reported using heatmaps.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep mutational scans for ACE2 binding, RBD expression, and antibody escape in the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 receptor-binding domains.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 continues to acquire mutations in the spike receptor-binding domain (RBD) that impact ACE2 receptor binding, folding stability, and antibody recognition. Deep mutational scanning prospectively characterizes the impacts of mutations on these biochemical properties, enabling rapid assessment of new mutations seen during viral surveillance. However, the effects of mutations can change as the virus evolves, requiring updated deep mutational scans. We determined the impacts of all single amino acid mutations in the Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 RBDs on ACE2-binding affinity, RBD folding, and escape from binding by the LY-CoV1404 (bebtelovimab) monoclonal antibody. In contrast, the Omicron substitution Q493R exhibits no sign of entrenchment, with the derived state, R493, being as unfavorable for ACE2 binding in Omicron RBDs as in Wuhan-Hu-1. Likely for this reason, the R493Q reversion has occurred in Omicron sub-variants including BA.4/BA.5 and BA.2.75, where the affinity buffer from R493Q reversion may potentiate concurrent antigenic change. Consistent with prior studies, we find that Omicron RBDs have reduced expression, and identify candidate stabilizing mutations that ameliorate this deficit. Last, our maps highlight a broadening of the sites of escape from LY-CoV1404 antibody binding in BA.1 and BA.2 compared to the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 background. These BA.1 and BA.2 deep mutational scanning datasets identify shifts in the RBD mutational landscape and inform ongoing efforts in viral surveillance.

title: EGFP N-terminal codon nucleotide scores
shortDescription: Nucleotide scores for the start codon of EGFP and its effect on an N-terminal fusion.

experiment.title: EGFP N-terminal codon
experiment.shortDescription: Mutagenesis of the start codon of EGFP and its effect on an N-terminal fusion.
experiment.abstractText: This is a dataset demonstrating the use of landing pad cell lines to generate recombinant mammalian cells. The experiment measured the effect of mutating the start codon of an EGFP construct with an N-terminal ubiquitin fusion. Once the ubiquitin is removed by cellular DUBs, the protein exposes a new N-terminal amino acid, which may target the protein for degradation.
experiment.methodText: Plasmids with an NNN N-terminal codon were created and introduced into HEK293T cells. Cells were sorted into four equally sized bins based on fluorescence and the genomic DNA containing the NNN codon was sequenced using Illumina amplicon sequencing.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A platform for functional assessment of large variant libraries in mammalian cells.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Sequencing-based, massively parallel genetic assays have revolutionized our ability to quantify the relationship between many genotypes and a phenotype of interest. Unfortunately, variant library expression platforms in mammalian cells are far from ideal, hindering the study of human gene variants in their physiologically relevant cellular contexts. Here, we describe a platform for phenotyping variant libraries in transfectable mammalian cell lines in two steps. First, a landing pad cell line with a genomically integrated, Tet-inducible cassette containing a Bxb1 recombination site is created. Second, a single variant from a library of transfected, promoter-less plasmids is recombined into the landing pad in each cell. Thus, every cell in the recombined pool expresses a single variant, allowing for parallel, sequencing-based assessment of variant effect. We describe a method for incorporating a single landing pad into a defined site of a cell line of interest, and show that our approach can be used generate more than 20 000 recombinant cells in a single experiment. Finally, we use our platform in combination with a sequencing-based assay to explore the N-end rule by simultaneously measuring the effects of all possible N-terminal amino acids on protein expression.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Matreyek KA, et al. A platform for functional assessment of large variant libraries in mammalian cells. Nucleic Acids Res. 2017; 45:e102.

experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for EHEE_rd1_0101.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of EHEE_rd1_0101 protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is EHEE_rd1_0101.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: EHEE_rd1_0101 chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of EHEE_rd1_0101.

experiment.title: EHEE_rd1_0101 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of EHEE_rd1_0101.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of EHEE_rd1_0101 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is EHEE_rd1_0101.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of EHEE_rd4_0044 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is EHEE_rd4_0044.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: ELF3 Pointed domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ELF3 Pointed domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: ELF3 Pointed domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ELF3 Pointed domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Pointed domain in ELF3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P78545_PF02198_50.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Missense variant effect map for human CPOX under mercury exposure
shortDescription: Missense variant effect map for human CPOX via functional complementation in yeast under mercury exposure

experiment.title: Environment-dependent landscapes of coding variant impacts on CPOX
experiment.shortDescription: We systematically assessed CPOX variant functions with and without mercury, which can increase the penetrance of CPOX variants. By combining comprehensive codon mutagenesis with large-scale multiplexed functional assays, we experimentally measured the impacts of nearly all possible CPOX missense variants.
experiment.abstractText: Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP) — caused by variants in coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX) — can be diagnosed via genome sequencing. However, 74% of clinically-reported CPOX missense variants are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) due to lack of evidence. CPOX variant classification is further complicated by environment-dependence: For example, the CPOX variant p.Asn272His (c.814A>C) is classified as benign yet has been associated with HCP-like symptoms in the context of mercury exposure. Here we measured the functional impact of nearly all possible CPOX amino acid substitutions in both the presence and absence of mercury. The resulting CPOX variant effect maps reflect known protein structure and mutational tolerance patterns while also offering new sequence-structure-function insights. Scores from this atlas not only distinguish pathogenic from benign variants but also identify mercury-dependent variant impacts, thus informing our clinical, structural, and functional understanding of CPOX deficiency and illustrating the value of systematic context-dependent multiplexed assays of genetic variant effects.
experiment.methodText: Scores were generated from raw data using the tileseqMut and tileseqMave pipelines. For a variant to be included in the score set, a minimum of 10 reads per variant were necessary in the non-select condition. The scores were scaled to 0 and 1 based on the centered distributions of the nonsense and synonymous scores, respectively. Biological replicate scores were averaged and error calculated using an inverse-variance weighted average of scores, with weights proportional to the combined standard deviation computed from the weighted variances and degrees of freedom. Use of inverse-variance weighted averages provided greater weights for scores with lower uncertainty. For variants with no replicate, the standard error and ‘degrees of freedom’ were taken directly from the existing biological replicate. Score columns include the variant (hgvs_pro), the functional score, standard error of score (se), degrees of freedom (df), log-likelihood ratios of pathogenicity (LLRp), and the conversion of LLRps to ACMG-compatible evidence strengths (evidence_weight). LLRp confidence intervals can be found in the supplemental manuscript files.

title: EP300 Coactivator CBP, KIX domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the EP300 Coactivator CBP, KIX domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: EP300 Coactivator CBP, KIX domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the EP300 Coactivator CBP, KIX domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Coactivator CBP, KIX domain in EP300 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q09472_PF02172_567.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Ephrin type-B receptor 2 SAM domain.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Ephrin type-B receptor 2 SAM domain protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1F0M.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: EPRS1 WHEP-TRS domain domainome 1.0

experiment.title: EPRS1 WHEP-TRS domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the EPRS1 WHEP-TRS domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the WHEP-TRS domain in EPRS1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P07814_PF00458_827.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Biopolymer transport protein ExbD.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Biopolymer transport protein ExbD protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2PFU.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 260 variants that failed validation.

experiment.title: exbD trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Biopolymer transport protein ExbD.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Biopolymer transport protein ExbD protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2PFU.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.shortDescription: Saturation mutagenesis for exonic base effects on splicing, AC-rich RNA-seq enhancer sequence.
experiment.abstractText: Saturation mutagenesis was conducted to determine the role of exonic sequences in splicing of a human RNA transcript. Minigene variants were assayed for splicing in human HEK293 cells. Ten different variant minigenes were tested, each differing by a six-nucleotide sequence at positions 5-10 in the exon. This record describes the sequence for an AC-rich RNA-seq enhancer sequence.
experiment.methodText:
A custom synthesized 60-bp 1760,00 element microarray was purchased from Aligent. Variant minigenes were constructed using primer extension PCR. The microarray wild type clusters were present in a higher number to provide the denominator sufficient for later analysis. The 3’ end of the 60-mer was constant and the remaining 47 nucleotides were specified as wild type or variants of WT-1 exon 5. The full minigene library was constructed by three-fragment overlap extension PCR and transfected into HEK293 cells.

Two independent transfections were performed.
 
Input DNA and reverse-transcribed RNA were amplified and prepared for sequencing. Sequencing was carried out using Illumina with 74 base pair reads.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Saturation mutagenesis reveals manifold determinants of exon definition.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: To illuminate the extent and roles of exonic sequences in the splicing of human RNA transcripts, we conducted saturation mutagenesis of a 51-nt internal exon in a three-exon minigene. All possible single and tandem dinucleotide substitutions were surveyed. Using high-throughput genetics, 5560 minigene molecules were assayed for splicing in human HEK293 cells. Up to 70% of mutations produced substantial (greater than twofold) phenotypes of either increased or decreased splicing. Of all predicted secondary structural elements, only a single 15-nt stem-loop showed a strong correlation with splicing, acting negatively. The in vitro formation of exon-protein complexes between the mutant molecules and proteins associated with spliceosome formation (U2AF35, U2AF65, U1A, and U1-70K) correlated with splicing efficiencies, suggesting exon definition as the step affected by most mutations. The measured relative binding affinities of dozens of human RNA binding protein domains as reported in the CISBP-RNA database were found to correlate either positively or negatively with splicing efficiency, more than could fit on the 51-nt test exon simultaneously. The large number of these functional protein binding correlations point to a dynamic and heterogeneous population of pre-mRNA molecules, each responding to a particular collection of binding proteins.

experiment.title: Exonic splicing for SRSF1 (ASF/SF2) binding site
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation mutagenesis for exonic base effects on splicing, similar to an SRSF1 (ASF/SF2) binding site.
experiment.abstractText: Saturation mutagenesis was conducted to determine the role of exonic sequences in splicing of a human RNA transcript. Minigene variants were assayed for splicing in human HEK293 cells. Ten different variant minigenes were tested, each differing by a six-nucleotide sequence at positions 5-10 in the exon. This record describes a sequence similar to an SRSF1 (ASF/SF2) binding site.
experiment.methodText:
A custom synthesized 60-bp 1760,00 element microarray was purchased from Aligent. Variant minigenes were constructed using primer extension PCR. The microarray wild type clusters were present in a higher number to provide the denominator sufficient for later analysis. The 3’ end of the 60-mer was constant and the remaining 47 nucleotides were specified as wild type or variants of WT-1 exon 5. The full minigene library was constructed by three-fragment overlap extension PCR and transfected into HEK293 cells.

Two independent transfections were performed.
 
Input DNA and reverse-transcribed RNA were amplified and prepared for sequencing. Sequencing was carried out using Illumina with 74 base pair reads.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Saturation mutagenesis reveals manifold determinants of exon definition.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: To illuminate the extent and roles of exonic sequences in the splicing of human RNA transcripts, we conducted saturation mutagenesis of a 51-nt internal exon in a three-exon minigene. All possible single and tandem dinucleotide substitutions were surveyed. Using high-throughput genetics, 5560 minigene molecules were assayed for splicing in human HEK293 cells. Up to 70% of mutations produced substantial (greater than twofold) phenotypes of either increased or decreased splicing. Of all predicted secondary structural elements, only a single 15-nt stem-loop showed a strong correlation with splicing, acting negatively. The in vitro formation of exon-protein complexes between the mutant molecules and proteins associated with spliceosome formation (U2AF35, U2AF65, U1A, and U1-70K) correlated with splicing efficiencies, suggesting exon definition as the step affected by most mutations. The measured relative binding affinities of dozens of human RNA binding protein domains as reported in the CISBP-RNA database were found to correlate either positively or negatively with splicing efficiency, more than could fit on the 51-nt test exon simultaneously. The large number of these functional protein binding correlations point to a dynamic and heterogeneous population of pre-mRNA molecules, each responding to a particular collection of binding proteins.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Ke S, et al. Saturation mutagenesis reveals manifold determinants of exon definition. Saturation mutagenesis reveals manifold determinants of exon definition. 2018; 28:11-24. doi: 10.1101/gr.219683.116

experiment.title: Experimental fitness of TEM-1 β-lactamase
experiment.shortDescription: Experimental fitness of variants in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene in the presence of ampicillin.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment measured the experimental fitness of variants in the TEM-1 $\beta$-lactamase gene in _Escherichia coli_. Fitness measurements were estimated based on growth under increasing concentrations of ampicillin using a band-pass selection system.
experiment.methodText:
The variant library was constructed using PFunkel comprehensive codon mutagenesis. The gene was mutagenized and assayed as three sub-region (codons 1-96, 97-192, and 193-287). One NNN-containing mutagenic primer was used per codon. Library construction is described in detail in (Firnberg and Ostermeier, 2012), where the library used in these experiments is referred to as "CCM-2."

The band-pass selection system is described in (Sohka et al., 2009). Briefly, cells are plated on media containing Tet and a variable concentration of Amp. If TEM-1 activity is too low for the Amp concentration, cells will not proliferate. If TEM-1 activity is too high, no cell wall damage will occur and TetC (which confers Tet resistance) will not be produced. Therefore cells should only grow if the TEM-1 variant's activity level matches the Amp concentration.

Sequencing was performed using 454 GS-FLX.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The current paradigm for tuning synthetic biological systems is through re-engineering system components. Biological systems designed with the inherent ability to be tuned by external stimuli will be more versatile. We engineered Escherichia coli cells to behave as an externally tunable band-pass filter for enzyme activity and small molecules. The band's location can be positioned within a range of 4 orders of magnitude simply by the addition of compounds to the growth medium. Inclusion in the genetic network of an enzyme-substrate pair that functions as an attenuator is a generalizable strategy that enables this tunability. The genetic circuit enabled bacteria growth to be patterned in response to chemical gradients in nonintuitive ways and facilitated the isolation of engineered allosteric enzymes. The application of this strategy to other biological systems will increase their utility for biotechnological applications and their usefulness as a tool for gaining insight into nature's underlying design principles.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.publicationJournal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Sohka T, et al. An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2009; 106:10135-40.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: We introduce PFunkel, a versatile method for extensive, researcher-defined DNA mutagenesis using a ssDNA or dsDNA template. Once the template DNA is prepared, the method can be completed in a single day in a single tube, and requires no intermediate DNA purification or sub-cloning. PFunkel can be used for site-directed mutagenesis at an efficiency approaching 100%. More importantly, PFunkel allows researchers the unparalleled ability to efficiently construct user-defined libraries. We demonstrate the creation of a library with site-saturation at four distal sites simultaneously at 70% efficiency. We also employ PFunkel to create a comprehensive codon mutagenesis library of the TEM-1 ß-lactamase gene. We designed this library to contain 18,081 members, one for each possible codon substitution in the gene (287 positions in TEM-1 x 63 possible codon substitutions). Deep sequencing revealed that ∼97% of the designed single codon substitutions are present in the library. From such a library we identified 18 previously unreported adaptive mutations that each confer resistance to the ß-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam. Three of these mutations confer resistance equal to or higher than that of the most resistant reported TEM-1 allele and have the potential to emerge clinically.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E and Ostermeier M. PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis. PloS one. 2012; 7:e52031.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Mutations are central to evolution, providing the genetic variation upon which selection acts. A mutation's effect on the suitability of a gene to perform a particular function (gene fitness) can be positive, negative, or neutral. Knowledge of the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of mutations is fundamental for understanding evolutionary dynamics, molecular-level genetic variation, complex genetic disease, the accumulation of deleterious mutations, and the molecular clock. We present comprehensive DFEs for point and codon mutants of the Escherichia coli TEM-1 β-lactamase gene and missense mutations in the TEM-1 protein. These DFEs provide insight into the inherent benefits of the genetic code's architecture, support for the hypothesis that mRNA stability dictates codon usage at the beginning of genes, an extensive framework for understanding protein mutational tolerance, and evidence that mutational effects on protein thermodynamic stability shape the DFE. Contrary to prevailing expectations, we find that deleterious effects of mutation primarily arise from a decrease in specific protein activity and not cellular protein levels.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E, et al. A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape. Molecular biology and evolution. 2014; 31:1581-92.

experiment.shortDescription: Experimental fitness of variants in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene in the presence of ampicillin.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment measured the experimental fitness of variants in the TEM-1 $\beta$-lactamase gene in _Escherichia coli_. Fitness measurements were estimated based on growth under increasing concentrations of ampicillin using a band-pass selection system.
experiment.methodText:
The variant library was constructed using PFunkel comprehensive codon mutagenesis. The gene was mutagenized and assayed as three sub-region (codons 1-96, 97-192, and 193-287). One NNN-containing mutagenic primer was used per codon. Library construction is described in detail in (Firnberg and Ostermeier, 2012), where the library used in these experiments is referred to as "CCM-2."

The band-pass selection system is described in (Sohka et al., 2009). Briefly, cells are plated on media containing Tet and a variable concentration of Amp. If TEM-1 activity is too low for the Amp concentration, cells will not proliferate. If TEM-1 activity is too high, no cell wall damage will occur and TetC (which confers Tet resistance) will not be produced. Therefore cells should only grow if the TEM-1 variant's activity level matches the Amp concentration.

Sequencing was performed using 454 GS-FLX.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The current paradigm for tuning synthetic biological systems is through re-engineering system components. Biological systems designed with the inherent ability to be tuned by external stimuli will be more versatile. We engineered Escherichia coli cells to behave as an externally tunable band-pass filter for enzyme activity and small molecules. The band's location can be positioned within a range of 4 orders of magnitude simply by the addition of compounds to the growth medium. Inclusion in the genetic network of an enzyme-substrate pair that functions as an attenuator is a generalizable strategy that enables this tunability. The genetic circuit enabled bacteria growth to be patterned in response to chemical gradients in nonintuitive ways and facilitated the isolation of engineered allosteric enzymes. The application of this strategy to other biological systems will increase their utility for biotechnological applications and their usefulness as a tool for gaining insight into nature's underlying design principles.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.publicationJournal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Sohka T, et al. An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2009; 106:10135-40.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: We introduce PFunkel, a versatile method for extensive, researcher-defined DNA mutagenesis using a ssDNA or dsDNA template. Once the template DNA is prepared, the method can be completed in a single day in a single tube, and requires no intermediate DNA purification or sub-cloning. PFunkel can be used for site-directed mutagenesis at an efficiency approaching 100%. More importantly, PFunkel allows researchers the unparalleled ability to efficiently construct user-defined libraries. We demonstrate the creation of a library with site-saturation at four distal sites simultaneously at 70% efficiency. We also employ PFunkel to create a comprehensive codon mutagenesis library of the TEM-1 ß-lactamase gene. We designed this library to contain 18,081 members, one for each possible codon substitution in the gene (287 positions in TEM-1 x 63 possible codon substitutions). Deep sequencing revealed that ∼97% of the designed single codon substitutions are present in the library. From such a library we identified 18 previously unreported adaptive mutations that each confer resistance to the ß-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam. Three of these mutations confer resistance equal to or higher than that of the most resistant reported TEM-1 allele and have the potential to emerge clinically.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E and Ostermeier M. PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis. PloS one. 2012; 7:e52031.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Mutations are central to evolution, providing the genetic variation upon which selection acts. A mutation's effect on the suitability of a gene to perform a particular function (gene fitness) can be positive, negative, or neutral. Knowledge of the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of mutations is fundamental for understanding evolutionary dynamics, molecular-level genetic variation, complex genetic disease, the accumulation of deleterious mutations, and the molecular clock. We present comprehensive DFEs for point and codon mutants of the Escherichia coli TEM-1 β-lactamase gene and missense mutations in the TEM-1 protein. These DFEs provide insight into the inherent benefits of the genetic code's architecture, support for the hypothesis that mRNA stability dictates codon usage at the beginning of genes, an extensive framework for understanding protein mutational tolerance, and evidence that mutational effects on protein thermodynamic stability shape the DFE. Contrary to prevailing expectations, we find that deleterious effects of mutation primarily arise from a decrease in specific protein activity and not cellular protein levels.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E, et al. A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape. Molecular biology and evolution. 2014; 31:1581-92.

experiment.title: F9 MultiSTEP F9 Gla domain
experiment.shortDescription: MultiSTEP assay for coagulation factor IX (F9) surface expression using a carboxylation-sensitive antibody to the F9 Gla domain.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment describes results from Multiplexed Surface Tethering of Extracellular Proteins (MultiSTEP), a method for assaying secreted proteins via human cell surface display. In this experiment, MultiSTEP was applied to coagulation factor IX (F9). The antibody used in this experiment targeted the γ-carboxylated F9 Gla domain.
experiment.methodText: The assay was performed in Freestyle 293-F cells with an engineered landing pad. Each variant protein included a 10 amino acid linker, a strep II protein tag, another 10-amino acid linker, and a single-pass transmembrane domain of CD28. Libraries were ordered from TWIST in three partially overlapping tiles. Barcodes were added to the full-length sequences and sequenced with PacBio to resolve the barcode-variant associations. After antibody staining, cells were FACS sorted and barcodes in each bin were sequenced using Illumina NextSeq.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Multiplex, multimodal mapping of variant effects in secreted proteins.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Despite widespread advances in DNA sequencing, the functional consequences of most genetic variants remain poorly understood. Multiplexed Assays of Variant Effect (MAVEs) can measure the function of variants at scale, and are beginning to address this problem. However, MAVEs cannot readily be applied to the ~10% of human genes encoding secreted proteins. We developed a flexible, scalable human cell surface display method, Multiplexed Surface Tethering of Extracellular Proteins (MultiSTEP), to measure secreted protein variant effects. We used MultiSTEP to study the consequences of missense variation in coagulation factor IX (FIX), a serine protease where genetic variation can cause hemophilia B. We combined MultiSTEP with a panel of antibodies to detect FIX secretion and post-translational modification, measuring a total of 44,816 effects for 436 synonymous variants and 8,528 of the 8,759 possible missense variants. 49.6% of possible F9 missense variants impacted secretion, post-translational modification, or both. We also identified functional constraints on secretion within the signal peptide and for nearly all variants that caused gain or loss of cysteine. Secretion scores correlated strongly with FIX levels in hemophilia B and revealed that loss of secretion variants are particularly likely to cause severe disease. Integration of the secretion and post-translational modification scores enabled reclassification of 63.1% of F9 variants of uncertain significance in the My Life, Our Future hemophilia genotyping project. Lastly, we showed that MultiSTEP can be applied to a wide variety of secreted proteins. Thus, MultiSTEP is a multiplexed, multimodal, and generalizable method for systematically assessing variant effects in secreted proteins at scale.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Popp NA, et al. Multiplex, multimodal mapping of variant effects in secreted proteins. bioRxiv. 2025; (Unknown volume):(Unknown pages). 10.1101/2024.04.01.587474

title: F9 predictor scores
shortDescription: Predictor trained on MultiSTEP assays for coagulation factor IX (F9)

experiment.title: F9 predictor scores
experiment.shortDescription: Predictor trained on MultiSTEP assays for coagulation factor IX (F9)
experiment.abstractText: A variant library was introduced into Freestyle 293-F suspension cells equipped with a landing pad, with F9 tethered to the cell surface (C terminus fused to CD28 type I transmembrane domain with a flexible linker). Multiple antibody-based assays were performed to assess different aspects of F9 expression and modification: antibodies specific for F9 gamma-carboxylation and gla motif gamma-carboxylation were used to evaluate this post-translational modification, while antibodies against the heavy chain, light chain, and strep 2 tag of F9 were employed to indirectly assess F9 secretion. The results from these complementary assays were subsequently used to train a Random Forest Classifier.
experiment.methodText: The results of five complementary MultiSTEP assays were used to train a Random Forest Classifier.
