title: rplI (K12M) chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of 50S ribosomal protein L9 (K12M).

experiment.title: rplI (K12M) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of 50S ribosomal protein L9 (K12M).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of 50S ribosomal protein L9 (K12M) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2HBB.pdb_K12M.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: RSL24D1 Ribosomal protein L24e-related domainome 1.0

experiment.title: RSL24D1 Ribosomal protein L24e-related from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the RSL24D1 Ribosomal protein L24e-related from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Ribosomal protein L24e-related in RSL24D1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9UHA3_PF01246_2.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

The identifier used in the original study is P02633_PF01023_1.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Saturation Genome Editing of BARD1 scores
shortDescription: We used saturation genome editing to measure the effect of 9,128 BARD1 SNVs and 2,048 3-base pair deletions on BARD1-dependent HAP1 cell survival

experiment.title: Saturation Genome Editing of BARD1
experiment.shortDescription: We used saturation genome editing to measure the effect of 9,128 BARD1 SNVs and 2,048 3-base pair deletions on BARD1-dependent HAP1 cell survival.
experiment.abstractText: Systematic interrogation of the functional consequences of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) is critical to interpretation of clinical genetic testing. While some loss-of-function (LoF) mutations in the tumor suppressor BARD1 are linked to increased risk of inherited breast cancers, the overwhelming majority of variants in BARD1 have unknown impact. We applied Saturation Genome Editing (SGE) to assess 9,128 SNVs and 2,048 in-frame deletions for their effect of cell survival and RNA expression. We find that 13% of missense variants are LoF. SGE scores are highly concordant with ClinVar annotations, and LoF variants are significantly enriched in breast cancer cohorts. BARD1 SGE scores provide strong evidence for variant classification. We link SGE scores to BARD1 protein structure to link specific functions to BRCA1/BARD1 tumor suppression. Together, these results elucidate the clinical picture of BARD1 variation at both nucleotide and protein levels.
experiment.methodText: Functional scores for 9,128 SNVs and 2,048 3-bp deletions were calculated by applying a negative binomial regression model to variant counts across all sampled time points and replicates. Variants near 0 represent no change, loss of function variants have progressively more negative scores.

experiment.title: Saturation genome editing of PALB2 exon 10 in haploid HAP1 cells
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation genome editing of PALB2 exon 10 in haploid HAP1 cells using cell survival as a readout, performed to validate the cDNA-based PARPi screen results.
experiment.abstractText: Loss-of-function variants in PALB2 give rise to defects in DNA damage repair by homologous recombination (HR), increasing the risk of breast cancer in female carriers. However, genetic testing frequently reveals missense variants of uncertain significance (VUS) for which the impact on protein function and cancer risk are unclear. Here we assay 84% of all possible missense variants in 11 out of 13 PALB2 exons using site-saturation functional screens with PARP inhibitor sensitivity as a readout for HR. These exons encode the coiled-coil and WD40 domains, which we identify as the minimal regions required for HR. Furthermore, we reveal the functional impact of 6718 missense variants, classifying 3904 variants as functional (58%), 2422 as intermediate (36%), and 392 as damaging (6%). A burden-type analysis shows that damaging missense variants in PALB2 are associated with a significantly increased risk of breast cancer, similar to that observed for truncating variants. These results will be valuable for the classification of PALB2 missense VUS and clinical management of carriers.
experiment.methodText: SGE was used to introduce all unique SNVs in the PALB2 exon 10 region (p.G1000 to p.I1037 of the WD40 domain) in haploid HAP1 cells. Cells were co-transfected with variant library and Cas9/sgRNA using Turbofectin 8.0 (Origene). Cells were selected in puromycin (1 µg/ml) for 3 days. Cells were harvested at day 5 (24 hrs after puromycin selection) and day 20 post-transfection, and genomic DNA was extracted. The target region was amplified by PCR to add barcodes for multiplexing and PCR products were sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq.

experiment.title: Saturation Genome Editing of SBDS
experiment.shortDescription: We used saturation genome editing to measure the effect of 2,675 SBDS SNVs and 640 3-base pair deletions on SBDS-dependent HAP1 cell survival.
experiment.abstractText: Genetic variants in the SBDS gene are associated with the rare inherited disease Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome (SDS). Many variants that cause rare diseases like SDS are single nucleotide variants (SNVs) with uncertain pathogenicity. Such variants of uncertain significance (VUS) are problematic in the clinic because they cannot inform diagnoses and interventions. Functional data can provide evidence for classifying variants as pathogenic or benign. Saturation Genome Editing (SGE) was applied to assess the functional impact of all possible missense variants and trinucleotide deletions of SBDS to generate evidence on their pathogenicity to improve information available to clinicians and patients. SGE on all 5 exons of SBDS generated a total of 3,315 variant scores. We identify 93.3% of stop gain variants (111 of 119) and 87.5% of splice site variants (63 of 72) as functionally abnormal. Of 1,580 missense variants, 146 (9.24%) score as loss-of-function, 1,423 (90.1%) as functionally normal, and 11 (0.70%) as indeterminate. SGE scores are highly concordant with ClinVar annotations, where 79.2% of assayed clinically known pathogenic variants (19 of 24) correctly score as functionally abnormal and all 91 known benign variants correctly score as functionally normal. Taken together, these suggest that SGE is an effective assay for SBDS.

experiment.title: Saturation Genome Editing of VHL in HAP1 cells
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation Genome Editing was performed to assess effects of VHL SNVs on growth in HAP1 cells.
experiment.abstractText:
Reproduced from Buckley et al. 2023, bioRxiv:

To maximize the impact of precision medicine approaches, it is critical to accurately identify genetic variants in cancer-associated genes with functional consequences. Yet, our knowledge of rare variants conferring clinically relevant phenotypes and the mechanisms through which they act remains highly limited. A tumor suppressor gene exemplifying the challenge of variant interpretation is VHL. VHL encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates the cellular response to hypoxia. Germline pathogenic variants in VHL predispose patients to tumors including clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and pheochromocytoma, and somatic VHL mutations are frequently observed in sporadic renal cancer. Here, we optimize and apply Saturation Genome Editing (SGE) to assay nearly all possible single nucleotide variants (SNVs) across VHL’s coding sequence. To delineate mechanisms, we quantify mRNA dosage effects over time and compare effects in isogenic cell lines. Function scores for 2,268 VHL SNVs identify a core set of pathogenic alleles driving ccRCC with perfect accuracy, inform differential risk across tumor types, and reveal novel mechanisms by which variants impact function. These results have immediate utility for classifying VHL variants encountered in both germline testing and tumor profiling and illustrate how precise functional measurements can resolve pleiotropic and dosage-dependent genotype-phenotype relationships across complete genes.
experiment.methodText: SGE was performed in HAP1 cell to measure SNV effects on cell growth due and VHL transcript levels. Seven libraries spanning the three coding exons of VHL and one intronic region were generated and assayed in parallel. Variants frequencies over time were quantified via direct sequencing of gDNA and cDNA. Function scores for each variant were calculated as the normalized log2-ratio of day 20 frequency over day 6 frequency. RNA scores were calculated as the log2-ratio of each coding variant in cDNA over gDNA (sampled from the same time point). Final function scores and RNA scores were generated by averaging across two independent transfection replicates.

experiment.title: Saturation genome essentiality screen of DDX3X in HAP1 cells
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation genome essentiality screen of DDX3X in HAP1 cells (log fold change at day 15)
experiment.abstractText: Loss-of-function of _DDX3X_ is a leading cause of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) in females. _DDX3X_ is also a somatically mutated cancer driver gene proposed to have tumour promoting and suppressing effects. We perform saturation genome editing of _DDX3X_, testing in vitro the functional impact of 12,776 nucleotide variants. We identify 3432 functionally abnormal variants, in three distinct classes. We train a machine learning classifier to identify functionally abnormal variants of NDD-relevance. This classifier has at least 97% sensitivity and 99% specificity to detect variants pathogenic for NDD, substantially out-performing in silico predictors, and resolving up to 93% of variants of uncertain significance. Moreover, functionally-abnormal variants can account for almost all of the excess nonsynonymous _DDX3X_ somatic mutations seen in _DDX3X_-driven cancers. Systematic maps of variant effects generated in experimentally tractable cell types have the potential to transform clinical interpretation of both germline and somatic disease-associated variation.
experiment.methodText: This study uses saturation genome editing (SGE) based essentiality screen to determine _DDX3X_ function.  HAP1 cells were transfected with sgRNA and HDR template library plasmids, followed by puromycin selection for two days. Cell pellets were harvested at several time points (Days 4, 7, 11, 15, and 21). Genomic DNA was extracted from these samples and direct sequencing was used to determine the variant frequency at each time point.

experiment.title: Saturation mutagenesis MPRA of BCL11A enhancer
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation mutagenesis MPRA of BCL11A enhancer in HEL 92.1.7 cells.
experiment.abstractText:
This study performed saturation mutagenesis on disease-associated enhancer and promoter regions and measured the effect of each mutation using massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA). The data describe potentially pathogenic mutations as well as the density of putative functional bases in each of the regulatory elements.

As described by <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/505362v1>
experiment.methodText:
Sequences containing mutations were generated using error-prone PCR. Each library contained 50,000-2,000,000 constructs per target, which included nearly all possible single nucleotide changes as well as many single base pair deletions. Variants were tagged with 15 or 20 base pair barcodes 3' of the target region. Promoters were inserted into pGL4.11 vectors and enhancers were inserted into pGL4.23 enhancers such that they would drive expression of the luciferase reporter gene. RNA barcodes were counted using targeted RT-PCR and Illumina sequencing, and DNA barcodes were counted using targeted PCR and Illumina sequencing. Long variant sequences were associate with barcodes using subassembly.

As described by <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/505362v1>

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Saturation mutagenesis of twenty disease-associated regulatory elements at single base-pair resolution.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The majority of common variants associated with common diseases, as well as an unknown proportion of causal mutations for rare diseases, fall in noncoding regions of the genome. Although catalogs of noncoding regulatory elements are steadily improving, we have a limited understanding of the functional effects of mutations within them. Here, we perform saturation mutagenesis in conjunction with massively parallel reporter assays on 20 disease-associated gene promoters and enhancers, generating functional measurements for over 30,000 single nucleotide substitutions and deletions. We find that the density of putative transcription factor binding sites varies widely between regulatory elements, as does the extent to which evolutionary conservation or integrative scores predict functional effects. These data provide a powerful resource for interpreting the pathogenicity of clinically observed mutations in these disease-associated regulatory elements, and comprise a rich dataset for the further development of algorithms that aim to predict the regulatory effects of noncoding mutations.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Kircher M, et al. Saturation mutagenesis of twenty disease-associated regulatory elements at single base-pair resolution. Nat Commun. 2019; 10:3583.

experiment.title: Saturation mutagenesis MPRA of F9 promoter
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation mutagenesis MPRA of F9 promoter in HepG2 cells.
experiment.abstractText:
This study performed saturation mutagenesis on disease-associated enhancer and promoter regions and measured the effect of each mutation using massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA). The data describe potentially pathogenic mutations as well as the density of putative functional bases in each of the regulatory elements.

As described by <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/505362v1>
experiment.methodText:
Sequences containing mutations were generated using error-prone PCR. Each library contained 50,000-2,000,000 constructs per target, which included nearly all possible single nucleotide changes as well as many single base pair deletions. Variants were tagged with 15 or 20 base pair barcodes 3' of the target region. Promoters were inserted into pGL4.11 vectors and enhancers were inserted into pGL4.23 enhancers such that they would drive expression of the luciferase reporter gene. RNA barcodes were counted using targeted RT-PCR and Illumina sequencing, and DNA barcodes were counted using targeted PCR and Illumina sequencing. Long variant sequences were associate with barcodes using subassembly.

As described by <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/505362v1>

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Saturation mutagenesis of twenty disease-associated regulatory elements at single base-pair resolution.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The majority of common variants associated with common diseases, as well as an unknown proportion of causal mutations for rare diseases, fall in noncoding regions of the genome. Although catalogs of noncoding regulatory elements are steadily improving, we have a limited understanding of the functional effects of mutations within them. Here, we perform saturation mutagenesis in conjunction with massively parallel reporter assays on 20 disease-associated gene promoters and enhancers, generating functional measurements for over 30,000 single nucleotide substitutions and deletions. We find that the density of putative transcription factor binding sites varies widely between regulatory elements, as does the extent to which evolutionary conservation or integrative scores predict functional effects. These data provide a powerful resource for interpreting the pathogenicity of clinically observed mutations in these disease-associated regulatory elements, and comprise a rich dataset for the further development of algorithms that aim to predict the regulatory effects of noncoding mutations.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Kircher M, et al. Saturation mutagenesis of twenty disease-associated regulatory elements at single base-pair resolution. Nat Commun. 2019; 10:3583.

This study performed saturation mutagenesis on disease-associated enhancer and promoter regions and measured the effect of each mutation using massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA). The data describe potentially pathogenic mutations as well as the density of putative functional bases in each of the regulatory elements.

As described by <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/505362v1>
experiment.methodText:
Sequences containing mutations were generated using error-prone PCR. Each library contained 50,000-2,000,000 constructs per target, which included nearly all possible single nucleotide changes as well as many single base pair deletions. Variants were tagged with 15 or 20 base pair barcodes 3' of the target region. Promoters were inserted into pGL4.11 vectors and enhancers were inserted into pGL4.23 enhancers such that they would drive expression of the luciferase reporter gene. RNA barcodes were counted using targeted RT-PCR and Illumina sequencing, and DNA barcodes were counted using targeted PCR and Illumina sequencing. Long variant sequences were associate with barcodes using subassembly.

As described by <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/505362v1>

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Saturation mutagenesis of twenty disease-associated regulatory elements at single base-pair resolution.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The majority of common variants associated with common diseases, as well as an unknown proportion of causal mutations for rare diseases, fall in noncoding regions of the genome. Although catalogs of noncoding regulatory elements are steadily improving, we have a limited understanding of the functional effects of mutations within them. Here, we perform saturation mutagenesis in conjunction with massively parallel reporter assays on 20 disease-associated gene promoters and enhancers, generating functional measurements for over 30,000 single nucleotide substitutions and deletions. We find that the density of putative transcription factor binding sites varies widely between regulatory elements, as does the extent to which evolutionary conservation or integrative scores predict functional effects. These data provide a powerful resource for interpreting the pathogenicity of clinically observed mutations in these disease-associated regulatory elements, and comprise a rich dataset for the further development of algorithms that aim to predict the regulatory effects of noncoding mutations.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Kircher M, et al. Saturation mutagenesis of twenty disease-associated regulatory elements at single base-pair resolution. Nat Commun. 2019; 10:3583.

experiment.title: Saturation mutagenesis of FGFR kinase domains in MCF10A and NCI-H1581 cells
experiment.shortDescription: High-throughput overexpression screen of saturation mutagenesis libraries covering the kinase domain of FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3 und FGFR4, resulting in a comprehensive catalogue for FGFR drug sensitivity and resistance.
experiment.abstractText:
Variants of unknown significance represent one of the biggest challenges for genomics-based precision oncology. High throughput functional genomics is thus essential to characterize the vast number of cancer mutations and tailor the most promising treatment accordingly.
Aberrantly activated fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) frequently drive tumorigenesis with a variety of genetic aberrations across a wide range of tumor entities. Approved selective inhibitors (FGFRis) are available. However, it remains largely unknown which of the many different point mutations affecting FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3 or FGFR4 are druggable, i.e. activating FGFR signaling while not mediating FGFRi resistance thereby substantially limiting the therapeutic potential of approved FGFRis.
Here, we implemented a saturation mutational scanning platform to screen all 11520 possible point mutations covering the kinase domains of FGFR1-4. In pooled positive selection screens, we identified 474 activating mutations and 738 resistance-mediating mutations to the FGFR inhibitors pemigatinib and/or futibatinib - with many clustered in particular structural elements. Combining these comprehensive datasets revealed 301 druggable FGFR point mutations analogous to a strong PS3/BS3 evidence level. Notably, mutations in the same codon or the corresponding mutations in different FGFRs could strongly differ in their impact, thus underlining the necessity for a saturation approach to study each mutation individually. The screens also identified loss-of-function mutations and FGFR2-specific activating nonsense mutations. Importantly, the functional screens identified 97% of acquired resistance mutations in a clinical trial.
In summary, we provide a comprehensive and clinically highly relevant catalog of every single druggable point mutations in the FGFR kinase domains which is readily available for clinical decision support to select the optimal cancer therapy and to push the boundaries of approved inhibitor applications.
experiment.methodText:
Design of a saturation mutagenesis overexpression library covering the kinase domain of FGFR1-4. Due to the size limitations for pooled oligo libraries (oPools with a maximum length of 300 nt, TWIST Bioscience), we divided each kinase domain into four pools, each covering 80 amino acids, resulting in 16 independent libraries for FGFR1-4. oPools with a total of 720 sequences per library, covering every possible substitution mutation at the nucleotide in the respective sequence, were designed and ordered. The libraries were cloned into lentiviral backbones and lentiviruses were produced. Plasmid libraries were analyzed for coverage using NGS and later used for normalization.
For activation, a positive selection screen was established in which MCF10A cells were infected with lentiviruses with an MOI < 0.3 and the transduced cells were then incubated for 2–3 weeks with medium lacking growth factors. For resistance, a second positive selection screen was established using the FGFR inhibitor-sensitive lung cancer cell line NCI-H1581. The cells were infected with lentiviruses at a MOI < 0.3 and the transduced cells were incubated in the presence of a FGFR inhibitor (pemigatinib or futibatinib) for 1–2 weeks. In both assays, the cells were harvested at the end of the experiment and the gDNA was extracted.
The target region (region in the overexpressed FGFR cds that contains the mutations) was amplified and labeled with Illumina adapters. NGS analysis was performed using the Illumina MiSeq platform and paired-end sequencing with a read length of 210 nt. All samples were sequenced with a coverage of at least 300 reads per point mutation in the reference library.
For the plasmid libraries, we sequenced 3 independent technical replicates. For the resistance screenings, 3 independent biological replicates were performed and for the activation screenings, 4 independent biological replicates were performed.

experiment.title: Saturation mutagenesis of FGFR kinase domains in MCF10A and NCI-H1581 cells
experiment.shortDescription: High-throughput overexpression screen of saturation mutagenesis libraries covering the kinase domain of FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3 und FGFR4, resulting in a comprehensive catalogue for FGFR drug sensitivity and resistance.
experiment.abstractText:
Variants of unknown significance represent one of the biggest challenges for genomics-based precision oncology. High throughput functional genomics is thus essential to characterize the vast number of cancer mutations and tailor the most promising treatment accordingly.
Aberrantly activated fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) frequently drive tumorigenesis with a variety of genetic aberrations across a wide range of tumor entities. Approved selective inhibitors (FGFRis) are available. However, it remains largely unknown which of the many different point mutations affecting FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3 or FGFR4 are druggable, i.e. activating FGFR signaling while not mediating FGFRi resistance thereby substantially limiting the therapeutic potential of approved FGFRis.
Here, we implemented a saturation mutational scanning platform to screen all 11520 possible point mutations covering the kinase domains of FGFR1-4. In pooled positive selection screens, we identified 474 activating mutations and 738 resistance-mediating mutations to the FGFR inhibitors pemigatinib and/or futibatinib - with many clustered in particular structural elements. Combining these comprehensive datasets revealed 301 druggable FGFR point mutations analogous to a strong PS3/BS3 evidence level. Notably, mutations in the same codon or the corresponding mutations in different FGFRs could strongly differ in their impact, thus underlining the necessity for a saturation approach to study each mutation individually. The screens also identified loss-of-function mutations and FGFR2-specific activating nonsense mutations. Importantly, the functional screens identified 97% of acquired resistance mutations in a clinical trial.
In summary, we provide a comprehensive and clinically highly relevant catalog of every single druggable point mutations in the FGFR kinase domains which is readily available for clinical decision support to select the optimal cancer therapy and to push the boundaries of approved inhibitor applications.
experiment.methodText:
Design of a saturation mutagenesis overexpression library covering the kinase domain of FGFR1-4. Due to the size limitations for pooled oligo libraries (oPools with a maximum length of 300 nt, TWIST Bioscience), we divided each kinase domain into four pools, each covering 80 amino acids, resulting in 16 independent libraries for FGFR1-4. oPools with a total of 720 sequences per library, covering every possible substitution mutation at the nucleotide in the respective sequence, were designed and ordered. The libraries were cloned into lentiviral backbones and lentiviruses were produced. Plasmid libraries were analyzed for coverage using NGS and later used for normalization.
For activation, a positive selection screen was established in which MCF10A cells were infected with lentiviruses with an MOI < 0.3 and the transduced cells were then incubated for 2–3 weeks with medium lacking growth factors. For resistance, a second positive selection screen was established using the FGFR inhibitor-sensitive lung cancer cell line NCI-H1581. The cells were infected with lentiviruses at a MOI < 0.3 and the transduced cells were incubated in the presence of a FGFR inhibitor (pemigatinib or futibatinib) for 1–2 weeks. In both assays, the cells were harvested at the end of the experiment and the gDNA was extracted.
The target region (region in the overexpressed FGFR cds that contains the mutations) was amplified and labeled with Illumina adapters. NGS analysis was performed using the Illumina MiSeq platform and paired-end sequencing with a read length of 210 nt. All samples were sequenced with a coverage of at least 300 reads per point mutation in the reference library.
For the plasmid libraries, we sequenced 3 independent technical replicates. For the resistance screenings, 3 independent biological replicates were performed and for the activation screenings, 4 independent biological replicates were performed.

Due to the size limitations for pooled oligo libraries (oPools with a maximum length of 300 nt, TWIST Bioscience), we divided each kinase domain into four pools, each covering 80 amino acids, resulting in 16 independent libraries for FGFR1-4. oPools with a total of 720 sequences per library, covering every possible substitution mutation at the nucleotide in the respective sequence, were designed and ordered. The libraries were cloned into lentiviral backbones and lentiviruses were produced. Plasmid libraries were analyzed for coverage using NGS and later used for normalization.
For activation, a positive selection screen was established in which MCF10A cells were infected with lentiviruses with an MOI < 0.3 and the transduced cells were then incubated for 2–3 weeks with medium lacking growth factors. For resistance, a second positive selection screen was established using the FGFR inhibitor-sensitive lung cancer cell line NCI-H1581. The cells were infected with lentiviruses at a MOI < 0.3 and the transduced cells were incubated in the presence of a FGFR inhibitor (pemigatinib or futibatinib) for 1–2 weeks. In both assays, the cells were harvested at the end of the experiment and the gDNA was extracted.
The target region (region in the overexpressed FGFR cds that contains the mutations) was amplified and labeled with Illumina adapters. NGS analysis was performed using the Illumina MiSeq platform and paired-end sequencing with a read length of 210 nt. All samples were sequenced with a coverage of at least 300 reads per point mutation in the reference library.
For the plasmid libraries, we sequenced 3 independent technical replicates. For the resistance screenings, 3 independent biological replicates were performed and for the activation screenings, 4 independent biological replicates were performed.

experiment.title: Saturation mutagenesis of FGFR kinase domains in MCF10A and NCI-H1581 cells
experiment.shortDescription: High-throughput overexpression screen of saturation mutagenesis libraries covering the kinase domain of FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3 und FGFR4, resulting in a comprehensive catalogue for FGFR drug sensitivity and resistance.
experiment.abstractText:
Variants of unknown significance represent one of the biggest challenges for genomics-based precision oncology. High throughput functional genomics is thus essential to characterize the vast number of cancer mutations and tailor the most promising treatment accordingly.
Aberrantly activated fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) frequently drive tumorigenesis with a variety of genetic aberrations across a wide range of tumor entities. Approved selective inhibitors (FGFRis) are available. However, it remains largely unknown which of the many different point mutations affecting FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3 or FGFR4 are druggable, i.e. activating FGFR signaling while not mediating FGFRi resistance thereby substantially limiting the therapeutic potential of approved FGFRis.
Here, we implemented a saturation mutational scanning platform to screen all 11520 possible point mutations covering the kinase domains of FGFR1-4. In pooled positive selection screens, we identified 474 activating mutations and 738 resistance-mediating mutations to the FGFR inhibitors pemigatinib and/or futibatinib - with many clustered in particular structural elements. Combining these comprehensive datasets revealed 301 druggable FGFR point mutations analogous to a strong PS3/BS3 evidence level. Notably, mutations in the same codon or the corresponding mutations in different FGFRs could strongly differ in their impact, thus underlining the necessity for a saturation approach to study each mutation individually. The screens also identified loss-of-function mutations and FGFR2-specific activating nonsense mutations. Importantly, the functional screens identified 97% of acquired resistance mutations in a clinical trial.
In summary, we provide a comprehensive and clinically highly relevant catalog of every single druggable point mutations in the FGFR kinase domains which is readily available for clinical decision support to select the optimal cancer therapy and to push the boundaries of approved inhibitor applications.

title: Scores from saturation prime editing essentiality screen of BRCA2 in locally haploidized HEK293T cells
shortDescription: Saturation prime editing essentiality screen of BRCA2 in locally haploidized HEK293T cells

experiment.title: Saturation prime editing essentiality screen of BRCA2 in locally haploidized HEK293T cells
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation prime editing essentiality screen of BRCA2 in locally haploidized HEK293T cells
experiment.abstractText: High-throughput functional characterization of genetic variants in their endogenous locus has so far been possible only with methods that rely on homology-directed repair, which are limited by low editing efficiencies. Here, we adapted CRISPR prime editing for high-throughput variant classification and combined it with a strategy that allows for haploidization of any locus, which simplifies variant interpretation. We demonstrate the utility of saturation prime editing (SPE) by applying it to the NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 1 gene (_NPC1_), mutations in which cause the lysosomal storage disorder Niemann-Pick disease type C. Our data suggest that _NPC1_ is very sensitive to genetic perturbation, with 410 of 706 assayed missense mutations being classified as deleterious, and that the derived function score of variants is reflective of diverse molecular defects. We further applied our approach to the _BRCA2_ gene, demonstrating that SPE is translatable to other genes with an appropriate cellular assay. In sum, we show that SPE allows for efficient, accurate functional characterization of genetic variants.
experiment.methodText: A cell survival assay was used to measure _BRCA2_ essentiality.  Saturation prime editing was used to introduce _BRCA2_ variants into locally haploidized HEK293T cells.  Cells were harvested every two days between days 6 and 16. Genomic DNA from both time points was amplified and sequenced using Illumina NextSeq 500/MiSeq to determine variant frequency.

experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.title: SCN5A response to veratridine+brevetoxin+ouabain mixture
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of human SCN5A by measuring response to veratridine+brevetoxin+ouabain drugs.
experiment.abstractText: Deep mutational scan of 12 amino acids in voltage-sensing helix 4 of human SCN5A, screened for functional protein by challenging HEK293T cells with drug mixture of veratridine+brevetoxin+ouabain.
experiment.methodText:
Comprehensive mutagenesis of the 12-amino-acid region (1621-1632aa) of the voltage-sensing helix 4 of human SCN5A, using inverse polymerase chain reaction with degenerate primers. Inserted 18-mer random barcodes into the plasmids, resulting in 7205 unique barcoded plasmids.

Mutants were screened transformed into HEK293T cells and selected for functional protein by challenging cells with a drug mixture of veratridine+brevetoxin+ouabain. The relative function under drugs of 253 mutations were measured. Six replicates were performed.

experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SCRIB PDZ domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the PDZ domain in SCRIB using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q14160_PF00595_857.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: sda combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Sporulation inhibitor sda.

experiment.title: sda combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Sporulation inhibitor sda.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Sporulation inhibitor sda protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1PV0.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 222 variants that failed validation.

title: sda chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of Sporulation inhibitor sda.

experiment.title: sda trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Sporulation inhibitor sda.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Sporulation inhibitor sda protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1PV0.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: Sequence requirement of S505N-induced constitutive activation
shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the S505N TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for its constitutive activation. This dataset contains scores for synonymous wildtype.

experiment.title: Sequence requirements for S505N-induced constitutive activation
experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for constitutive signaling, with S505N hTpoR as base sequence.
experiment.abstractText: The human thrombopoietin receptor (hTpoR/MPL) plays a crucial role in platelet production and its continuous activation induces thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. S505N and W515K hTpoR mutations are common among these patients, while the mechanism remain unknown. We therefore seek a deeper understanding of the sequence requirement of these disease causative mutations using DMS.
experiment.methodText:
The variant libraries were constructed using HiFi assembly with degenerate oligo pools targeting the transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions of TpoR. We selected the libraries on cytokine dependent cell lines, where cell growth depended on TpoR signaling to measure constitutive activation of TpoR. 
 
Cells were harvested after selection and RNA extracted to generate cDNA, which was indexed and prepared for direct Illumina sequencing. Raw sequenced data were trimmed and deduplicated before being analyzed with the DiMSum pipeline. We ensured at least two biological replicates were performed per datasets.
 
Functional scores were derived by comparing non-treated cells against plasmids library. Functional scores were normalised so that the mean of nonsense variants was set to 0 (non-functional) and the mean of synonymous variants (functional) was set to 1.

shortDescription: Profile surface presentation level of hTpoR variants using DMS. This dataset contains scores for protein variants.

experiment.title: Sequence requirements for surface expression of hTpoR variants
experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for surface presentation
experiment.abstractText: The human thrombopoietin receptor (hTpoR/MPL) plays a crucial role in platelet production and is the target of several biologic and small-molecule agonists used to treat thrombocytopenia. Mutations that cause constitutive hTpoR signalling through JAK2 can drive myeloproliferative diseases such as essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Several of the above drugs, and most disease-associated hTpoR mutations, act at or near the transmembrane (TM) domain, and specific TM and/or juxtamembrane (JM) structural transitions have been implicated in their mechanisms of action. Whether these non-native stimuli have shared or distinct structural mechanisms, and how these relate to activation by Tpo, remain unclear, and there is no high-resolution structure of the intact receptor that visualizes this crucial region. We employed deep mutational scanning to interrogate sequence-function relationships in the hTpoR TM-JM regions in response to four classes of stimuli: the native ligand Tpo, three small-molecule agonists eltrombopag, avatrombopag and lusutrombopag, a peptide mimic of the biologic agonist romiplostim and two disease-associated mutations S505N and W515K
experiment.methodText:
The variant libraries were constructed using overlap extension PCR with degenerate oligos targeting the transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions of TpoR. We selected the libraries based on TpoR surface staining to measure protein abundance.
 
Cells were harvested after selection and RNA extracted to generate cDNA, which was indexed and prepared for direct Illumina sequencing. Raw sequenced data were trimmed and deduplicated before being analyzed with the DiMSum pipeline. We ensured at least two biological replicates were performed per datasets.
 
Functional scores were derived by comparing Surface expression levels (high vs. low) and were normalised so that the mean of nonsense variants was set to 0 (poor surface presentation) and the mean of synonymous variants (normal surface presentation) was set to 1.

title: SETD2 WW domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SETD2 WW domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SETD2 WW domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SETD2 WW domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the WW domain in SETD2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9BYW2_PF00397_2382.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Scores from SGE of BRCA2 exon 13
shortDescription: Saturation mutagenesis of BRCA2 exon 13

experiment.title: SGE of BRCA2 exon 13
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation mutagenesis of BRCA2 exon 13
experiment.abstractText: The unknown pathogenicity of a significant number of variants found in cancer-related genes is attributed to limited epidemiological data, resulting in their classification as variant of uncertain significance (VUS). To date, Breast Cancer gene-2 (_BRCA2_) has the highest number of VUSs, which has necessitated the development of several robust functional assays to determine their functional significance. Here we report the use of a humanized-mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC) line expressing a single copy of the human _BRCA2_ for a CRISPR-Cas9-based high-throughput functional assay. As a proof-of-principle, we have saturated 11 codons encoded by BRCA2 exons 3, 18, 19 and all possible single-nucleotide variants in exon 13 and multiplexed these variants for their functional categorization. Specifically, we used a pool of 180-mer single-stranded donor DNA to generate all possible combination of variants. Using a high throughput sequencing-based approach, we show a significant drop in the frequency of non-functional variants, whereas functional variants are enriched in the pool of the cells. We further demonstrate the response of these variants to the DNA-damaging agents, cisplatin and olaparib, allowing us to use cellular survival and drug response as parameters for variant classification. Using this approach, we have categorized 599 _BRCA2_ variants including 93-single nucleotide variants (SNVs) across the 11 codons, of which 28 are reported in ClinVar. We also functionally categorized 252 SNVs from exon 13 into 188 functional and 60 non-functional variants, demonstrating that saturation genome editing (SGE) coupled with drug sensitivity assays can enhance functional annotation of _BRCA2_ VUS.
experiment.methodText: A BRCA2 variant library was introduced into PL2F7/F7 mouse embryonic stem cells harboring a single-copy human BRCA2 transgene. These cells were derived from PL2F7 cells (Brca2cko/ko) by integrating a 127kb BAC containing full-length human BRCA2 at chromosome 12 position A3, with endogenous mouse Brca2 deleted by Cre-mediated recombination. Cells were nucleofected with 3μg sgRNA/Cas9 plasmid and 6μg of 180-mer ssODN library. Following nucleofection, 3x10^7 cells were cultured on feeder cells for 72 hours, then replated and maintained until day 14. Cell pellets were harvested at day 3 and day 14. Genomic DNA was extracted and amplicon sequencing (1-3 million reads/sample) was performed to determine variant frequency at each time point, with function scores calculated as log2(day14/day3) ratios.

title: Scores from sGE of BRCA2 exons 15–26 in humanized mouse embryonic stem cells
shortDescription: SGE CRISPR-Cas9 based knock-in assay in exons 15 to 26 in a humanized mouse embryonic stem cell line

experiment.title: SGE of BRCA2 exons 15–26 in humanized mouse embryonic stem cells
experiment.shortDescription: SGE CRISPR-Cas9 based knock-in assay in exons 15 to 26 in a humanized mouse embryonic stem cell line
experiment.abstractText: Sequencing-based genetic tests have uncovered a vast array of _BRCA2_ sequence variants. Owing to limited clinical, familial and epidemiological data, thousands of variants are considered to be variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Here we have utilized CRISPR-Cas9-based saturation genome editing in a humanized mouse embryonic stem cell line to determine the functional effect of VUS. We have categorized nearly all possible single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the region that encodes the carboxylate-terminal DNA-binding domain of _BRCA2_. We have generated function scores for 6,551 SNVs, covering 96.4% of possible SNVs in exons 15-26 spanning _BRCA2_ residues 2479-3216. These variants include 1,282 SNVs that are categorized as missense VUS in the clinical variant database ClinVar, with 77.2% of these classified as benign and 20.4% classified as pathogenic using our functional score. Our assay provides evidence that 3,384 of the SNVs in the region are benign and 776 are pathogenic. Our classification aligns closely with pathogenicity data from ClinVar, orthogonal functional assays and computational meta predictors. We have integrated our embryonic stem cell-based _BRCA2_-saturation genome editing dataset with other available evidence and utilized the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines for clinical classification of all possible SNVs. This classification is available as a sequence-function map and serves as a valuable resource for interpreting unidentified variants in the population and for physicians and genetic counsellors to assess _BRCA2_ VUS in patients.
experiment.methodText: A cell survival assay was used to measure _BRCA2_ essentiality. A mouse ES cell line expressing a single copy of human _BRCA2_ was transfected with sgRNA-Cas9 plasmids and an ssODN oligonucleotide library. Cells were harvested at day 3 and day 14. Direct sequencing was then used to determine the frequency of each variant at each time point.

title: Table S1. Functional Scoring CARD11 Ibrutinib SGE
shortDescription: CARD11 CARD domain

experiment.title: SGE of CARD11 CARD domain in diploid cells
experiment.shortDescription: CARD11 CARD domain
experiment.abstractText: CARD11 encodes an adaptor protein that expresses dominant-negative and gain-of-function variants associated with distinct immunodeficiencies. Here, we used a “cloning-free” saturation genome editing approach in a diploid cell line to simultaneously score variants for decreased or increased function in the region of CARD11 associated with immunodeficiency.
experiment.methodText: Variants were introduced into the endogenous CARD11 locus of TMD8 cells with Cas9, sgRNA, and an ~150bp ssODN repair template. Cells were expanded for 14 days with or without ibrutinib and variant copy numbers were determined by illumina sequencing. Scores are calculated based on the ratio of variant reads in day 14 cells versus day 0 (pretreatment).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Multiplexed Functional Assessment of Genetic Variants in CARD11.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Genetic testing has increased the number of variants identified in disease genes, but the diagnostic utility is limited by lack of understanding variant function. CARD11 encodes an adaptor protein that expresses dominant-negative and gain-of-function variants associated with distinct immunodeficiencies. Here, we used a "cloning-free" saturation genome editing approach in a diploid cell line to simultaneously score 2,542 variants for decreased or increased function in the region of CARD11 associated with immunodeficiency. We also described an exon-skipping mechanism for CARD11 dominant-negative activity. The classification of reported clinical variants was sensitive (94.6%) and specific (88.9%), which rendered the data immediately useful for interpretation of seven coding and splicing variants implicated in immunodeficiency found in our clinic. This approach is generalizable for variant interpretation in many other clinically actionable genes, in any relevant cell type.

title: SH3D19 SH3 domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SH3D19 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SH3D19 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SH3D19 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in SH3D19 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q5HYK7_PF00018_664.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SHOX Homeobox domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SHOX Homeobox domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SHOX Homeobox domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Homeobox domain in SHOX using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O15266_PF00046_119.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Scores from site-saturation functional screen of PALB2 missense variants in mES cells
shortDescription: Site-saturation fuctional screen of PALB2 missense variants in the CC and WD40 domains in mouse embryonic stem cells using PARPi sensitivity as a readout for homologous recombination

experiment.title: Site-saturation functional screen of PALB2 missense variants in mES cells
experiment.shortDescription: Site-saturation fuctional screen of PALB2 missense variants in the CC and WD40 domains in mouse embryonic stem cells using PARPi sensitivity as a readout for homologous recombination
experiment.abstractText: Loss-of-function variants in _PALB2_ give rise to defects in DNA damage repair by homologous recombination (HR), increasing the risk of breast cancer in female carriers. However, genetic testing frequently reveals missense variants of uncertain significance (VUS) for which the impact on protein function and cancer risk are unclear. Here we assay 84% of all possible missense variants in 11 out of 13 _PALB2_ exons using site-saturation functional screens with PARP inhibitor sensitivity as a readout for HR. These exons encode the coiled-coil and WD40 domains, which we identify as the minimal regions required for HR. Furthermore, we reveal the functional impact of 6718 missense variants, classifying 3904 variants as functional (58%), 2422 as intermediate (36%), and 392 as damaging (6%). A burden-type analysis shows that damaging missense variants in _PALB2_ are associated with a significantly increased risk of breast cancer, similar to that observed for truncating variants. These results will be valuable for the classification of _PALB2_ missense VUS and clinical management of carriers.
experiment.methodText: A cDNA-based site-saturation screen was used to measure _PALB2_ function via PARPi sensitivity as a readout for homologous recombination. Palb2-knockout mouse embryonic stem cells were used to express _PALB2_ cDNA variant libraries which were at the Rosa26 locus via recombination-mediated cassette exchange. Cells expressing _PALB2_ variants were treated with PARP inhibitor (olaparib), and next-generation sequencing was used to determine the frequency of each variant in treated vs. untreated conditions. Depletion scores were generated using Enrich2.

Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: SMARCA4 BRK domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SMARCA4 BRK domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SMARCA4 BRK domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SMARCA4 BRK domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the BRK domain in SMARCA4 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P51532_PF07533_612.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

title: SMN Tudor domain combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Survival motor neuron protein Tudor domain.

experiment.title: SMN Tudor domain combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Survival motor neuron protein Tudor domain.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Survival motor neuron protein Tudor domain protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1MHN.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: SMN Tudor domain trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Survival motor neuron protein Tudor domain.

experiment.title: SMN Tudor domain trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Survival motor neuron protein Tudor domain.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Survival motor neuron protein Tudor domain protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1MHN.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: SORBS1 combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Sorbin and SH3 domain-containing protein 1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Sorbin and SH3 domain-containing protein 1 protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2O2W.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 39 variants that failed validation.

title: SORBS1 trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Sorbin and SH3 domain-containing protein 1.

experiment.title: SORBS1 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Sorbin and SH3 domain-containing protein 1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Sorbin and SH3 domain-containing protein 1 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2O2W.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.title: spa combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Immunoglobulin G-binding protein A.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Immunoglobulin G-binding protein A protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is v2_2M5A.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: spa (pross1) trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Protein A (pross1).

experiment.title: spa (pross1) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Protein A (pross1).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Protein A (pross1) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2B88.pdb_pross1.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: SpCas9 negative selection
shortDescription: Negative (off-target) selection of SpCas9 in a bacterial selection system.

experiment.title: SpCas9 negative selection
experiment.shortDescription: Negative (off-target) selection of SpCas9 in a bacterial selection system.
experiment.abstractText: Deep mutational scanning was used on a library of 1.9x10^7 *Streptococcus pyogenes* Cas9 (SpCas9) variants to infer the effects of each mutation and screen for functional changes. A selection system in *E. coli* was established to differentiate between active and inactive mutant variants of SpCas9. The biological system used positive and negative selection to assay SpCas9 nuclease function in order to gather information about amino acids that allow SpCas9 to cleave DNA.
experiment.methodText: Negative selection plasmids US0hisB-pyrF- were used to perform selection of SpCas9 variants by generating electrocompetent cells. These cells were electroporated and plated on both selection and control plates. The SpCas9 mutant library was cloned and extrapolated to be transformed into positive and negative selection competent cells. Following recovery, the transformations were used to perform titrations for negative selection, positive selection, and controls. Specific mutant cloning was performed by generating overlapping fragments necessary to produce chosen mutation combinations. Following that, the cells were pooled together and analyzed using Flow cytometry on a Becton Dickinson FACSAria. Next generation sequencing was performed using an Illuman NextSeq using 2x150bp paired-end reads.

title: spg (F53D) trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Immunoglobulin G-binding protein G (F53D).

experiment.title: spg (F53D) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Immunoglobulin G-binding protein G (F53D).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Immunoglobulin G-binding protein G (F53D) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1GB4.pdb_F53D.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.
