title: Selection of loss-of-function SPOP via yeast survival assay
shortDescription: An amino acid level deep mutational scan of human SPOP using yeast survival assay.

experiment.title: SPOP yeast growth inhibition
experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scan of the human SPOP using yeast growth inhibition reveals comprehensive functional landscape of variants.
experiment.abstractText: To comprehensively characterize the functional landscape of SPOP alteration, we performed a deep mutational screening (DMS), elucidating the functionality of 7,933 out of 8,228 possible single amino acid changes (96.4% coverage). Leveraging the observation that overexpression of human SPOP leads to yeast growth arrest, we assessed the functionality of each variant using a yeast proliferation assay.
experiment.methodText: DMS library was synthesized through tile-based cloning. We observed that expression of wild-type SPOP inhibits yeast growth, whereas depletion of specific functional regions within wild-type SPOP, namely the MATH, BTB, and 3-box domains, rescues it. To take advantage of the complementary strengths of both platforms, we analyze our mutant libraries using short-read and long-read sequencing.

title: SPTA1 SH3 domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SPTA1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SPTA1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SPTA1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in SPTA1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P02549_PF00018_979.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Spectrin alpha chain, non-erythrocytic 1 (A10S) protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 5FWB.pdb_A10S.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

experiment.title: SPTAN1 (A10S) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Spectrin alpha chain, non-erythrocytic 1 (A10S).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Spectrin alpha chain, non-erythrocytic 1 (A10S) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 5FWB.pdb_A10S.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: SPTAN1 SH3 domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SPTAN1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SPTAN1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SPTAN1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in SPTAN1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P07751_PF00018_968.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: SQSTM1 Sequestosome-1, UBA domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SQSTM1 Sequestosome-1, UBA domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SQSTM1 Sequestosome-1, UBA domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SQSTM1 Sequestosome-1, UBA domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Sequestosome-1, UBA domain in SQSTM1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q13501_PF16577_389.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: SRC SH3 domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SRC SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: SRC SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SRC SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in SRC using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P12931_PF00018_87.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: Stability selection of PyKS
experiment.shortDescription: Selecting on pyrrolidine ketide synthase (PyKS) with higher protein stability by GFP fusing.
experiment.abstractText: This study tested the variant effects of pyrrolidine ketide synthase (PyKS) whose wildtype has low protein stability. The PyKS single mutation library is generated with the fluorescent protein GFP fused and selected by FACS. Mutants with high protein stability will have higher fluorescence intensity.
experiment.methodText:
The variant library in this study is generated using nicking mutagenesis with NNK primers and expressed in E.col. Variants were generated in five non-overlapping tiles, covering residues 8-78, 79-156, 157-234, 235-312, and 313-388 (UniProt coordinates).

Cells were sorted using FACS on a BD Influx cell sorter into a reference population and a selected population, where the selected population were in the top 8-10% of GFP intensity. Variant counts in each population were determined by deep sequencing on an Illumina MiSeq with 250bp paired-end reads.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: An Automated Data-Driven Pipeline for Improving Heterologous Enzyme Expression.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Enzymes are the ultimate entities responsible for chemical transformations in natural and engineered biosynthetic pathways. However, many natural enzymes suffer from suboptimal functional expression due to poor intrinsic protein stability. Further, stability enhancing mutations often come at the cost of impaired function. Here we demonstrate an automated protein engineering strategy for stabilizing enzymes while retaining catalytic function using deep mutational scanning coupled to multiple-filter based screening and combinatorial mutagenesis. We validated this strategy by improving the functional expression of a Type III polyketide synthase from the Atropa belladonna biosynthetic pathway for tropane alkaloids. The best variant had a total of 8 mutations with over 25-fold improved activity over wild-type in E. coli cell lysates, an improved melting temperature of 11.5 ± 0.6 °C, and only minimal reduction in catalytic efficiency. We show that the multiple-filter approach maintains acceptable sensitivity with homology modeling structures up to 4 Å RMS. Our results highlight an automated protein engineering tool for improving the stability and solubility of difficult to express enzymes, which has impact for biotechnological applications.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: High-resolution sequence-function mapping of full-length proteins.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Comprehensive sequence-function mapping involves detailing the fitness contribution of every possible single mutation to a gene by comparing the abundance of each library variant before and after selection for the phenotype of interest. Deep sequencing of library DNA allows frequency reconstruction for tens of thousands of variants in a single experiment, yet short read lengths of current sequencers makes it challenging to probe genes encoding full-length proteins. Here we extend the scope of sequence-function maps to entire protein sequences with a modular, universal sequence tiling method. We demonstrate the approach with both growth-based selections and FACS screening, offer parameters and best practices that simplify design of experiments, and present analytical solutions to normalize data across independent selections. Using this protocol, sequence-function maps covering full sequences can be obtained in four to six weeks. Best practices introduced in this manuscript are fully compatible with, and complementary to, other recently published sequence-function mapping protocols.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the STAU1 Double-stranded RNA-binding domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: STAU1 Double-stranded RNA-binding domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the STAU1 Double-stranded RNA-binding domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Double-stranded RNA-binding domain in STAU1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O95793_PF00035_183.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: STIM1 cEFhand domain DMS
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of STIM1 cEFhand domain in HEK293T cells to evaluate the effect of variants on cell survival.
experiment.abstractText: This study evaluated the variant effect of the STIM1 calcium binding domain cEFhand on cell survival. 706 single amino acid variants were characterized through this study in cells with or without a WT endogenous copy present.
experiment.methodText: Variants were constructed using site-saturation mutagenesis with tiled set of degenerate PCR primers (NNK) at each position of the STIM1 cEFhand domain. The variant library was recombined into either standard LP cells (HEK293T landing pad cells with endogenous STIM1 present) or knockout LP cells (HEK293T landing pad cells with endogenous STIM1 knocked out). Samples were taken 5, 7 and 9 days after transfection. Genomic DNA was extracted from cells, amplified with adapter primer pairs and samples were run on Illumina NextSeq 550 using a Mid Output 150 cycle kit. The experiment was done at least 5 separate times.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Comprehensive mutational characterization of the calcium-sensing STIM1 EF-hand reveals residues essential for structure and function
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract:
Calcium signaling is a fundamental molecular means of cellular regulation. Store operated calcium entry (SOCE) is a major intracellular signaling module, wherein calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum triggers transmembrane STIM1 proteins to conformationally shift and oligomerize to prompt calcium influx from the extracellular environment. STIM1 senses ER calcium concentrations with its canonical EF-hand domain, and missense variants can dysregulate SOCE and cause Tubular Aggregate Myopathy, Stormorken Syndrome or immunodeficiency. Few STIM1 EF-hand variants are characterized, obscuring how STIM1 sequence controls its function, and hampering clinical interpretation of STIM1 variants observed in patients.

We leveraged fitness costs caused by overexpression of STIM1 variants in cultured human cells to functionally characterize 706 of the 720 possible single amino acid variants of the STIM1 canonical EF-hand. The calcium-coordinating EF-hand residues exhibited varying mutational patterns. The trailing helix possessed a core of immutable residues, even depleting during library propagation in bacteria, implicating residues normally restraining STIM1 aggregation. The leading helix only exhibited toxicity in cells with endogenous STIM1, implicating a multimerization-dependent STIM1 regulatory module. No cytotoxic STIM1 variants were observed in healthy human populations. Some disease-associated variants had low scores, but most pathogenic variants were not overtly cytotoxic in our assay. We demonstrate that orthogonal measurements for STIM1 oligomerization, cytoplasmic calcium influx, and cellular stress complement the cytotoxicity phenotypes to enhance variant understanding. Collectively, these data reveal the complex molecular roles embedded in the STIM1 canonical EF-hand sequence for its function in promoting calcium signaling through SOCE.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Nonribosomal peptide synthetase StoC protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 6EWU.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: STOX1 Storkhead-box protein, winged-helix domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the STOX1 Storkhead-box protein, winged-helix domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: STOX1 Storkhead-box protein, winged-helix domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the STOX1 Storkhead-box protein, winged-helix domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Storkhead-box protein, winged-helix domain in STOX1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q6ZVD7_PF10264_112.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: sucB combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Dihydrolipoyllysine-residue succinyltransferase component of 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Dihydrolipoyllysine-residue succinyltransferase component of 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1W4H.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 131 variants that failed validation.

title: SUMO1 DMS-TileSeq
shortDescription: A Deep Mutational Scan of the human SUMO1 using functional complementation in yeast via DMS-TileSeq

experiment.title: SUMO1 yeast complementation
experiment.shortDescription: A Deep Mutational Scan of the human SUMO1 using functional complementation in yeast.
experiment.abstractText: Although we now routinely sequence human genomes, we can confidently identify only a fraction of the sequence variants that have a functional impact. Here, we developed a deep mutational scanning framework that produces exhaustive maps for human missense variants by combining random codon mutagenesis and multiplexed functional variation assays with computational imputation and refinement. We applied this framework to four proteins corresponding to six human genes: UBE2I (encoding SUMO E2 conjugase), SUMO1 (small ubiquitin-like modifier), TPK1 (thiamin pyrophosphokinase), and CALM1/2/3 (three genes encoding the protein calmodulin). The resulting maps recapitulate known protein features and confidently identify pathogenic variation. Assays potentially amenable to deep mutational scanning are already available for 57% of human disease genes, suggesting that DMS could ultimately map functional variation for all human disease genes.
experiment.methodText: A Deep Mutational Scan of SUMO1 using functional complementation in yeast was performed using DMS-TileSeq and a machine-learning method was used to impute the effects of missing variants and refine measurements of lower confidence. See [**Weile *et al.* 2017**](http://msb.embopress.org/content/13/12/957) for details.

title: Systematic characterization of indel variants using a yeast-based protein folding sensor
shortDescription: Protein folding of DHFR indel variants at 37 °C.

experiment.title: Systematic characterization of indel variants using a yeast-based protein folding sensor
experiment.shortDescription: Protein folding of DHFR indel variants using a protein folding sensor in yeast.
experiment.abstractText: This study assessed the protein folding of DHFR indel variants using a protein folding sensor in yeast. The protein folding was measured using the CPOP folding sensor in a ura5Δura10Δ strain.
experiment.methodText: The human DHFR sequence was divided into five tiles. For each tile, we generated an indel library comprising all possible single residue deletions as well as insertion of a single glycine residue at each position in that tile. The DHFR sequence outside each tile in the five libraries was wild-type. The DHFR libraries were inserted into the CPOP folding sensor and cloned into pAG415. The libraries were transformed into a ura5Δura10Δ strain. Cells were plated on SC-uracil medium with and without methotrexate at 30 °C and 37 °C to select for folding of DHFR indel variants. Based on the relative change in frequency, we calculated a CPOP folding score of each DHFR indel variant. The scores were calculated based on three replicates.

title: Combined score using three assays of TP53 activity that assess loss of function or dominant negative effect
shortDescription: Combined score using three assays of TP53 activity that assess loss of function or dominant negative effect

experiment.title: Systematic integration of multiplexed functional data (TP53)
experiment.shortDescription: Combined score using three assays of TP53 activity that assess loss of function or dominant negative effect
experiment.abstractText: Unlike most tumor suppressor genes, the most common genetic alterations in tumor protein p53 (_TP53_) are missense mutations. Mutant p53 protein is often abundantly expressed in cancers and specific allelic variants exhibit dominant-negative or gain-of-function activities in experimental models. To gain a systematic view of p53 function, we interrogated loss-of-function screens conducted in hundreds of human cancer cell lines and performed _TP53_ saturation mutagenesis screens in an isogenic pair of _TP53_ wild-type and null cell lines. We found that loss or dominant-negative inhibition of wild-type p53 function reliably enhanced cellular fitness. By integrating these data with the Catalog of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) mutational signatures database, we developed a statistical model that describes the _TP53_ mutational spectrum as a function of the baseline probability of acquiring each mutation and the fitness advantage conferred by attenuation of p53 activity. Collectively, these observations show that widely-acting and tissue-specific mutational processes combine with phenotypic selection to dictate the frequencies of recurrent _TP53_ mutations.
experiment.methodText: This combined score integrates data from three functional assays to provide a comprehensive measure of each TP53 variant's functional impact. It uses the Z-scores from the two nutlin-3 assays (which enrich for loss-of-function and dominant-negative alleles) and the Z-score from the etoposide assay (which enriches for wild-type-like alleles).

title: TAB3 Ubiquitin system component CUE domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TAB3 Ubiquitin system component CUE domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TAB3 Ubiquitin system component CUE domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TAB3 Ubiquitin system component CUE domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Ubiquitin system component CUE domain in TAB3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q8N5C8_PF02845_12.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

title: TAX1BP1 CALCOCO1/2, zinc finger UBZ1-type domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TAX1BP1 CALCOCO1/2, zinc finger UBZ1-type domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TAX1BP1 CALCOCO1/2, zinc finger UBZ1-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TAX1BP1 CALCOCO1/2, zinc finger UBZ1-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the CALCOCO1/2, zinc finger UBZ1-type domain in TAX1BP1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q86VP1_PF18112_729.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Tcerg1 FBP28WW domain combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for FBP28WW domain from Transcription elongation regulator 1 .

experiment.title: Tcerg1 FBP28WW domain combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for FBP28WW domain from Transcription elongation regulator 1 .
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of FBP28WW domain from Transcription elongation regulator 1  protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1E0L.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 50 variants that failed validation.

title: Tcerg1 FBP28WW domain chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of FBP28WW domain from Transcription elongation regulator 1 .

experiment.title: Tcerg1 FBP28WW domain trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of FBP28WW domain from Transcription elongation regulator 1 .
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of FBP28WW domain from Transcription elongation regulator 1  protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1E0L.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Transcription elongation regulator 1 (L453D mutant) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2N4R.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: TCERG1L FF domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TCERG1L FF domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TCERG1L FF domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TCERG1L FF domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the FF domain in TCERG1L using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q5VWI1_PF01846_448.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: TDP-43 toxicity
shortDescription: Deep mutational scanning of TDP-43 prion-like domain (AA 290-331) using a toxicity assay

experiment.title: TDP-43 toxicity
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scanning of TDP-43 prion-like domain using a toxicity assay.
experiment.abstractText: Insoluble protein aggregates are the hallmarks of many neurodegenerative diseases. For example, aggregates of TDP-43 occur in nearly all cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, whether aggregates cause cellular toxicity is still not clear, even in simpler cellular systems. We reasoned that deep mutagenesis might be a powerful approach to disentangle the relationship between aggregation and toxicity. We generated >50,000 mutations in the prion-like domain (PRD) of TDP-43 and quantified their toxicity in yeast cells. Surprisingly, mutations that increase hydrophobicity and aggregation strongly decrease toxicity. In contrast, toxic variants promote the formation of dynamic liquid-like condensates. Mutations have their strongest effects in a hotspot that genetic interactions reveal to be structured in vivo, illustrating how mutagenesis can probe the in vivo structures of unstructured proteins. Our results show that aggregation of TDP-43 is not harmful but protects cells, most likely by titrating the protein away from a toxic liquid-like phase.
experiment.methodText:
Variants for TDP-43 were constructed using a "doped" oligo for each of the TDP-43 libraries (290-331 and 332-373). Libraries were transformed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and TDP-43 expression was induced for 5-6 generations. Variant counts were processed with DiMSum (Faure et al. 2020) to obtain a toxicity score for each variant. 
See Bolognesi et al. 2019 for details.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Tudor domain in TDRD3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9H7E2_PF00567_554.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: Tec combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Tyrosine-protein kinase Tec.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Tyrosine-protein kinase Tec protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1GL5.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 306 variants that failed validation.

experiment.title: Tec trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Tyrosine-protein kinase Tec.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Tyrosine-protein kinase Tec protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1GL5.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.title: TEM-1 0.15 μg/ml cefotaxime
experiment.shortDescription: Effects of TEM-1 mutations on cefotaxime resistance at 0.15 μg/ml
experiment.abstractText: This study examined the fitness effects of single amino acid mutations in TEM-1 β-lactamase in *Escherichia coli* under selection for ampicillin resistance or cefotaxime resistance.
experiment.methodText:
The sequence was split into ten non-overlapping subgroups and saturation mutagenesis libraries were created for each using NNS PCR mutagenesis. The PCR products from the mutagenesis were mixed in equimolar ratios and ligated as a single library.

Cells were grown overnight to saturation under non-selective media and then diluted and grown in the presence of the antibiotic to perform the selection. 

Sequencing was performed using 75-bp paired-end Illumina reads.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Evolvability as a function of purifying selection in TEM-1 β-lactamase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Evolvability—the capacity to generate beneficial heritable variation—is a central property of biological systems. However, its origins and modulation by environmental factors have not been examined systematically. Here, we analyze the fitness effects of all single mutations in TEM-1 β-lactamase (4,997 variants) under selection for the wild-type function (ampicillin resistance) and for a new function (cefotaxime resistance). Tolerance to mutation in this enzyme is bimodal and dependent on the strength of purifying selection in vivo, a result that derives from a steep non-linear ampicillin-dependent relationship between biochemical activity and fitness. Interestingly, cefotaxime resistance emerges from mutations that are neutral at low levels of ampicillin but deleterious at high levels; thus the capacity to evolve new function also depends on the strength of selection. The key property controlling evolvability is an excess of enzymatic activity relative to the strength of selection, suggesting that fluctuating environments might select for high-activity enzymes.

title: TEM-15 Amp scores
shortDescription: Amino acid scores for TEM-15 (TEM-1 variant) fitness on Amp.

experiment.title: TEM-15 Amp
experiment.shortDescription: TEM-15 (TEM-1 variant) fitness on Amp.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment measured the experimental fitness of variants in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene in *Escherichia coli* on different backgrounds. Fitness measurements were estimated based on growth under increasing concentrations of ampicillin using a band-pass selection system.
experiment.methodText:
The variant library was constructed using PFunkel comprehensive codon mutagenesis. One NNN-containing mutagenic primer was used per codon.

This dataset describes variants on the TEM-15 background, which differs from TEM-1 by p.[Glu102Lys;Gly236Ser] (TEM-1 position not Ambler position).

The band-pass selection system is described in (Sohka et al., 2009). Briefly, cells are plated on media containing Tet and a variable concentration of Amp. If TEM-1 activity is too low for the Amp concentration, cells will not proliferate. If TEM-1 activity is too high, no cell wall damage will occur and TetC (which confers Tet resistance) will not be produced. Therefore cells should only grow if the TEM-1 variant’s activity level matches the Amp concentration.

Sequencing was performed using PacBio.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The current paradigm for tuning synthetic biological systems is through re-engineering system components. Biological systems designed with the inherent ability to be tuned by external stimuli will be more versatile. We engineered Escherichia coli cells to behave as an externally tunable band-pass filter for enzyme activity and small molecules. The band's location can be positioned within a range of 4 orders of magnitude simply by the addition of compounds to the growth medium. Inclusion in the genetic network of an enzyme-substrate pair that functions as an attenuator is a generalizable strategy that enables this tunability. The genetic circuit enabled bacteria growth to be patterned in response to chemical gradients in nonintuitive ways and facilitated the isolation of engineered allosteric enzymes. The application of this strategy to other biological systems will increase their utility for biotechnological applications and their usefulness as a tool for gaining insight into nature's underlying design principles.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.publicationJournal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Sohka T, et al. An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2009; 106:10135-40.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: We introduce PFunkel, a versatile method for extensive, researcher-defined DNA mutagenesis using a ssDNA or dsDNA template. Once the template DNA is prepared, the method can be completed in a single day in a single tube, and requires no intermediate DNA purification or sub-cloning. PFunkel can be used for site-directed mutagenesis at an efficiency approaching 100%. More importantly, PFunkel allows researchers the unparalleled ability to efficiently construct user-defined libraries. We demonstrate the creation of a library with site-saturation at four distal sites simultaneously at 70% efficiency. We also employ PFunkel to create a comprehensive codon mutagenesis library of the TEM-1 ß-lactamase gene. We designed this library to contain 18,081 members, one for each possible codon substitution in the gene (287 positions in TEM-1 x 63 possible codon substitutions). Deep sequencing revealed that ∼97% of the designed single codon substitutions are present in the library. From such a library we identified 18 previously unreported adaptive mutations that each confer resistance to the ß-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam. Three of these mutations confer resistance equal to or higher than that of the most resistant reported TEM-1 allele and have the potential to emerge clinically.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E and Ostermeier M. PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis. PloS one. 2012; 7:e52031.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Shifting Fitness and Epistatic Landscapes Reflect Trade-offs along an Evolutionary Pathway.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Nature repurposes proteins via evolutionary processes. Such adaptation can come at the expense of the original protein's function, which is a trade-off of adaptation. We sought to examine other potential adaptive trade-offs. We measured the effect on ampicillin resistance of ~12,500 unique single amino acid mutants of the TEM-1, TEM-17, TEM-19, and TEM-15 β-lactamase alleles, which constitute an adaptive path in the evolution of cefotaxime resistance. These protein fitness landscapes were compared and used to calculate epistatic interactions between these mutations and the two mutations in the pathway (E104K and G238S). This series of protein fitness landscapes provides a systematic, quantitative description of pairwise/tertiary intragenic epistasis involving adaptive mutations. We find that the frequency of mutations exhibiting epistasis increases along the evolutionary pathway. Adaptation moves the protein to a region in the fitness landscape characterized by decreased mutational robustness and increased ruggedness, as measured by fitness effects of mutations and epistatic interactions for TEM-1's original function. This movement to such a "fitness territory" has evolutionary consequences and is an important adaptive trade-off and cost of adaptation. Our systematic study provides detailed insight into the relationships between mutation, protein structure, protein stability, and epistasis and quantitatively depicts the different costs inherent in the evolution of new functions.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Steinberg B and Ostermeier M. Shifting Fitness and Epistatic Landscapes Reflect Trade-offs along an Evolutionary Pathway. Shifting Fitness and Epistatic Landscapes Reflect Trade-offs along an Evolutionary Pathway. 2016; 428:2730-43. doi: 10.1016/j.jmb.2016.04.033

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Mutations are central to evolution, providing the genetic variation upon which selection acts. A mutation's effect on the suitability of a gene to perform a particular function (gene fitness) can be positive, negative, or neutral. Knowledge of the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of mutations is fundamental for understanding evolutionary dynamics, molecular-level genetic variation, complex genetic disease, the accumulation of deleterious mutations, and the molecular clock. We present comprehensive DFEs for point and codon mutants of the Escherichia coli TEM-1 β-lactamase gene and missense mutations in the TEM-1 protein. These DFEs provide insight into the inherent benefits of the genetic code's architecture, support for the hypothesis that mRNA stability dictates codon usage at the beginning of genes, an extensive framework for understanding protein mutational tolerance, and evidence that mutational effects on protein thermodynamic stability shape the DFE. Contrary to prevailing expectations, we find that deleterious effects of mutation primarily arise from a decrease in specific protein activity and not cellular protein levels.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E, et al. A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape. Molecular biology and evolution. 2014; 31:1581-92.

experiment.title: TEM-1 625 μg/ml Amp
experiment.shortDescription: Effects of TEM-1 mutations on ampicillin resistance at 625 μg/ml
experiment.abstractText: This study examined the fitness effects of single amino acid mutations in TEM-1 β-lactamase in *Escherichia coli* under selection for ampicillin resistance or cefotaxime resistance.
experiment.methodText:
The sequence was split into ten non-overlapping subgroups and saturation mutagenesis libraries were created for each using NNS PCR mutagenesis. The PCR products from the mutagenesis were mixed in equimolar ratios and ligated as a single library.

Cells were grown overnight to saturation under non-selective media and then diluted and grown in the presence of the antibiotic to perform the selection. Two replicate selections were performed.

Sequencing was performed using 75-bp paired-end Illumina reads.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Evolvability as a function of purifying selection in TEM-1 β-lactamase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Evolvability—the capacity to generate beneficial heritable variation—is a central property of biological systems. However, its origins and modulation by environmental factors have not been examined systematically. Here, we analyze the fitness effects of all single mutations in TEM-1 β-lactamase (4,997 variants) under selection for the wild-type function (ampicillin resistance) and for a new function (cefotaxime resistance). Tolerance to mutation in this enzyme is bimodal and dependent on the strength of purifying selection in vivo, a result that derives from a steep non-linear ampicillin-dependent relationship between biochemical activity and fitness. Interestingly, cefotaxime resistance emerges from mutations that are neutral at low levels of ampicillin but deleterious at high levels; thus the capacity to evolve new function also depends on the strength of selection. The key property controlling evolvability is an excess of enzymatic activity relative to the strength of selection, suggesting that fluctuating environments might select for high-activity enzymes.

A mutation's effect on the suitability of a gene to perform a particular function (gene fitness) can be positive, negative, or neutral. Knowledge of the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of mutations is fundamental for understanding evolutionary dynamics, molecular-level genetic variation, complex genetic disease, the accumulation of deleterious mutations, and the molecular clock. We present comprehensive DFEs for point and codon mutants of the Escherichia coli TEM-1 β-lactamase gene and missense mutations in the TEM-1 protein. These DFEs provide insight into the inherent benefits of the genetic code's architecture, support for the hypothesis that mRNA stability dictates codon usage at the beginning of genes, an extensive framework for understanding protein mutational tolerance, and evidence that mutational effects on protein thermodynamic stability shape the DFE. Contrary to prevailing expectations, we find that deleterious effects of mutation primarily arise from a decrease in specific protein activity and not cellular protein levels.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E, et al. A comprehensive, high-resolution map of a gene's fitness landscape. Molecular biology and evolution. 2014; 31:1581-92.

title: TEM-19 Amp scores
shortDescription: Amino acid scores for TEM-19 (TEM-1 variant) fitness on Amp.

experiment.title: TEM-19 Amp
experiment.shortDescription: TEM-19 (TEM-1 variant) fitness on Amp.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment measured the experimental fitness of variants in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene in *Escherichia coli* on different backgrounds. Fitness measurements were estimated based on growth under increasing concentrations of ampicillin using a band-pass selection system.
experiment.methodText:
The variant library was constructed using PFunkel comprehensive codon mutagenesis. One NNN-containing mutagenic primer was used per codon.

This dataset describes variants on the TEM-19 background, which differs from TEM-1 by p.Gly236Ser (TEM-1 position not Ambler position).

The band-pass selection system is described in (Sohka et al., 2009). Briefly, cells are plated on media containing Tet and a variable concentration of Amp. If TEM-1 activity is too low for the Amp concentration, cells will not proliferate. If TEM-1 activity is too high, no cell wall damage will occur and TetC (which confers Tet resistance) will not be produced. Therefore cells should only grow if the TEM-1 variant’s activity level matches the Amp concentration.

Sequencing was performed using PacBio.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The current paradigm for tuning synthetic biological systems is through re-engineering system components. Biological systems designed with the inherent ability to be tuned by external stimuli will be more versatile. We engineered Escherichia coli cells to behave as an externally tunable band-pass filter for enzyme activity and small molecules. The band's location can be positioned within a range of 4 orders of magnitude simply by the addition of compounds to the growth medium. Inclusion in the genetic network of an enzyme-substrate pair that functions as an attenuator is a generalizable strategy that enables this tunability. The genetic circuit enabled bacteria growth to be patterned in response to chemical gradients in nonintuitive ways and facilitated the isolation of engineered allosteric enzymes. The application of this strategy to other biological systems will increase their utility for biotechnological applications and their usefulness as a tool for gaining insight into nature's underlying design principles.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.publicationJournal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Sohka T, et al. An externally tunable bacterial band-pass filter. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2009; 106:10135-40.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: We introduce PFunkel, a versatile method for extensive, researcher-defined DNA mutagenesis using a ssDNA or dsDNA template. Once the template DNA is prepared, the method can be completed in a single day in a single tube, and requires no intermediate DNA purification or sub-cloning. PFunkel can be used for site-directed mutagenesis at an efficiency approaching 100%. More importantly, PFunkel allows researchers the unparalleled ability to efficiently construct user-defined libraries. We demonstrate the creation of a library with site-saturation at four distal sites simultaneously at 70% efficiency. We also employ PFunkel to create a comprehensive codon mutagenesis library of the TEM-1 ß-lactamase gene. We designed this library to contain 18,081 members, one for each possible codon substitution in the gene (287 positions in TEM-1 x 63 possible codon substitutions). Deep sequencing revealed that ∼97% of the designed single codon substitutions are present in the library. From such a library we identified 18 previously unreported adaptive mutations that each confer resistance to the ß-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam. Three of these mutations confer resistance equal to or higher than that of the most resistant reported TEM-1 allele and have the potential to emerge clinically.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Firnberg E and Ostermeier M. PFunkel: efficient, expansive, user-defined mutagenesis. PloS one. 2012; 7:e52031.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Shifting Fitness and Epistatic Landscapes Reflect Trade-offs along an Evolutionary Pathway.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Nature repurposes proteins via evolutionary processes. Such adaptation can come at the expense of the original protein's function, which is a trade-off of adaptation. We sought to examine other potential adaptive trade-offs. We measured the effect on ampicillin resistance of ~12,500 unique single amino acid mutants of the TEM-1, TEM-17, TEM-19, and TEM-15 β-lactamase alleles, which constitute an adaptive path in the evolution of cefotaxime resistance. These protein fitness landscapes were compared and used to calculate epistatic interactions between these mutations and the two mutations in the pathway (E104K and G238S). This series of protein fitness landscapes provides a systematic, quantitative description of pairwise/tertiary intragenic epistasis involving adaptive mutations. We find that the frequency of mutations exhibiting epistasis increases along the evolutionary pathway. Adaptation moves the protein to a region in the fitness landscape characterized by decreased mutational robustness and increased ruggedness, as measured by fitness effects of mutations and epistatic interactions for TEM-1's original function. This movement to such a "fitness territory" has evolutionary consequences and is an important adaptive trade-off and cost of adaptation. Our systematic study provides detailed insight into the relationships between mutation, protein structure, protein stability, and epistasis and quantitatively depicts the different costs inherent in the evolution of new functions.

experiment.title: TEM-1 single-codon deletions
experiment.shortDescription: Effect of single-codon deletions on TEM-1 fitness
experiment.abstractText: This study characterized the effect of single-codon insertion and deletion events on the function of TEM-1 beta-lactamase in the presence of varying concentrations of ampicillin.
experiment.methodText: The library of mutants containing all possible nucleotide deletions was generated using a forward primer with a 3-base deletion on the 5’ end and a compatible reverse primer. TEM-1 variants were expressed on a pSkunk2 plasmid. The selection was performed using a band-pass genetic circuit, set up such that the cells will only grow if the activity of the TEM-1 variant protein matches the concentration of Amp present. If the activity is too low or too high for the Amp concentration, the cells will fail to grow. High-throughput sequencing was performed using PacBio.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Fitness Effects of Single Amino Acid Insertions and Deletions in TEM-1 β-Lactamase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Short insertions and deletions (InDels) are a common type of mutation found in nature and a useful source of variation in protein engineering. InDel events have important consequences in protein evolution, often opening new pathways for adaptation. However, much less is known about the effects of InDels compared to point mutations and amino acid substitutions. In particular, deep mutagenesis studies on the distribution of fitness effects of mutations have focused almost exclusively on amino acid substitutions. Here, we present a near-comprehensive analysis of the fitness effects of single amino acid InDels in TEM-1 β-lactamase. While we found InDels to be largely deleterious, partially overlapping deletion-tolerant and insertion-tolerant regions were observed throughout the protein, especially in unstructured regions and at the end of helices. The signal sequence of TEM-1 tolerated InDels more than the mature protein. Most regions of the protein tolerated insertions more than deletions, but a few regions tolerated deletions more than insertions. We examined the relationship between InDel tolerance and a variety of measures to help understand its origin. These measures included evolutionary variation in β-lactamases, secondary structure identity, tolerance to amino acid substitutions, solvent accessibility, and side-chain weighted contact number. We found secondary structure, weighted contact number, and evolutionary variation in class A beta-lactamases to be the somewhat predictive of InDel fitness effects.

title: TEM-1 unselected
shortDescription: Effects of TEM-1 mutations under no selection

experiment.title: TEM-1 unselected
experiment.shortDescription: Effects of TEM-1 mutations under no selection
experiment.abstractText: This study examined the fitness effects of single amino acid mutations in TEM-1 β-lactamase in *Escherichia coli* under selection for ampicillin resistance or cefotaxime resistance.
experiment.methodText:
The sequence was split into ten non-overlapping subgroups and saturation mutagenesis libraries were created for each using NNS PCR mutagenesis. The PCR products from the mutagenesis were mixed in equimolar ratios and ligated as a single library.

Cells were grown overnight to saturation under non-selective media and then diluted and grown in the absence of antibiotic. Two replicate selections were performed.

Sequencing was performed using 75-bp paired-end Illumina reads.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Evolvability as a function of purifying selection in TEM-1 β-lactamase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Evolvability—the capacity to generate beneficial heritable variation—is a central property of biological systems. However, its origins and modulation by environmental factors have not been examined systematically. Here, we analyze the fitness effects of all single mutations in TEM-1 β-lactamase (4,997 variants) under selection for the wild-type function (ampicillin resistance) and for a new function (cefotaxime resistance). Tolerance to mutation in this enzyme is bimodal and dependent on the strength of purifying selection in vivo, a result that derives from a steep non-linear ampicillin-dependent relationship between biochemical activity and fitness. Interestingly, cefotaxime resistance emerges from mutations that are neutral at low levels of ampicillin but deleterious at high levels; thus the capacity to evolve new function also depends on the strength of selection. The key property controlling evolvability is an excess of enzymatic activity relative to the strength of selection, suggesting that fluctuating environments might select for high-activity enzymes.

title: TERF2 SANT/Myb domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TERF2 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TERF2 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TERF2 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SANT/Myb domain in TERF2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q15554_PF00249_489.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: TFG PB1 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TFG PB1 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the PB1 domain in TFG using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q92734_PF00564_6.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).
