experiment.title: The energetic and allosteric landscape for KRAS inhibition
experiment.shortDescription: To quantify the impact of >26,000 mutations on the folding of KRAS and its binding to six interaction partners and to quantify how mutations tune the binding specificity of a signalling protein and map the inhibitory allosteric sites.
experiment.abstractText: Thousands of proteins have now been genetically-validated as therapeutic targets in hundreds of human diseases. However, very few have actually been successfully targeted and many are considered ‘undruggable’. This is particularly true for proteins that function via protein-protein interactions: direct inhibition of binding interfaces is difficult, requiring the identification of allosteric sites. However, most proteins have no known allosteric sites and a comprehensive allosteric map does not exist for any protein. Here we address this shortcoming by charting multiple global atlases of inhibitory allosteric communication in KRAS, a protein mutated in 1 in 10 human cancers. We quantified the impact of >26,000 mutations on the folding of KRAS and its binding to six interaction partners. Genetic interactions in double mutants allowed us to perform biophysical measurements at scale, inferring >22,000 causal free energy changes, a similar number of measurements as the total made for proteins to date. These energy landscapes quantify how mutations tune the binding specificity of a signalling protein and map the inhibitory allosteric sites for an important therapeutic target. Allosteric propagation is particularly effective across the central beta sheet of KRAS and multiple surface pockets are genetically-validated as allosterically active, including a distal pocket in the C-terminal lobe of the protein. Allosteric mutations typically inhibit binding to all tested effectors but they can also change the binding specificity, revealing the regulatory, evolutionary and therapeutic potential to tune pathway activation. Using the approach described here it should be possible to rapidly and comprehensively identify allosteric target sites in many important proteins.

experiment.title: The functional landscape of coding variation in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene LDLR.
experiment.shortDescription: Functional assessment of LDLR missense variants on LDL uptake in the presence of VLDL.
experiment.abstractText: Variants in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene LDLR can raise circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentrations and increase the risk of premature atherosclerosis. Definitive classifications are lacking for nearly half of clinically encountered LDLR missense variants.
experiment.methodText: We applied a multiplexed in vitro assay measuring the binding and internalization of LDL particles in the presence of VLDL. Barcoded cDNA libraries collectively containing nearly all possible single amino acid substitutions in LDLR were introduced at a genomically integrated Bxb1 “landing pad” in HeLa cells lacking endogenous LDLR. Cells were selected for LDL uptake via fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Functional scores were calculated by comparing barcode abundance in selected and unselected populations and scaled such that scores of 0 and 1 correspond to the median behaviour of nonsense and synonymous variants.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: The functional landscape of coding variation in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene LDLR
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract:
Variants in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene
                    LDLR
                    —the most important genetic driver of cardiovascular disease—can raise circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentrations and increase the risk of premature atherosclerosis. Definitive classifications are lacking for nearly half of clinically encountered
                    LDLR
                    missense variants, limiting interventions that reduce disease burden. Here, we tested the impact of ~17,000 (nearly all possible)
                    LDLR
                    missense coding variants on both LDLR cell-surface abundance and LDL uptake, yielding sequence–function maps that recapitulate known biochemistry, offer functional insights, and provide evidence for interpreting clinical variants. Functional scores correlated with hyperlipidemia phenotypes in prospective human cohorts and augmented polygenic scores to improve risk inference, highlighting the potential of this resource to accelerate familial hypercholesterolemia diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

experiment.title: The functional landscape of coding variation in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene LDLR.
experiment.shortDescription: Functional assessment of LDLR missense variants on LDLR cell-surface abundance.
experiment.abstractText: Variants in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene LDLR can raise circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentrations and increase the risk of premature atherosclerosis. Definitive classifications are lacking for nearly half of clinically encountered LDLR missense variants.
experiment.methodText: We applied a multiplexed in vitro assay measuring LDLR cell-surface abundance via immunofluorescence. Barcoded cDNA libraries collectively containing nearly all possible single amino acid substitutions in LDLR were introduced at a genomically integrated Bxb1 “landing pad” in HeLa cells lacking endogenous LDLR. Cells were selected for LDL uptake via fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Functional scores were calculated by comparing barcode abundance in selected and unselected populations and scaled such that scores of 0 and 1 correspond to the median behaviour of nonsense and synonymous variants.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: The functional landscape of coding variation in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene LDLR
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract:
Variants in the familial hypercholesterolemia gene
                    LDLR
                    —the most important genetic driver of cardiovascular disease—can raise circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentrations and increase the risk of premature atherosclerosis. Definitive classifications are lacking for nearly half of clinically encountered
                    LDLR
                    missense variants, limiting interventions that reduce disease burden. Here, we tested the impact of ~17,000 (nearly all possible)
                    LDLR
                    missense coding variants on both LDLR cell-surface abundance and LDL uptake, yielding sequence–function maps that recapitulate known biochemistry, offer functional insights, and provide evidence for interpreting clinical variants. Functional scores correlated with hyperlipidemia phenotypes in prospective human cohorts and augmented polygenic scores to improve risk inference, highlighting the potential of this resource to accelerate familial hypercholesterolemia diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Thiamin biosynthesis sulfur carrier protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Thiamin biosynthesis sulfur carrier protein protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2K5P.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 78 variants that failed validation.

title: THO1 SAP domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the THO1 SAP domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: THO1 SAP domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the THO1 SAP domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SAP domain in THO1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P40040_PF02037_1.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: tnC4 combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Troponin C.

experiment.title: tnC4 combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Troponin C.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Troponin C protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2K2A.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 150 variants that failed validation.

title: tnC4 chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of Troponin C.

experiment.title: tnC4 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Troponin C.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Troponin C protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2K2A.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: TNNC2 EF-hand domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TNNC2 EF-hand domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TNNC2 EF-hand domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TNNC2 EF-hand domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the EF-hand domain in TNNC2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P02585_PF13499_1.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

title: TP53 ABE8e tiling screen with activity based selection (Etoposide arm)
shortDescription: Z-scores from a base editing screen employing ABE8e tiling TP53 under Etoposide challenge to identify mutations that can be introduced with base editing to disrupt protein function. This screen employs activity-based selection and corrects for self-editing to enhance resolution and accuracy.

experiment.title: TP53 base editing tiling screen with activity-based selection (Etoposide arm)
experiment.shortDescription:
Z-scores of base editing guides tiling TP53 (ENST00000269305.9)
 under Etoposide challenge to identify mutations that can be introduced with base editing to disrupt protein function. This screen employs activity-based selection and corrects for self-editing to enhance resolution and accuracy.
experiment.abstractText: Base editing is a CRISPR-based technology that enables high-throughput, nucleotide-level functional interrogation of the genome, which is essential for understanding the genetic basis of human disease and informing therapeutic development. We have developed a co-selection method that enriches for cells with high base editing activity, substantially increasing editing efficiency at a target locus. We evaluate this activity-based selection method by tiling guide RNAs across TP53, demonstrating its enhanced capacity to pinpoint specific mutations and protein regions of functional importance.
experiment.methodText: Guide abundance is measured at the Day 21 timepoint and corrected for self-editing (see [GitHub](github.com/ellkap/Base-editor-activity-based-selection) for implementation). We filtered out sgRNAs for which the log-normalized reads per million of the pDNA was > 3 standard deviations below the mean. Log fold change in sgRNA abundance is calculated for the Etoposide arm relative to the no drug arm. We then calculated z-scores relative to the intergenic control sgRNAs and averaged between replicates.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Activity-based selection for enhanced base editor mutational scanning
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: BSTRACTBase editing is a CRISPR-based technology that enables high-throughput, nucleotide-level functional interrogation of the genome, which is essential for understanding the genetic basis of human disease and informing therapeutic development. Base editing screens have emerged as a powerful experimental approach, yet significant cell-to-cell variability in editing efficiency introduces noise that may obscure meaningful results. Here, we develop a co-selection method that enriches for cells with high base editing activity, substantially increasing editing efficiency at a target locus. We evaluate this activity-based selection method against a traditional screening approach by tiling guide RNAs acrossTP53, demonstrating its enhanced capacity to pinpoint specific mutations and protein regions of functional importance. We anticipate that this modular selection method will enhance the resolution of base editing screens across many applications.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Activity-based selection for enhanced base editor mutational scanning
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: BSTRACTBase editing is a CRISPR-based technology that enables high-throughput, nucleotide-level functional interrogation of the genome, which is essential for understanding the genetic basis of human disease and informing therapeutic development. Base editing screens have emerged as a powerful experimental approach, yet significant cell-to-cell variability in editing efficiency introduces noise that may obscure meaningful results. Here, we develop a co-selection method that enriches for cells with high base editing activity, substantially increasing editing efficiency at a target locus. We evaluate this activity-based selection method against a traditional screening approach by tiling guide RNAs acrossTP53, demonstrating its enhanced capacity to pinpoint specific mutations and protein regions of functional importance. We anticipate that this modular selection method will enhance the resolution of base editing screens across many applications.

title: TP63 Sterile alpha motif domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TP63 Sterile alpha motif domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TP63 Sterile alpha motif domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TP63 Sterile alpha motif domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Sterile alpha motif domain in TP63 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9H3D4_PF07647_545.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: TPK1 DMS-TileSeq
shortDescription: A Deep Mutational Scan of human TPK1 using functional complementation in yeast via DMS-TileSeq.

experiment.title: TPK1 yeast complementation
experiment.shortDescription: A Deep Mutational Scan of human thiamin pyrophosphokinase (TPK1) using functional complementation in yeast.
experiment.abstractText: Although we now routinely sequence human genomes, we can confidently identify only a fraction of the sequence variants that have a functional impact. Here, we developed a deep mutational scanning framework that produces exhaustive maps for human missense variants by combining random codon mutagenesis and multiplexed functional variation assays with computational imputation and refinement. We applied this framework to four proteins corresponding to six human genes: UBE2I (encoding SUMO E2 conjugase), SUMO1 (small ubiquitin-like modifier), TPK1 (thiamin pyrophosphokinase), and CALM1/2/3 (three genes encoding the protein calmodulin). The resulting maps recapitulate known protein features and confidently identify pathogenic variation. Assays potentially amenable to deep mutational scanning are already available for 57% of human disease genes, suggesting that DMS could ultimately map functional variation for all human disease genes.
experiment.methodText: A Deep Mutational Scan of TPK1 (thiamin pyrophosphokinase) using functional complementation in yeast was performed using DMS-TileSeq and a machine-learning method was used to impute the effects of missing variants and refine measurements of lower confidence. See [**Weile *et al.* 2017**](http://msb.embopress.org/content/13/12/957) for details.

title: TPMT VAMP-seq
shortDescription: Amino acid scores for variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) applied to TPMT.

experiment.title: TPMT VAMP-seq
experiment.shortDescription: Variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) applied to TPMT.
experiment.abstractText: This study demonstrated variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq), a technique for measuring the effect of protein variants on abundance using fluorescence. VAMP-seq is a generally-applicable assay for protein stability that can identify loss-of-function variants.
experiment.methodText: Barcoded variant libraries were created using inverse PCR. Barcodes were associated with full-length variants using Pacific Biosciences SMRT sequencing to generate long reads. Each protein variant is fused to EGFP so that its abundance can be tracked using fluorescence. Cells were sorted into bins using FACS based on the ratio of EGFP to mCherry.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Multiplex assessment of protein variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Determining the pathogenicity of genetic variants is a critical challenge, and functional assessment is often the only option. Experimentally characterizing millions of possible missense variants in thousands of clinically important genes requires generalizable, scalable assays. We describe variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq), which measures the effects of thousands of missense variants of a protein on intracellular abundance simultaneously. We apply VAMP-seq to quantify the abundance of 7,801 single-amino-acid variants of PTEN and TPMT, proteins in which functional variants are clinically actionable. We identify 1,138 PTEN and 777 TPMT variants that result in low protein abundance, and may be pathogenic or alter drug metabolism, respectively. We observe selection for low-abundance PTEN variants in cancer, and show that p.Pro38Ser, which accounts for ~10% of PTEN missense variants in melanoma, functions via a dominant-negative mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate that VAMP-seq is applicable to other genes, highlighting its generalizability.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Matreyek KA, et al. Multiplex assessment of protein variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing. Nat. Genet. 2018; 50:874-882.

title: TpoR activation by high dosage of avatrombopag
shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for ligand-induced activation. This dataset contains scores for synonymous wildtype.

experiment.title: TpoR activation by high dosage of avatrombopag
experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for ligand-induced activation
experiment.abstractText: The human thrombopoietin receptor (hTpoR/MPL) plays a crucial role in platelet production and is the target of several biologic and small-molecule agonists used to treat thrombocytopenia. Mutations that cause constitutive hTpoR signalling through JAK2 can drive myeloproliferative diseases such as essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Several of the above drugs, and most disease-associated hTpoR mutations, act at or near the transmembrane (TM) domain, and specific TM and/or juxtamembrane (JM) structural transitions have been implicated in their mechanisms of action. Whether these non-native stimuli have shared or distinct structural mechanisms, and how these relate to activation by Tpo, remain unclear, and there is no high-resolution structure of the intact receptor that visualizes this crucial region. We employed deep mutational scanning to interrogate sequence-function relationships in the hTpoR TM-JM regions in response to four classes of stimuli: the native ligand Tpo, three small-molecule agonists eltrombopag, avatrombopag and lusutrombopag, a peptide mimic of the biologic agonist romiplostim and two disease-associated mutations S505N and W515K.
experiment.methodText:
The variant libraries were constructed using overlap extension PCR with degenerate oligos targeting the transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions of TpoR. We selected the libraries on cytokine dependent cell lines, where cell growth depended on TpoR activation to measure function in the context of different stimuli.
Cells were harvested after selection and RNA extracted to generate cDNA, which was indexed and prepared for direct Illumina sequencing. Raw sequenced data were trimmed and deduplicated before being analyzed with the DiMSum pipeline. We ensured at least two biological replicates were performed per datasets.
Functional scores were derived by comparing agonist-treated cells against IL3 treated (non-selective) controls. Functional scores were normalised so that the mean of nonsense variants was set to 0 (non-functional) and the mean of synonymous variants (functional) was set to 1.

experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for ligand-induced activation
experiment.abstractText: The human thrombopoietin receptor (hTpoR/MPL) plays a crucial role in platelet production and is the target of several biologic and small-molecule agonists used to treat thrombocytopenia. Mutations that cause constitutive hTpoR signalling through JAK2 can drive myeloproliferative diseases such as essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Several of the above drugs, and most disease-associated hTpoR mutations, act at or near the transmembrane (TM) domain, and specific TM and/or juxtamembrane (JM) structural transitions have been implicated in their mechanisms of action. Whether these non-native stimuli have shared or distinct structural mechanisms, and how these relate to activation by Tpo, remain unclear, and there is no high-resolution structure of the intact receptor that visualizes this crucial region. We employed deep mutational scanning to interrogate sequence-function relationships in the hTpoR TM-JM regions in response to four classes of stimuli: the native ligand Tpo, three small-molecule agonists eltrombopag, avatrombopag and lusutrombopag, a peptide mimic of the biologic agonist romiplostim and two disease-associated mutations S505N and W515K.
experiment.methodText:
The variant libraries were constructed using overlap extension PCR with degenerate oligos targeting the transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions of TpoR. We selected the libraries on cytokine dependent cell lines, where cell growth depended on TpoR activation to measure function in the context of different stimuli.
Cells were harvested after selection and RNA extracted to generate cDNA, which was indexed and prepared for direct Illumina sequencing. Raw sequenced data were trimmed and deduplicated before being analyzed with the DiMSum pipeline. We ensured at least two biological replicates were performed per datasets.
Functional scores were derived by comparing agonist-treated cells against IL3 treated (non-selective) controls. Functional scores were normalised so that the mean of nonsense variants was set to 0 (non-functional) and the mean of synonymous variants (functional) was set to 1.

experiment.title: TpoR activation by low dosage of eltrombopag
experiment.shortDescription: Deep Mutational Scanning of the TpoR transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains to explore sequence requirements for ligand-induced activation
experiment.abstractText: The human thrombopoietin receptor (hTpoR/MPL) plays a crucial role in platelet production and is the target of several biologic and small-molecule agonists used to treat thrombocytopenia. Mutations that cause constitutive hTpoR signalling through JAK2 can drive myeloproliferative diseases such as essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Several of the above drugs, and most disease-associated hTpoR mutations, act at or near the transmembrane (TM) domain, and specific TM and/or juxtamembrane (JM) structural transitions have been implicated in their mechanisms of action. Whether these non-native stimuli have shared or distinct structural mechanisms, and how these relate to activation by Tpo, remain unclear, and there is no high-resolution structure of the intact receptor that visualizes this crucial region. We employed deep mutational scanning to interrogate sequence-function relationships in the hTpoR TM-JM regions in response to four classes of stimuli: the native ligand Tpo, three small-molecule agonists eltrombopag, avatrombopag and lusutrombopag, a peptide mimic of the biologic agonist romiplostim and two disease-associated mutations S505N and W515K.
experiment.methodText:
The variant libraries were constructed using overlap extension PCR with degenerate oligos targeting the transmembrane and juxtamembrane regions of TpoR. We selected the libraries on cytokine dependent cell lines, where cell growth depended on TpoR activation to measure function in the context of different stimuli.
Cells were harvested after selection and RNA extracted to generate cDNA, which was indexed and prepared for direct Illumina sequencing. Raw sequenced data were trimmed and deduplicated before being analyzed with the DiMSum pipeline. We ensured at least two biological replicates were performed per datasets.
Functional scores were derived by comparing agonist-treated cells against IL3 treated (non-selective) controls. Functional scores were normalised so that the mean of nonsense variants was set to 0 (non-functional) and the mean of synonymous variants (functional) was set to 1.

title: TRIM26 B-box-type zinc finger domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TRIM26 B-box-type zinc finger domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TRIM26 B-box-type zinc finger domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TRIM26 B-box-type zinc finger domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the B-box-type zinc finger domain in TRIM26 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q12899_PF00643_97.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study used variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) to measure protein abundance using fluorescence of TSC2. This assay identifies variants that are loss of function due to loss of abundance/stability.
experiment.methodText: This meta-analysis combines the two domain-level score analysis and adds functional classes. Variant functional classes were determined using a GMM approach.

experiment.title: TSC2 RapGAP
experiment.shortDescription: VAMP-seq assay for the TSC2 RapGAP domain.
experiment.abstractText: This study used variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) to measure protein abundance using fluorescence in the RapGAP domain of TSC2. This assay identifies variants that are loss of function due to loss of abundance/stability.
experiment.methodText: The variant library was ordered from Twist Biosciences and assembled into a plasmid along with the variant barcode. These plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells containing a Bxb1 Tet-on landing pad for stable integration. Cells were sorted using FACS and barcodes from each bin were sequenced using Illumina. Barcode-variant associates were resolved using PacBio long read sequencing and analysed using Pacybara.

title: TSC2 Tuberin Domain Scores
shortDescription: Scores for the TSC2 Tuberin domain VAMP-seq assay.

experiment.title: TSC2 Tuberin
experiment.shortDescription: VAMP-seq assay for the TSC2 Tuberin domain.
experiment.abstractText: This study used variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing (VAMP-seq) to measure protein abundance using fluorescence in the Tuberin domain of TSC2. This assay identifies variants that are loss of function due to loss of abundance/stability.
experiment.methodText: The variant library was ordered from Twist Biosciences and assembled into a plasmid along with the variant barcode. These plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells containing a Bxb1 Tet-on landing pad for stable integration. Cells were sorted using FACS and barcodes from each bin were sequenced using Illumina. Barcode-variant associates were resolved using PacBio long read sequencing and analysed using Pacybara.

title: TTC3 Zinc finger, RING-type domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TTC3 Zinc finger, RING-type domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: TTC3 Zinc finger, RING-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the TTC3 Zinc finger, RING-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, RING-type domain in TTC3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P53804_PF13639_1957.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12.

experiment.title: Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 4AME.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 39 variants that failed validation.

title: Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 isoform chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 isoform.

experiment.title: Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 isoform trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 isoform.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Type-3 ice-structuring protein HPLC 12 isoform protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1EKL.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: UBE2I joint data
shortDescription: A joint Deep Mutational Scan dataset of the human SUMO E2 conjugase UBE2I using functional complementation in yeast, combining DMS-BarSeq and DMS-TileSeq

experiment.title: UBE2I yeast complementation
experiment.shortDescription: A Deep Mutational Scan of the human SUMO E2 conjugase UBE2I using functional complementation in yeast.
experiment.abstractText: Although we now routinely sequence human genomes, we can confidently identify only a fraction of the sequence variants that have a functional impact. Here, we developed a deep mutational scanning framework that produces exhaustive maps for human missense variants by combining random codon mutagenesis and multiplexed functional variation assays with computational imputation and refinement. We applied this framework to four proteins corresponding to six human genes: UBE2I (encoding SUMO E2 conjugase), SUMO1 (small ubiquitin-like modifier), TPK1 (thiamin pyrophosphokinase), and CALM1/2/3 (three genes encoding the protein calmodulin). The resulting maps recapitulate known protein features and confidently identify pathogenic variation. Assays potentially amenable to deep mutational scanning are already available for 57% of human disease genes, suggesting that DMS could ultimately map functional variation for all human disease genes.
experiment.methodText: A Deep Mutational Scan of UBE2I using functional complementation in yeast was performed using two different methods: DMS-BarSeq and DMS-TileSeq, both datasets were combined and a machine-learning method was used to impute the effects of missing variants and refine measurements of lower confidence. See [**Weile *et al.* 2017**](http://msb.embopress.org/content/13/12/957) for details.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the UBE2K Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: UBE2K Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the UBE2K Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Ubiquitin-associated domain in UBE2K using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P61086_PF00627_158.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: UBE4B combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Ubiquitin conjugation factor E4 B.

experiment.title: UBE4B combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Ubiquitin conjugation factor E4 B.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Ubiquitin conjugation factor E4 B protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 3L1X.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 384 variants that failed validation.

title: UBE4B trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Ubiquitin conjugation factor E4 B.

experiment.title: UBE4B trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Ubiquitin conjugation factor E4 B.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Ubiquitin conjugation factor E4 B protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 3L1X.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.title: Ubiquitin E1 binding, excess E1
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of ubiquitin measuring binding to E1 with yeast display with excess E1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the effect of single amino acid changes in ubiquitin on binding to E1 (Uba1). Combined with work from a previous study on the effect of ubiquitin mutations on yeast growth rate, this showed that ubiquitin-E1 binding was not linearly related to growth rate and that mutations in ubiquitin are likely to affect multiple function that modulate growth rate.
experiment.methodText:
This experiment used the same library of ubiquitin variants as previously described in Roscoe et al. 2013. The ubiqutin variants were displayed as C-terminal fusions with Aga2-HA and reacted with E1. Bound cells were isolated using FACS and deep sequencing was used to quantify enrichment or depletion of cells in the bound population.

The excess E1 assay was performed on two separate sub-regions of ubiquitin.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Systematic exploration of ubiquitin sequence, E1 activation efficiency, and experimental fitness in yeast.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The complexity of biological interaction networks poses a challenge to understanding the function of individual connections in the overall network. To address this challenge, we developed a high-throughput reverse engineering strategy to analyze how thousands of specific perturbations (encompassing all point mutations in a central gene) impact both a specific edge (interaction to a directly connected node) and an overall network function. We analyzed the effects of ubiquitin mutations on activation by the E1 enzyme and compared these to effects on yeast growth rate. Using this approach, we delineated ubiquitin mutations that selectively impacted the ubiquitin-E1 edge. We find that the elasticity function relating the efficiency of ubiquitin-E1 interaction to growth rate is non-linear and that a greater than 50-fold decrease in E1 activation efficiency is required to reduce growth rate by 2-fold. Despite the robustness of fitness to decreases in E1 activation efficiency, the effects of most ubiquitin mutations on E1 activation paralleled the effects on growth rate. Our observations indicate that most ubiquitin mutations that disrupt E1 activation also disrupt other functions. The structurally characterized ubiquitin-E1 interface encompasses the interfaces of ubiquitin with most other known binding partners, and we propose that this enables E1 in wild-type cells to selectively activate ubiquitin protein molecules capable of binding to other partners from the cytoplasmic pool of ubiquitin protein that will include molecules with chemical damage and/or errors from transcription and translation.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Roscoe BP and Bolon DN. Systematic exploration of ubiquitin sequence, E1 activation efficiency, and experimental fitness in yeast. J. Mol. Biol. 2014; 426:2854-70.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Analyses of the effects of all ubiquitin point mutants on yeast growth rate.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The amino acid sequence of a protein governs its function. We used bulk competition and focused deep sequencing to investigate the effects of all ubiquitin point mutants on yeast growth rate. Many aspects of ubiquitin function have been carefully studied, which enabled interpretation of our growth analyses in light of a rich structural, biophysical and biochemical knowledge base. In one highly sensitive cluster on the surface of ubiquitin, almost every amino acid substitution caused growth defects. In contrast, the opposite face tolerated virtually all possible substitutions. Surface locations between these two faces exhibited intermediate mutational tolerance. The sensitive face corresponds to the known interface for many binding partners. Across all surface positions, we observe a strong correlation between burial at structurally characterized interfaces and the number of amino acid substitutions compatible with robust growth. This result indicates that binding is a dominant determinant of ubiquitin function. In the solvent-inaccessible core of ubiquitin, all positions tolerated a limited number of substitutions, with hydrophobic amino acids especially interchangeable. Some mutations null for yeast growth were previously shown to populate folded conformations indicating that, for these mutants, subtle changes to conformation caused functional defects. The most sensitive region to mutation within the core was located near the C-terminus that is a focal binding site for many critical binding partners. These results indicate that core mutations may frequently cause functional defects through subtle disturbances to structure or dynamics.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Roscoe BP, et al. Analyses of the effects of all ubiquitin point mutants on yeast growth rate. J. Mol. Biol. 2013; 425:1363-77.

Surface locations between these two faces exhibited intermediate mutational tolerance. The sensitive face corresponds to the known interface for many binding partners. Across all surface positions, we observe a strong correlation between burial at structurally characterized interfaces and the number of amino acid substitutions compatible with robust growth. This result indicates that binding is a dominant determinant of ubiquitin function. In the solvent-inaccessible core of ubiquitin, all positions tolerated a limited number of substitutions, with hydrophobic amino acids especially interchangeable. Some mutations null for yeast growth were previously shown to populate folded conformations indicating that, for these mutants, subtle changes to conformation caused functional defects. The most sensitive region to mutation within the core was located near the C-terminus that is a focal binding site for many critical binding partners. These results indicate that core mutations may frequently cause functional defects through subtle disturbances to structure or dynamics.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Systematic exploration of ubiquitin sequence, E1 activation efficiency, and experimental fitness in yeast.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The complexity of biological interaction networks poses a challenge to understanding the function of individual connections in the overall network. To address this challenge, we developed a high-throughput reverse engineering strategy to analyze how thousands of specific perturbations (encompassing all point mutations in a central gene) impact both a specific edge (interaction to a directly connected node) and an overall network function. We analyzed the effects of ubiquitin mutations on activation by the E1 enzyme and compared these to effects on yeast growth rate. Using this approach, we delineated ubiquitin mutations that selectively impacted the ubiquitin-E1 edge. We find that the elasticity function relating the efficiency of ubiquitin-E1 interaction to growth rate is non-linear and that a greater than 50-fold decrease in E1 activation efficiency is required to reduce growth rate by 2-fold. Despite the robustness of fitness to decreases in E1 activation efficiency, the effects of most ubiquitin mutations on E1 activation paralleled the effects on growth rate. Our observations indicate that most ubiquitin mutations that disrupt E1 activation also disrupt other functions. The structurally characterized ubiquitin-E1 interface encompasses the interfaces of ubiquitin with most other known binding partners, and we propose that this enables E1 in wild-type cells to selectively activate ubiquitin protein molecules capable of binding to other partners from the cytoplasmic pool of ubiquitin protein that will include molecules with chemical damage and/or errors from transcription and translation.

experiment.title: Ubiquitin yeast growth
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of ubiquitin in a yeast growth assay
experiment.abstractText: This study performed a bulk growth competition experiment measuring the effect of point mutations on ubiquitin structure and function. The results were consistent with previous studies of individual mutants as well as Alanine-scanning. Positions were clustered by their tolerance of mutations and highly sensitive regions were mapped.
experiment.methodText: Variant construction, DNA sequencing, and analysis was conducted using EMPIRIC [Hietpas et al.]. Variants were transformed into the Sub328 ubiquitin shutoff strain, which produces sufficient ubiquitin in galactose but not in dextrose. The competition assay was therefore performed in dextrose media, whereas the libraries were constructed and maintained in galactose media.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Experimental illumination of a fitness landscape.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The genes of all organisms have been shaped by selective pressures. The relationship between gene sequence and fitness has tremendous implications for understanding both evolutionary processes and functional constraints on the encoded proteins. Here, we have exploited deep sequencing technology to experimentally determine the fitness of all possible individual point mutants under controlled conditions for a nine-amino acid region of Hsp90. Over the past five decades, limited glimpses into the relationship between gene sequence and function have sparked a long debate regarding the distribution, relative proportion, and evolutionary significance of deleterious, neutral, and advantageous mutations. Our systematic experimental measurement of fitness effects of Hsp90 mutants in yeast, evaluated in the light of existing population genetic theory, are remarkably consistent with a nearly neutral model of molecular evolution.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Hietpas RT, et al. Experimental illumination of a fitness landscape. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 2011; 108:7896-901.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the UBQLN3 Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: UBQLN3 Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the UBQLN3 Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Ubiquitin-associated domain in UBQLN3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9H347_PF00627_613.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

shortDescription: Model combined scores for E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR5 .

experiment.title: UBR5 combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR5 .
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR5  protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1I2T.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 39 variants that failed validation.

title: UBR5 chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR5 .

experiment.title: UBR5 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR5 .
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase UBR5  protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1I2T.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Uncharacterized protein (L8K) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 6NS8.pdb_L8K.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: Unregulated-Ras
shortDescription: Selection result of Ras mutants expressed without the GAP or the GEF

experiment.title: Unregulated-Ras
experiment.shortDescription: Selection result of Ras mutants expressed without the GAP or the GEF
experiment.abstractText: The authors used saturation mutagenesis to study the variant effect of Ras, without the regulation of GTPase activating protein (GAP) or guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF). The variants were selected using a bacterial two-hybrid strategy.
experiment.methodText: The RAS mutant library was generated by oligonucleotide-directed mutagenesis. The mutant library was transfected into bacteria without GAP or GEF expression and the functioning RAS protein which will bind to GTP as well as Raf. The binding of these molecules can trigger the transcription of an antibiotic resistant factor. The library was separated into three sub-libraries in order to cover the whole RAS gene length which ranges from the residue 2-56, 57-111, and 112-166. These samples were selected individually. The samples in different sub-libraries were barcoded and pooled together for MiSeq sequencing.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deconstruction of the Ras switching cycle through saturation mutagenesis.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Ras proteins are highly conserved signaling molecules that exhibit regulated, nucleotide-dependent switching between active and inactive states. The high conservation of Ras requires mechanistic explanation, especially given the general mutational tolerance of proteins. Here, we use deep mutational scanning, biochemical analysis and molecular simulations to understand constraints on Ras sequence. Ras exhibits global sensitivity to mutation when regulated by a GTPase activating protein and a nucleotide exchange factor. Removing the regulators shifts the distribution of mutational effects to be largely neutral, and reveals hotspots of activating mutations in residues that restrain Ras dynamics and promote the inactive state. Evolutionary analysis, combined with structural and mutational data, argue that Ras has co-evolved with its regulators in the vertebrate lineage. Overall, our results show that sequence conservation in Ras depends strongly on the biochemical network in which it operates, providing a framework for understanding the origin of global selection pressures on proteins.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Bandaru P, et al. Deconstruction of the Ras switching cycle through saturation mutagenesis. Elife. 2017; 6:None.

experiment.title: USH1C PDZ domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the USH1C PDZ domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the PDZ domain in USH1C using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9Y6N9_PF00595_207.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: VarChAMP_Imaging_Morphological_Change_May_2025
shortDescription: Cell morphological changes from images of cells.

experiment.title: VarChAMP_Imaging_May_2025
experiment.shortDescription: Protein localization & abundance and cell morphological changes from images of cells.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured protein subcellular localization and abundance, and cell morphological changes using fluorescence microscopy.
experiment.methodText: Entry clones of alleles were transferred using Gateway technology into a mammalian expression pLenti6.2 plasmid containing a C-terminal mNeonGreen fusion (plasmid modified from Addgene 87075). Inserts were verified by restriction digestion and clones that did not produce the expected digestion pattern were omitted from further analysis. Lentiviral constructs were packaged in HEK 293T cells seeded in 96-well plates, then viral supernatant was transferred to spinfect U2OS cells seeded in 384-well plates (4x technical replicates were performed by administering the same viral supernatant to 4 different wells, all viral production and infection was repeated for on a separate day 2x biological replicates). 48 hrs following infection, cells were selected for infection and protein overexpression by applying puromycin for 48 hrs. Cells were then stained with 500 nM MitoTracker Deep Red 1 hr prior to paraformaldehyde fixation. Blocking, permeabilization and staining (8.25 nM Alexa Fluor™ 568 Phalloidin, 1 ug/mL Hoechst 33342, 1.5 ug/mL WGA Alexa Fluor 555) was then performed in one step. All confocal images were captured on a Perkin Elmer Opera Phenix Microscope (20X water objective, 384 wells, 9 fields).

title: Amino acid scores for Aβ42 variants
shortDescription: Amino acid level scores for molecular determinants of Aβ aggregation with deep mutational scanning

experiment.title: Variants of Aβ42 affecting aggregation
experiment.shortDescription: Molecular determinants of Aβ aggregation with Deep Mutational Scanning
experiment.abstractText: This experiment measured the molecular determinants of A$\beta$ 42 aggregation in a cell-based system, by combining a yeast DHFR aggregation assay with deep mutational scanning. The effect of 791 of the 798 possible single amino acid substitutions on the aggregation propensity of A$\beta$ 42 was measured using a yeast growth-based aggregation assay.
experiment.methodText: The variant library was cloned using in vivo assembly. To measure A$\beta$ aggregation by yeast growth rate, A$\beta$ was fused to dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) via a short peptide linker. DHFR is required for growth and the activity of the fusion protein depends on the solubility of A$\beta$. When treated with DHFR inhibitor methotrexate, yeast with soluble A$\beta$ variants grow more rapidly that those with aggregating A$\beta$ variants. High-throughput DNA sequencing was used to measure the frequency of each variant. Six time points (including the starting time point) were measured during the course of the assay. Three replicate assays were performed.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. experiment.title: VIL1 trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Villin-1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Villin-1 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 1VII.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.
