title: VIM-2 0.031 µg/mL MEM at 37C
shortDescription: Amino acid scores for deep mutational scan of VIM-2 metallo-β-lactamase at 0.031 µg/mL meropenem at 37C

experiment.title: VIM-2 0.031 µg/mL MEM at 37C
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of VIM-2 metallo-β-lactamase at 0.031 µg/mL meropenem at 37C
experiment.abstractText: Saturation mutagenesis of VIM-2 metallo-β-lactamase was performed to determine substrate recognition and better understand the ability to recognize new substrates. The VIM-2 signal peptide plays a role in expression and transport and was included in the analysis. Relative fitness was determined in the presence of three antibiotics (ampicillin, cefotaxime, and meropenem).
experiment.methodText:
The variant library was constructed using degenerate NNN codons introduced by PCR to generate libraries of single amino acid mutations. Seven libraries were constructed, each with 39 consecutive codons (33 for the last library) to enable fully-overlapping 150-bp paired-end sequencing using Illumina NextSeq.

Two replicate selections were performed for each library.

An additional GGA (Gly) codon was introduced immediately after the start codon in order to create an NcoI restriction site for cloning into the pIDR2 (chloramphenicol resistance) plasmid.

The variant library was transformed into E.coli (E. cloni 10G strain) and selected for chloramphenicol resistance. These cells containing the VIM-2 plasmid were then split into 7 different groups for antibiotic selection.

This record describes the selection performed on VIM-2 at 0.031 µg/mL meropenem at 37C.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Comprehensive exploration of the translocation, stability and substrate recognition requirements in VIM-2 lactamase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) degrade a broad spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics, and are a major disseminating source for multidrug resistant bacteria. Despite many biochemical studies in diverse MBLs, molecular understanding of the roles of residues in the enzyme's stability and function, and especially substrate specificity, is lacking. Here, we employ deep mutational scanning (DMS) to generate comprehensive single amino acid variant data on a major clinical MBL, VIM-2, by measuring the effect of thousands of VIM-2 mutants on the degradation of three representative classes of β-lactams (ampicillin, cefotaxime, and meropenem) and at two different temperatures (25°C and 37°C). We revealed residues responsible for expression and translocation, and mutations that increase resistance and/or alter substrate specificity. The distribution of specificity-altering mutations unveiled distinct molecular recognition of the three substrates. Moreover, these function-altering mutations are frequently observed among naturally occurring variants, suggesting that the enzymes have continuously evolved to become more potent resistance genes.

The variant library was transformed into E.coli (E. cloni 10G strain) and selected for chloramphenicol resistance. These cells containing the VIM-2 plasmid were then split into 7 different groups for antibiotic selection.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Comprehensive exploration of the translocation, stability and substrate recognition requirements in VIM-2 lactamase.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) degrade a broad spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics, and are a major disseminating source for multidrug resistant bacteria. Despite many biochemical studies in diverse MBLs, molecular understanding of the roles of residues in the enzyme's stability and function, and especially substrate specificity, is lacking. Here, we employ deep mutational scanning (DMS) to generate comprehensive single amino acid variant data on a major clinical MBL, VIM-2, by measuring the effect of thousands of VIM-2 mutants on the degradation of three representative classes of β-lactams (ampicillin, cefotaxime, and meropenem) and at two different temperatures (25°C and 37°C). We revealed residues responsible for expression and translocation, and mutations that increase resistance and/or alter substrate specificity. The distribution of specificity-altering mutations unveiled distinct molecular recognition of the three substrates. Moreover, these function-altering mutations are frequently observed among naturally occurring variants, suggesting that the enzymes have continuously evolved to become more potent resistance genes.

experiment.title: VKOR carboxylation activity
experiment.shortDescription: Carboxylation activity of VKOR variants by substrate surface expression.
experiment.abstractText: This study tested the carboxylation activity change of vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) variants. The functioning VKOR is able to carboxylate Factor IX domain which is secreted and retained on the cell surface. By culturing the cells with fluorophore-labeled carboxylation-specific antibody, the impact of VKOR variants to its carboxylation activity can be determined by FACS.
experiment.methodText: The variant library is generated by mutagenesis primers through PCR which contains 697 missense mutations. Each bin is deeply sequenced and the final abundance scores are calculated.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Multiplexed measurement of variant abundance and activity reveals VKOR topology, active site and human variant impact.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) drives the vitamin K cycle, activating vitamin K-dependent blood clotting factors. VKOR is also the target of the widely used anticoagulant drug, warfarin. Despite VKOR's pivotal role in coagulation, its structure and active site remain poorly understood. In addition, VKOR variants can cause vitamin K-dependent clotting factor deficiency or alter warfarin response. Here, we used multiplexed, sequencing-based assays to measure the effects of 2,695 VKOR missense variants on abundance and 697 variants on activity in cultured human cells. The large-scale functional data, along with an evolutionary coupling analysis, supports a four transmembrane domain topology, with variants in transmembrane domains exhibiting strongly deleterious effects on abundance and activity. Functionally constrained regions of the protein define the active site, and we find that, of four conserved cysteines putatively critical for function, only three are absolutely required. Finally, 25% of human VKOR missense variants show reduced abundance or activity, possibly conferring warfarin sensitivity or causing disease.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Chiasson MA, et al. Multiplexed measurement of variant abundance and activity reveals VKOR topology, active site and human variant impact. Elife. 2020; 9:None.

title: VKOR protein stability
shortDescription: VKOR protein stability measured by VAMP-seq.

experiment.title: VKOR protein stability
experiment.shortDescription: VKOR protein stability measured by VAMP-seq.
experiment.abstractText: This study tested the impact of vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) variants affecting protein abundance using VAMP-seq. The mutated VKOR are fused with eGFP and variants leading to misfolded proteins will cause a decrease in fluorescence intensity. The variant library is expressed in human HEK293T cells and selected by FACS to indicate the variant effects.
experiment.methodText: The variant is generated by mutagenesis primers through PCR which is barcoded and covers 92.5% of all possible variants. This library is introduced to HEK293T cells using a landing pad. The cell line also expresses mCherry from an internal ribosomal entry site as a control for protein expression. Individual cells are then sorted using FACS to four bins according to the relative intensity of eGFP and mCherry. Each bin is deeply sequenced and the final abundance scores are calculated.

title: WBP4 U1-C, C2H2-type zinc finger domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the WBP4 U1-C, C2H2-type zinc finger domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: WBP4 U1-C, C2H2-type zinc finger domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the WBP4 U1-C, C2H2-type zinc finger domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the U1-C, C2H2-type zinc finger domain in WBP4 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O75554_PF06220_8.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of NEDD4-like E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase WWP1.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of NEDD4-like E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase WWP1 protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2OP7.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: WWP1 WW domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the WWP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: WWP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the WWP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the WW domain in WWP1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9H0M0_PF00397_343.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Putative periplasmic protein.

experiment.title: yahO trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Putative periplasmic protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Putative periplasmic protein protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2MA4.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: YAP1 WW domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the YAP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: YAP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the YAP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the WW domain in YAP1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P46937_PF00397_165.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: Enrich2 nucleotide variant scores for YAP65 WW domain
shortDescription: Nucleotide variant scores for deep mutational scan of the hYAP65 WW domain using phage display calculated by Enrich2.

experiment.title: YAP65 WW domain
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of the hYAP65 WW domain using phage display.
experiment.abstractText: This was the first published deep mutational scan. The experiment quantified binding affinity between the human YAP65 (YAP1) WW domain and a peptide binding partner using phage display. The phage display selection was tuned such that the enrichment in each round was moderate, allowing inefficient binders to be maintained in the population and subsequently quantified.
experiment.methodText: The target sequence was a codon-optimized human YAP65 WW domain. The variant library was constructed using doped oligo synthesis, with 0.7% of each non-target base at each position. The phage display was performed using T7 phage and selection for binding to biotinylated GTPPPPYTVG peptide attached to streptavidin-coated magnetic beads. Paired-end Illumina sequencing was performed such that both forward and reverse reads fully overlapped the variable region.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: High-resolution mapping of protein sequence-function relationships.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: We present a large-scale approach to investigate the functional consequences of sequence variation in a protein. The approach entails the display of hundreds of thousands of protein variants, moderate selection for activity and high-throughput DNA sequencing to quantify the performance of each variant. Using this strategy, we tracked the performance of >600,000 variants of a human WW domain after three and six rounds of selection by phage display for binding to its peptide ligand. Binding properties of these variants defined a high-resolution map of mutational preference across the WW domain; each position had unique features that could not be captured by a few representative mutations. Our approach could be applied to many in vitro or in vivo protein assays, providing a general means for understanding how protein function relates to sequence.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Fowler DM, et al. High-resolution mapping of protein sequence-function relationships. Nat. Methods. 2010; 7:741-6.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A fundamental protein property, thermodynamic stability, revealed solely from large-scale measurements of protein function.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: The ability of a protein to carry out a given function results from fundamental physicochemical properties that include the protein's structure, mechanism of action, and thermodynamic stability. Traditional approaches to study these properties have typically required the direct measurement of the property of interest, oftentimes a laborious undertaking. Although protein properties can be probed by mutagenesis, this approach has been limited by its low throughput. Recent technological developments have enabled the rapid quantification of a protein's function, such as binding to a ligand, for numerous variants of that protein. Here, we measure the ability of 47,000 variants of a WW domain to bind to a peptide ligand and use these functional measurements to identify stabilizing mutations without directly assaying stability. Our approach is rooted in the well-established concept that protein function is closely related to stability. Protein function is generally reduced by destabilizing mutations, but this decrease can be rescued by stabilizing mutations. Based on this observation, we introduce partner potentiation, a metric that uses this rescue ability to identify stabilizing mutations, and identify 15 candidate stabilizing mutations in the WW domain. We tested six candidates by thermal denaturation and found two highly stabilizing mutations, one more stabilizing than any previously known mutation. Thus, physicochemical properties such as stability are latent within these large-scale protein functional data and can be revealed by systematic analysis. This approach should allow other protein properties to be discovered.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.publicationJournal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Araya CL, et al. A fundamental protein property, thermodynamic stability, revealed solely from large-scale measurements of protein function. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 2012; 109:16858-63.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A statistical framework for analyzing deep mutational scanning data.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Deep mutational scanning is a widely used method for multiplex measurement of functional consequences of protein variants. We developed a new deep mutational scanning statistical model that generates error estimates for each measurement, capturing both sampling error and consistency between replicates. We apply our model to one novel and five published datasets comprising 243,732 variants and demonstrate its superiority in removing noisy variants and conducting hypothesis testing. Simulations show our model applies to scans based on cell growth or binding and handles common experimental errors. We implemented our model in Enrich2, software that can empower researchers analyzing deep mutational scanning data.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.referenceHtml: Rubin AF, et al. A statistical framework for analyzing deep mutational scanning data. Genome Biol. 2017; 18:150.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Cold-shock protein, DNA-binding domain in YBX2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9Y2T7_PF00313_86.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: ydgH combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for Putative periplasmic protein.

experiment.title: ydgH combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for Putative periplasmic protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Putative periplasmic protein protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2M2J.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases. Removed 234 variants that failed validation.

title: ydgH chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of Putative periplasmic protein.

experiment.title: ydgH trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of Putative periplasmic protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of Putative periplasmic protein protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2M2J.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: Yeast growth Hsp82 (Hsp90)
shortDescription: Amino acid scores for yeast growth assay of Hsp82 (yeast Hsp90) covering the first 231 positions.

experiment.title: Yeast growth Hsp82 (Hsp90)
experiment.shortDescription: Yeast growth assay of Hsp82 (yeast Hsp90) covering the first 231 positions.
experiment.abstractText: Systematic mutagenesis was used to create a mutant library of Hsp82 (yeast Hsp90) genes from yeast across the gene to assess protein fitness.
experiment.methodText:
Fully randomized codons (NNN codons) were generated for each position and inserted into plasmids using a cassette ligation strategy. 

The assay was performed in p414ADHΔTER, which has a reduced level of Hsp82 and therefore sensitized the yeast.

Two biological replicates were performed for positions 12-21 and 92-101.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Systematic Mutant Analyses Elucidate General and Client-Specific Aspects of Hsp90 Function.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: To probe the mechanism of the Hsp90 chaperone that is required for the maturation of many signaling proteins in eukaryotes, we analyzed the effects of all individual amino acid changes in the ATPase domain on yeast growth rate. The sensitivity of a position to mutation was strongly influenced by proximity to the phosphates of ATP, indicating that ATPase-driven conformational changes impose stringent physical constraints on Hsp90. To investigate how these constraints may vary for different clients, we performed biochemical analyses on a panel of Hsp90 mutants spanning the full range of observed fitness effects. We observed distinct effects of nine Hsp90 mutations on activation of v-src and glucocorticoid receptor (GR), indicating that different chaperone mechanisms can be utilized for these clients. These results provide a detailed guide for understanding Hsp90 mechanism and highlight the potential for inhibitors of Hsp90 that target a subset of clients.

title: zf-CHCC domain-containing protein combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for zf-CHCC domain-containing protein.

experiment.title: zf-CHCC domain-containing protein combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for zf-CHCC domain-containing protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of zf-CHCC domain-containing protein protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2JRR.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: zf-CHCC domain-containing protein chymotrypsin digestion
shortDescription: Chymotrypsin digestion of zf-CHCC domain-containing protein.

experiment.title: zf-CHCC domain-containing protein trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of zf-CHCC domain-containing protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of zf-CHCC domain-containing protein protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2JRR.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: ZHER2 Affibody (alternative) combined scores
shortDescription: Model combined scores for ZHER2 Affibody (alternative).

experiment.title: ZHER2 Affibody (alternative) combined scores
experiment.shortDescription: Model combined scores for ZHER2 Affibody (alternative).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of ZHER2 Affibody (alternative) protein variants with both trypsin and chymotripsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2KZJ.pdb.
experiment.methodText: The score column is the dG value calculated using the coupled model, calculated from the counts across replicates and proteases. dG values were fit directly using a Bayesian model, assuming that each sequence has a shared dG value that is shared across both proteases.

title: ZHER2 Affibody (alternative) trypsin digestion
shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of ZHER2 Affibody (alternative).

experiment.title: ZHER2 Affibody (alternative) trypsin digestion
experiment.shortDescription: Trypsin digestion of ZHER2 Affibody (alternative).
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the digestion of ZHER2 Affibody (alternative) protein variants with trypsin to measure the effect of these variants on folding. The target accession used in the original study is 2KZJ.pdb.
experiment.methodText: Sequences were reverse-transcribed and codon optimized using E. coli codon frequencies. Oligo libraries containing mutations were purchased from Agilent or Twist. The libraries were transcribed and translated using cDNA display such that proteins are attached to the cDNA at the C-terminus and have a PA tag at the N-terminus. The protein-cDNA complexes were purified and subjected to a protease assay such that only undigested molecules would retain the PA tag and the cDNA linkage. High-throughput Illumina sequencing was used to quantify the amount of each variant after the assay.

title: Zika E protein DMS
shortDescription: Site preference scores for deep mutational scan of the Zika Virus E protein.

experiment.title: Zika E protein DMS
experiment.shortDescription: Deep mutational scan of the Zika Virus E protein.
experiment.abstractText: This study presents a neutralization based assay to assess mutations’ in the E protein in the viral envelope of Zika Virus (ZIKV). E protein genes were used to detect variant interactions' effect on viral neutralization by monoclonal antibodies. DMS measured 9,576 possible amino acid mutations that contribute to 31,752 possible mutant codon sequences within the E protein. Variant infectivity was determined by a TCID50 assay.
experiment.methodText:
Mutant plasmid libraries were created by cloning the entire E protein coding sequence into a single plasmid of Zika virus, strain MR766. 

Mutagenesis was performed to generate single amino acid mutations on the E protein gene through NNN PCR. Three fully independent biological replicates were performed.

293T cells were used to produce pools of virus genomes encoding all E protein mutants. Functional variants were selected by infecting Vero cells at low MOI. Input viruses were washed away and infection was allowed to continue for 3 or 4 rounds of additional infection, leading to enrichment of functional variants.

Viral RNA was extracted from the Vero cell population, reverse-transcribed, and sequenced using barcoded sub-amplicon sequencing.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Deep Mutational Scanning Comprehensively Maps How Zika Envelope Protein Mutations Affect Viral Growth and Antibody Escape.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Functional constraints on viral proteins are often assessed by examining sequence conservation among natural strains, but this approach is relatively ineffective for Zika virus because all known sequences are highly similar. Here, we take an alternative approach to map functional constraints on Zika virus's envelope (E) protein by using deep mutational scanning to measure how all amino acid mutations to the E protein affect viral growth in cell culture. The resulting sequence-function map is consistent with existing knowledge about E protein structure and function but also provides insight into mutation-level constraints in many regions of the protein that have not been well characterized in prior functional work. In addition, we extend our approach to completely map how mutations affect viral neutralization by two monoclonal antibodies, thereby precisely defining their functional epitopes. Overall, our study provides a valuable resource for understanding the effects of mutations to this important viral protein and also offers a roadmap for future work to map functional and antigenic selection to Zika virus at high resolution.

secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Software for the analysis and visualization of deep mutational scanning data.
secondaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Deep mutational scanning is a technique to estimate the impacts of mutations on a gene by using deep sequencing to count mutations in a library of variants before and after imposing a functional selection. The impacts of mutations must be inferred from changes in their counts after selection.
RESULTS: I describe a software package, dms_tools, to infer the impacts of mutations from deep mutational scanning data using a likelihood-based treatment of the mutation counts. I show that dms_tools yields more accurate inferences on simulated data than simply calculating ratios of counts pre- and post-selection. Using dms_tools, one can infer the preference of each site for each amino acid given a single selection pressure, or assess the extent to which these preferences change under different selection pressures. The preferences and their changes can be intuitively visualized with sequence-logo-style plots created using an extension to weblogo.
CONCLUSIONS: dms_tools implements a statistically principled approach for the analysis and subsequent visualization of deep mutational scanning data.

experiment.title: ZMYM3 Zinc finger, MYM-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZMYM3 Zinc finger, MYM-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, MYM-type domain in ZMYM3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q14202_PF06467_405.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: ZNF81 Zinc finger C2H2-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZNF81 Zinc finger C2H2-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger C2H2-type domain in ZNF81 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P51508_PF00096_331.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.
